papers.abstract: Diffusion language models offer a promising path to efficient agents through parallel token generation. However, efficient interaction requires adapting both where computation is spent and how much text is generated. We introduce a metacognitive controller that guides diffusion generation according to the needs of the current response and the agent's interaction with the environment. It learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should extend, reducing overall computation within responses. Our controller, a lightweight plug-in for the diffusion backbone, is trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness and generation cost. This approach connects the agent's generation process to the interaction the agent serves. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate that our approach reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average compared with the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of our approach.
authors: Mingyu Zhao, Shuhang Lin, Ligong Han, Xiaojing Yu, Zhenting Wang, Yifei Pang, Yang Zhou, Dimitris N. Metaxas
bullets: Targets the challenge of reducing computation while preserving agent response quality.
Learns when to finalize tokens and how far generation should continue.
Trained on agent trajectories to balance correctness with generation cost.
Reduces inference FLOPs by 20.6% on average across five benchmarks versus the most efficient baseline, while maintaining competitive task accuracy.
Ablation studies support the controller’s effectiveness.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive token finalization and generation-length control reduce inference FLOPs for diffusion language agents, fitting efficient token-level computation.
papers.title: Metacognitive Decoding: Efficient Inference for Diffusion Language Agents
papers.tldr: A lightweight metacognitive controller makes diffusion language agents more efficient by adapting token finalization and response length to interaction needs.

papers.abstract: Current 3D scene understanding pipelines typically concatenate vast numbers of 3D object tokens with text tokens and feed the resulting sequence to a Large Language Model (LLM). However, existing 3D-LLMs for scene understanding encounter two major limitations: (i) excessive inclusion of task-irrelevant object data, introducing noise that reduces reasoning accuracy and increases hallucinations; and (ii) reliance solely on point cloud data, which inherently lacks the rich semantic information available in complementary 2D modalities, such as color, material properties, texture, and high-level contextual relationships. To address these challenges, we introduce 3D-SceneQ, a 3D LLM that unifies adaptive token pruning with multimodal semantic enrichment, markedly advancing scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding. Specifically, we propose a Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) module that adaptively selects task-relevant objects based on the intended meaning of user instructions, leveraging a learnable latent query to retain critical information while effectively suppressing irrelevant noise. In addition, we introduce a Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) module, which integrates 2D feature embeddings from pre-trained models into 3D representation to enrich object-level semantic information. Evaluations show that 3D-SceneQ outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks (e.g., +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D), demonstrating its remarkable capabilities in various 3D language reasoning tasks.
authors: Yongqi Shan, Lu Zhang, Jiazuo Yu, Yunzhi Zhuge, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Addresses noise from feeding large numbers of task-irrelevant 3D object tokens to LLMs.
Uses Query-Guided Adaptive Pruning (QGAP) to retain objects relevant to the user instruction.
Uses Multi-modal Object-level Feature Enhancement (MOFE) to integrate pretrained 2D features into 3D representations.
Outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks, including +5.7 CIDEr on Scan2Cap and +17.0 EM@1 on SQA3D.
Targets 3D scene understanding, reasoning, and grounding tasks.

papers.abstract: Pruned language models are judged almost entirely by accuracy and perplexity, which assumes that preserved output behaviour implies preserved internal computation. We test this assumption with a factorial pruning study on GPT-2, crossing two importance criteria (magnitude, random), two component types (attention heads, MLP neurons) and three sparsity levels (3%, 50%, 70%). Using the fully characterised indirect object identification (IOI) circuit as ground truth, we measure circuit integrity with activation patching, path patching and direct logit attribution. We find two qualitatively distinct failure modes. Magnitude head pruning >= zeroes the circuit: output-facing heads are removed, and the model falls to near-chance. Magnitude neuron pruning at 30% inverts it: all 26 circuit heads remain intact, but Name Mover contributions flip sign, and the model systematically prefers the wrong name (17.7% accuracy). Perplexity ranks it as less damaged than random head pruning (74.6 vs 140.1). A replication of the Greater-Than circuit shows that the critical component type depends on the circuit's architecture. These results show that output metrics and structural checks can both miss mechanistic damage, motivating circuit-level causal analysis as a complementary evaluation of compressed language models.
bullets: The study tests magnitude and random pruning of GPT-2 attention heads and MLP neurons across multiple sparsity levels.
Circuit integrity is evaluated using activation patching, path patching, and direct logit attribution, with IOI as the primary ground truth.
Magnitude head pruning can remove output-facing circuit heads and reduce performance to near chance.
Magnitude neuron pruning can leave all circuit heads intact while reversing Name Mover contributions, yielding systematically wrong predictions.
A Greater-Than circuit replication shows that pruning sensitivity depends on circuit architecture; circuit-level causal analysis is therefore needed alongside perplexity and structural checks.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates mechanistic failure modes of weight pruning in Transformers using mechanistic interpretability. This provides a deeper understanding of how pruning affects internal computation, relevant to LLMs and model efficiency.
papers.title: Mechanistic Failure Modes of Weight Pruning in Transformer Language Models
papers.tldr: Weight pruning can preserve or obscure output-level performance while severely damaging the internal circuits that produce model behavior.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has been widely adopted for aligning language models with human preferences. Recent empirical work has revealed that DPO induces remarkably sparse parameter updates, yet no theoretical explanation for this phenomenon has been offered. We analyze DPO's optimization dynamics under a neural tangent kernel linearization and show that the logistic structure of the DPO loss gives rise to an implicit maximum-margin bias. Building on this observation, we introduce the concept of dual sparsity: the DPO update direction is a sparse linear combination (data-level sparsity, driven by support vectors) of sparse gradient feature vectors (parameter-level sparsity, arising from gradient cancellation between preferred and dispreferred responses). We formalize this structure in our main theorem, bound the number of support pairs by a margin-dependent spectral quantity, and present a framework relating dual sparsity to weight disentanglement---a condition favorable for model merging. Experiments on GPT-2 Small and Medium and on 7--9B instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) with the Anthropic HH-RLHF and UltraFeedback datasets confirm both sources of sparsity, and experiments on GPT-2 show that DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to $35{\times}$ compared to supervised fine-tuning.
bullets: DPO’s logistic loss creates an implicit maximum-margin optimization bias.
Its update is sparse at two levels: support-vector-like data sparsity and gradient-cancellation-driven parameter sparsity.
A theorem bounds the number of support pairs using a margin-dependent spectral quantity.
The framework connects dual sparsity with weight disentanglement, a property useful for model merging.
Experiments across GPT-2 and several 7–9B instruction-tuned models confirm both sparsity mechanisms; on GPT-2, DPO reduces cross-task interference by up to 35× versus supervised fine-tuning.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) updates, providing a theoretical explanation for weight disentanglement. This connects alignment (LLMs) with efficiency (sparsity) and model merging.
papers.title: On the Sparsity of Direct Preference Optimization: Weight Disentanglement in the NTK Regime
papers.tldr: DPO’s sparse parameter updates are theoretically explained by dual sparsity in the NTK regime, which also promotes weight disentanglement and reduces cross-task interference.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multimodal capabilities but suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to the massive number of visual tokens. While token pruning is a promising solution, existing methods still suffer from two major drawbacks: 1) unreliable pruning criteria that fail to accurately localize task-specific regions due to inherent attention biases or query-agnostic designs, and 2) suboptimal pruning strategies that employ rigid, non-adaptive schedules, overlooking the dynamic evolution of token redundancy across different model depths. To address these challenges, we propose LearnPrunerV2, which extends the previous two-stage heuristic framework (LearnPruner) into a fully learnable architecture. Specifically, we integrate lightweight learnable modules into every layer of the VLM backbone, which estimate token importance by fusing intrinsic visual saliency with extrinsic query relevance captured via a shadow token. By uncovering a consistent staircase redundancy pattern across VLM layers, we further introduce Budget-Deterministic Pruning (BDP) to establish a hardware-friendly schedule with fixed per-layer budgets. Extensive experimental results across various benchmarks and VLMs demonstrate that LearnPrunerV2 consistently outperform previous state-of-the-art methods. Notably, LearnPrunerV2 preserves 99.8% of the original performance when pruning 77.8% of visual tokens on LLaVA-v1.5, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
authors: Rinyoichi Takezoe, Yaqian Li, Weiren Wang, Zihao Bo, Huihong Shi, Anzhou Hou, Mo Guang, Jiale Yan, Kaiwen Long
bullets: Targets excessive computation from the large number of visual tokens in VLMs.
Uses lightweight per-layer modules to estimate token importance from visual saliency and query relevance via a shadow token.
Introduces Budget-Deterministic Pruning, a fixed per-layer schedule guided by the observed staircase pattern of token redundancy.
Across benchmarks and VLMs, it reportedly outperforms prior state-of-the-art pruning methods.
On LLaVA-v1.5, it retains 99.8% of original performance while pruning 77.8% of visual tokens.

papers.title: LearnPrunerV2: Learnable Progressive Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models

papers.abstract: Diffusion vision-language models (DVLMs) process their entire input at every denoising step. Since visual tokens make up 89-97% of this input on the benchmarks we study, most of the decoding computation is spent repeatedly processing the same image. Visual token pruning methods partially relieve this burden by removing part of the visual tokens, but they lose the removed information and still process the remaining image at every step. To measure how often the image is actually needed, we compare LLaDA-V's predictions with and without the image at every decoding step and find that removing the image changes a token being unmasked at only 22.8% of steps on average and at as few as 7.9%. We therefore propose LOWN, a decoding method that decides at every step whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask. LOWN predicts the masked tokens without the image and processes the image only when this prediction disagrees with the last image-conditioned prediction. Agreement certifies the earlier prediction for reuse, and the number of certified tokens sets how many are unmasked in that step. We further observe that the need for the image differs across benchmarks, so LOWN's adaptive decision is needed rather than a fixed schedule. Without training or a tuned threshold, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V's score on ten benchmarks at 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average. LOWN also generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, composes orthogonally with visual token pruning, and runs under key-value caching for further efficiency gains. Code and project page are available at https://hyeon9698.github.io/LOWN/
authors: Donghyeon Cho, Joowon Kim, Seungho Shin, Eunho Yang
bullets: DVLMs repeatedly process mostly redundant visual tokens at every denoising step.
The method compares image-free and image-conditioned predictions to certify when prior predictions can be reused.
It adaptively decides both whether to process the image and how many tokens to unmask, without training or a tuned threshold.
Across ten benchmarks, LOWN retains 99.6% of LLaDA-V’s score while using 35.3% of the decoding FLOPs on average.
It generalizes across LLaDA-based DVLMs, combines with visual token pruning, and supports key-value caching.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.
authors: Yuqi Li, Chuanyue Yan, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Xiaoqin Feng, Junming Liu, Xi Xiao, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen, Yingli Tian
bullets: Video VLMs face high computation, latency, and memory costs on long visual sequences.
Methods are categorized by intervention stage: input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding.
Post-training quantization is treated as a cross-stage approach with different calibration requirements.
The survey examines how intervention location affects preservation of task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence.
Prior results and shared-setting experiments assess accuracy–latency trade-offs and highlight that local gains may not yield end-to-end speedups.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible generation through iterative masked denoising, but incur substantial inference cost because token representations are repeatedly recomputed across denoising steps. Existing cache-based methods reduce this cost by reusing intermediate results across denoising steps and recomputing only a subset of positions at each step, chosen either on a fixed schedule or by heuristic signals of change. Our trajectory experiments instead point to decoding trajectory as the more relevant quantity. Cached generation remains accurate when it stays close to the full-denoising trajectory, with errors concentrated around unmask-order deviations and reduced as longer reference prefixes are recovered. This suggests a more direct principle: limiting representation error helps, but keeping generation on the full-denoising trajectory is a more direct route to accurate decoding. We therefore formulate efficient dLLM inference as trajectory-guided querying. Rather than broadly repairing representation error, we use full-denoising trajectories to supervise which unresolved positions should receive limited fresh computation. Based on this formulation, we introduce TRACEQUERY, a lightweight sparse decoding framework that predicts a small set of near-future trajectory-relevant positions, queries only those candidates, and lets the backbone select which one to commit from their fresh predictions. TRACEQUERY delivers the strongest quality-computation trade-off among cache-based approaches, sustaining high accuracy with substantially fewer fresh token computations, and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and families. Code: https://github.com/fish1928/tracequery.git
bullets: dLLMs are expensive because token representations are repeatedly recomputed during iterative denoising.
The authors find that decoding accuracy depends more directly on staying close to the full-denoising trajectory than merely limiting representation error.
TRACEQUERY predicts a small set of future trajectory-relevant positions, computes fresh predictions only for them, and lets the backbone choose which position to commit.
It achieves the strongest quality–computation trade-off among cache-based methods and generalizes across tasks, model variants, and model families.
The approach relies on full-denoising trajectories as supervision for efficient sparse querying.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Two-stage ablation of TRACEQUERY. (b) Stage II fixes the selected configuration and evaluates alternative feature groups under closed-loop cached decoding. Figure 2: Overview of TRACEQUERY. Full denoising first provides an offline reference trajectory describing the future order of decoding decisions. The router is trained to recover the near-future portion of this trajectory from inexpensive signals available during decoding. At inference time, after step t commits At, the router ranks the remaining unresolved positions and selects a small query set Qt+1. Only these positions receive fresh computation, while other positions reuse cached representations. The backbone dLLM then makes the final commitment from the freshly queried candidates. Periodic broad recomputation is retained to control accumulated approximation error.

papers.abstract: Attention over tens of thousands of visual tokens dominates the inference of video diffusion transformers (DiTs). Existing methods reduce this cost through sparsity, low precision, or both, but use a single precision for all kept tiles. We observe that the output error introduced by approximation varies widely across tiles. Many tiles can be skipped with little error, others must be computed but gain little beyond low precision, and a few retain substantial error even at low precision. We present Triage, a training-free attention method that assigns each tile one of three approximation tiers: skipping it by replacing it with its block means, skimming it in NVFP4, or refining it with NVFP4 residual correction. A lightweight router predicts each tile's error under each tier from block statistics and moves a tile to a more accurate tier only when the predicted error reduction justifies the extra compute, with a single price setting this trade-off. A fused kernel executes all three tiers in a single pass on the FP4 tensor cores of RTX Blackwell GPUs. Across Wan2.2, HunyuanVideo, and LTX-2.5, Triage accelerates end-to-end generation by up to 2.32x over dense FlashAttention, and in each of five settings it runs faster than every baseline while reaching 0.3-3.0 dB higher PSNR than the highest-PSNR baseline.
authors: Yeonjae Kim, Omin Kwon, Seong Hoon Seo, Jae W. Lee
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over tens of thousands of video tokens.
Assigns each tile to skip, NVFP4 skim, or NVFP4 residual refinement.
A lightweight router uses block statistics and one price parameter to balance error against compute.
A fused kernel executes all tiers in one pass on RTX Blackwell FP4 tensor cores.
Across three video diffusion models and five settings, it achieves up to 2.32× end-to-end speedup and 0.3–3.0 dB higher PSNR than the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Deploying large vision-language models (LVLMs) on resource-constrained embodied agents for 3D visual question answering necessitates cloud-edge collaboration. However, offloading massive visual data to the cloud over bandwidth-limited and noisy channels introduces severe latency and transmission distortion. To address this, we propose TP-JSCC, an efficient token pruning and joint source-channel coding method for LVLMs-based 3D-VQA in Cloud-Edge Collaboration. First, we develop a Local and Global Semantics-based Hybrid Token Pruning (LGS-HTP) module to significantly reduce the visual token count. By decoupling foreground-background tokens and jointly selecting local and global semantics, LGS-HTP effectively reduces redundancy while preserving reasoning-critical tokens. Second, we introduce a lightweight Token Joint Source-Channel Coding (T-JSCC) module to further compress the pruned tokens and ensure their robust transmission over error-prone channels. By employing lightweight cascaded linear layers and Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)-adaptive mechanism, this module adapts to fluctuating channel conditions while maintaining minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments on ScanQA and SQA3D datasets indicate the exceptional efficiency and robustness of our approach. Specifically, on ScanQA validation set, the LGS-HTP module could achieve 90% pruning ratio while incurring less than a 1% CIDEr loss. Building on this, the T-JSCC further compresses the tokens by 18 times, resulting in an overall 180 times data volume reduction for robust transmission, while saving 90% in computational complexity for LVLM deployment. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuanhui0325/TP-JSCC.
authors: Zhengxin Li, Chongzhen Tian, Hui Yuan, Hao Liu, Sam Kwong
bullets: Targets latency and distortion caused by offloading large 3D visual inputs from resource-constrained agents.
LGS-HTP jointly selects local and global semantic tokens while separating foreground and background information.
T-JSCC applies lightweight compression with SNR adaptation to handle changing channel conditions.
On ScanQA validation, it prunes 90% of tokens with less than 1% CIDEr loss and achieves 18× further compression.
The combined approach reduces transmitted data volume by 180× and deployment computational complexity by 90%, as reported on ScanQA and SQA3D.

papers.abstract: Recent generic reference-based image generation models natively support multiple conditions by concatenating all reference image and text tokens into a joint sequence processed by a single Diffusion Transformer (DiT). However, this versatile paradigm comes at an efficiency cost: accommodating multiple references leads to a token explosion, incurring massive $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ computational complexity. Most acceleration methods operate inside the DiT, showing limited capability in reducing spatial redundancy and failing to alleviate peak VRAM. While some pre-model token reduction alternatives exist, they inevitably introduce external models. This raises a question: Is it possible to achieve acceleration and memory savings while preserving compatibility with in-model techniques and requiring no additional parameters? In this work, we realize this goal by proposing the early Token reduction via Downsampled self-Probing (ToDoPro). By executing a few denoising steps on spatially $2\times$ downsampled reference images, this cheap probing stage utilizes the DiT model itself to effectively and efficiently extract reference token importance. Using the probed importance, we apply a hierarchical reduction before the main denoising stage: we completely discard low-importance tokens, substitute mid-importance tokens with their downsampled counterparts to cheaply preserve global context, and keep high-importance tokens. Experiments across three base models and two benchmarks demonstrate that our early reduction accelerates inference significantly and mitigates peak GPU memory. Furthermore, we can improve generation quality by safely filtering out noisy, uninformative reference tokens, enabling the model to concentrate its limited attention capacity on genuinely useful tokens. The code will be released at https://github.com/scy639/ToDoPro
authors: Caiyi Sun, Yujing Sun, Siu-Ming Yiu
bullets: Addresses token explosion and quadratic compute from combining multiple image and text references.
Runs a few denoising steps on 2× downsampled references to estimate token importance without adding external models or parameters.
Hierarchically discards low-importance tokens, downsamples mid-importance tokens, and preserves high-importance tokens before full denoising.
Experiments on three base models and two benchmarks show significant inference acceleration and reduced peak GPU memory.
Filtering noisy, uninformative tokens can improve quality by focusing attention on useful references.

The compressed reference images then enter the main denoising stage, slashing end-to-end latency and activation VRAM while remaining compatible with in-model methods in (a).

papers.tldr: ToDoPro uses the DiT itself to identify and reduce redundant reference tokens early, accelerating reference-based image generation while lowering peak memory and potentially improving quality.

papers.abstract: Multi-modal video fusion aims to generate temporally coherent videos with salient targets and rich structural details by integrating complementary information from heterogeneous sensors. However, existing video fusion methods commonly rely on optical flow estimation and feature warping for inter-frame alignment and cross-frame information aggregation to maintain temporal consistency, thereby introducing considerable computational overhead and making the fusion performance vulnerable to flow estimation errors. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an efficient multi-modal video fusion network with dynamic region-guided temporal interaction. Specifically, the proposed spatio-temporal interaction module leverages the Test-Time Training paradigm to model temporal dependencies with linear complexity. Building on this design, the module restricts temporal modeling to key dynamic regions in the video sequence, as static background regions provide limited temporal cues. By excluding low-variation tokens from unnecessary temporal interaction, this selective strategy contributes to improved fusion quality and temporal consistency. In addition, leveraging the strong ability of pretrained MAE features to capture global structural dependencies, we introduce a feature-level temporal consistency constraint to suppress local flickering by aligning the inter-frame variation directions of the fused and source videos. We further propose a new MAE-based temporal metric that quantifies directional distance between their temporal variations within dynamic regions. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with existing state-of-the-art methods, our method achieves superior fusion quality and temporal consistency on multiple benchmark datasets, while exhibiting high computational efficiency under edge-device deployment settings.

Reports superior fusion quality and temporal consistency with high efficiency on edge-device settings across multiple benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Visual-token compression is usually evaluated by clean accuracy and efficiency, but these averages do not reveal failures that compression introduces under an image shift where the uncompressed model stays correct. We introduce VTC-AUDIT, which estimates this incremental risk only on pairs where the full model is correct on both images and the compressed model is correct on the clean image. The four arms then cross two binary choices: which image selects the retained token positions, and which image supplies the visual features. We audit three open 8-9B vision-language models on four tasks and eight pre-specified shifts. We evaluate two training-free compressors---hard-pruning DivPrune and prune-and-merge ApET---at a matched 25% retained-position budget, producing 708,000 inference records. Reselecting positions on the shifted image, rather than reusing the clean-image positions, raises the failure rate in all six model-compressor settings. The increase is 3.04-9.60 percentage points for DivPrune and 2.05-4.20 percentage points for ApET, with every 95% interval above zero. Repeating the audit on a separately resampled second manifest reproduces all six increases. In a pooled monitor audit across the four benchmarks, support Jaccard instability fails the practical AUROC criterion of 0.65 in all six settings, whereas clean compressed-model uncertainty clears it. Thus, support turnover is a weak ranking signal under the audited benchmark mixture, while clean compressed-model uncertainty is substantially more informative. These results suggest that future visual-token compression evaluations should report conditional reliability alongside clean accuracy and efficiency.
bullets: Measures incremental risk only when the full model remains correct under both clean and shifted images and the compressed model is correct on the clean image.
Crosses whether retained token positions and visual features come from the clean or shifted image, auditing hard-pruning and prune-and-merge compressors at a matched 25% budget.
Across three vision-language models, four tasks, and eight shifts, selecting positions from the shifted image increases failure rates in all six model–compressor settings.
The increases are reproduced on an independently resampled manifest, supporting the robustness of the finding.
Support Jaccard instability is a weak ranking signal, while clean compressed-model uncertainty is more informative in the pooled audit.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
authors: Sooyoung Kwon, Carlee Joe-Wong, Kyunghan Lee
bullets: Targets onboard VLA inference, where processing hundreds of visual tokens causes high prefill latency.
Finds that reuse is effective for low-drift tokens, while pruning is preferable for high-drift tokens.
Uses a calibrated drift threshold and cache age to classify tokens as reusable, invalid-and-recompute, or prune.
A fixed recomputation budget directly controls latency.

On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, remains within 3 percentage points of full recomputation while reducing Jetson AGX Orin prefill latency by up to 48%; with 7% of tokens recomputed, it exceeds the strongest LIBERO-Object baseline by 24.4 points.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models are costly to serve because they are large and because they generate long chains of thought (CoT). Weight pruning and CoT compression address these two costs separately, but they interfere in that pruning adds redundant reasoning on problems the model still solves and incomplete reasoning on those it no longer solves, and on harder problems makes the model less compressible by subsequent length-preference optimization. We trace this to a blind spot on each side: pruning criteria do not distinguish necessary from redundant reasoning, and preference-based CoT compression receives no training signal on problems a pruned model always or never solves. We propose Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD), which identifies neurons enriched in redundant reasoning by contrasting their activations on long and short correct solutions of the same problem and prunes them preferentially, and we extend preference pairs to the problems a pruned model always or never solves. Pruning 20\% of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the combination uses 8--22\% fewer thinking tokens on four math benchmarks than pruning with reasoning-aware calibration (RAC) followed by the same compression, with accuracy within 0.5 points.
authors: Tao Jing, Chen Kang, Feifei Zhai, Pengyuan Liu, Dong Yu
bullets: Pruning and chain-of-thought compression can interfere: pruning may induce redundant or incomplete reasoning and reduce later compressibility.
The method, Contrastive Set-Difference (CSD), contrasts neuron activations between long and short correct solutions to identify neurons associated with redundant reasoning.
It also adds preference-training pairs from problems a pruned model always solves or always fails to solve.
With 20% pruning of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the combined approach used 8–22% fewer thinking tokens across four math benchmarks than RAC followed by the same compression.
Accuracy remained within 0.5 percentage points of the comparison pipeline.

papers.abstract: Instruction-based image editors built on diffusion transformers run tens of denoising steps. Training-free acceleration either reuses features across steps (step caching) or stops computing the regions an edit leaves untouched (region freezing), and the two have been combined before. We ask how a high speed-up target should be split between them. On Qwen-Image-2.1, freezing does more than remove tokens: it lowers the cost of every step, so the step cache can reach the same overall speed-up with a conservative threshold that keeps its error small. A per-step cost model fitted on development runs predicts held-out latency with a median error of 4.0% and reproduces the speed ceilings of the region methods we re-implemented (2.73$\times$ predicted vs. 2.70$\times$ measured for RegionE). Driving frozen tokens to the model's one-step $x_0$ estimate beats returning them to the reference image on every development sample, and in 90% of measured cases the composed error stays below the sum of the two individual errors. The resulting method, FreezePlan, keeps five full steps and gives the rest of the budget to TaylorSeer. On a pre-registered test split it runs 5.05$\times$ faster end to end at 29.8 dB PSNR to the original output, with no significant drop in a VLM judge score; TaylorSeer at 5.02$\times$ reaches 23.5 dB. The curve extends to 5.99$\times$ at 28.0 dB. Swapping in the region selectors of prior methods under our schedule lowers median PSNR by only 0.5--0.6 dB, which places the gain in the schedule and budget split rather than in the selector.
bullets: Region freezing reduces the cost of every denoising step, allowing step caching to operate in a lower-error regime.
A fitted per-step cost model predicts held-out latency with 4.0% median error and accurately estimates method speed ceilings.
Using the model’s one-step x₀ estimate for frozen tokens outperforms restoring the reference image across development samples.
FreezePlan keeps five full steps and allocates the remaining computation budget to TaylorSeer.
On a preregistered test split, it achieves 5.05× end-to-end speedup at 29.8 dB PSNR with no significant VLM-judge score drop; it reaches 5.99× at 28.0 dB.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding significantly accelerates autoregressive text generation in Large Language Models (LLMs), but its efficacy depends largely on two key factors: the distributional alignment between the draft and the target model, and the draft model's latency during inference. However, existing approaches typically utilize independently pretrained small draft models or seek to prune the target model to a manually chosen architecture, thereby failing to explicitly balance the trade-off between draft model alignment and token generation efficiency. To address this gap, we formulate draft model design as an optimization problem and propose T2D, a framework that constructs draft models directly from the target model using latency-aware structured pruning and knowledge distillation. In this manner, T2D obtains draft models that are jointly optimized for both measured inference latency and cross-entropy loss on the target model's responses, resulting in superlative speculative decoding performance. Through extensive experiments on multi-domain speculative decoding benchmarks and across several target model families of differing scale, we demonstrate how T2D prunes up to 92\% of the target model to obtain highly performant draft models compared to competitive baselines. Moreover, draft models obtained via T2D can also be utilized by other speculative decoding token-alignment and knowledge distillation methods in a plug-and-play fashion, leading to further gains. Our findings underscore the importance of jointly navigating the draft model architecture-alignment frontier to unlock the full potential of speculative decoding for LLMs.
authors: Shahriar Kabir Nahin, Xiao Ye, Muhao Chen, Ben Zhou, Anshuman Chhabra
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between draft-model inference latency and distributional alignment with the target model.
Uses latency-aware structured pruning plus knowledge distillation to formulate draft-model design as an optimization problem.
Prunes up to 92% of the target model while maintaining strong speculative decoding performance across multiple domains and target-model scales.
The resulting draft models can plug into other token-alignment and distillation methods for additional gains.
Scope: effectiveness depends on measured latency and cross-entropy alignment with the target model’s responses.

papers.abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-centric tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic objects across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-centric representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at https://github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.
authors: Nhi Pham, Christopher Wewer, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer, Jan Eric Lenssen
bullets: Addresses the instability of patch-based and holistic tokens whose identities are tied to fixed image locations.
Learns tokens that track the same objects across motion, deformation, and partial occlusion.
Produces compact continuous latent representations for downstream flow-based video generation.
Matches class-conditional FVD on UCF-101 with 8× fewer latent tokens and lower latency.
Outperforms 1D tokenization baselines on Kinetics-600 frame prediction at low token budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method Overview. TrackTok encodes an input video V into a 1D set of object-centric, semantically persistent, latent tokens Z . Its encoder E is composed of semantic feature extraction with V-JEPA 2.1 [16], the construction of input-dependent queries Q using centroids of k-Means clusters C, and a ViT performing attention based on semantic similarity instead of spatial position. The decoder D reconstructs the three-dimensional RGB video from the 1D latent set Z .

For each sample, we apply PCA on token features and map the top three components to RGB as color for the corresponding token impact mask. The visualization highlights the semantic object alignment and temporal tracking of tokens learned by TrackTok in contrast to AdapTok’s or LARP’s tokens, which are dominated by high-frequency textures and edges. Both baselines also show degraded reconstruction quality at 128 tokens. Furthermore, leveraging only V-JEPA 2.1 without our cluster queries (CQ) still results in tokens encoding fixed regions of the video. Refer to Appendix E for more uncurated examples.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning substantially reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet existing methods are mostly training-free and plug-and-play. They treat the resulting performance drop as an inevitable cost of compression and pursue increasingly complex pruning rules. We rethink this view through two questions: how much of the loss can post-training rescue, and, building on this recovery, how can joint compression push pruning to its limit? We curate a 282K-sample post-training mixture covering general VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding, and post-train 36 configurations that drop or merge tokens under a unified protocol. Post-training rescues most of the loss, even for OCR and grounding, and its adaptation gain in closing the gap between the pruned and the dense model grows as the budget tightens. For joint compression, we find that the vision encoder, not the LLM, dominates prefill time in native-resolution MLLMs, so where tokens are removed matters more than how many: keeping 40% of tokens at the encoder runs faster than keeping 10% at the projector. Our best configuration prunes the encoder lightly and the projector aggressively, leaves the LLM intact, and keeps general understanding and reasoning at the dense level. It accelerates the LLM stage by 3.49x but the end-to-end time-to-first-token by only 1.54x, showing that LLM-stage speedups overstate end-to-end gains. We hope these findings offer insights for future research on joint visual token compression. Our data, protocol, and code will be released.
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Post-training largely restores pruning-induced performance loss, including on OCR and grounding tasks.
A 282K-sample mixture spanning VQA, reasoning, OCR, and grounding supports a unified evaluation of 36 compression configurations.
In native-resolution MLLMs, the vision encoder dominates prefill time, making encoder-side pruning more impactful than projector-side pruning.
The best setup lightly prunes the encoder, aggressively prunes the projector, and keeps the LLM unchanged while preserving general understanding and reasoning at dense-model levels.
A 3.49× LLM-stage speedup translates to only a 1.54× end-to-end time-to-first-token improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Rethinks visual token pruning in MLLMs, introducing post-training recovery and joint compression strategies, fitting Efficient AI and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: Rescuing Your Pruning: Rethinking Visual Token Pruning and Post-Training Recovery in MLLMs
papers.tldr: Post-training can recover most of the accuracy lost to visual token pruning, while pruning location—not just token count—is critical for end-to-end MLLM speed.

papers.abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs), which process both visual inputs and text queries, incur high inference costs due to the large number of visual tokens, making visual token pruning a natural approach for improving efficiency. Recent work has leveraged query information to guide token selection, often through heuristics derived from attention patterns or token dynamics. However, these approaches do not explicitly exploit the underlying structure of query-vision interactions. We address this gap by observing that the query-vision interaction matrix, naturally induced by the query and key projections already present in transformer attention, is effectively low-rank, with a small number of dominant latent interaction modes capturing query-relevant semantics. Motivated by this observation, we propose Query-Vision Decomposition (QViD), a novel training-free query-aware visual token pruning method that exploits this structure. Extensive experiments on both image and video understanding benchmarks show that QViD consistently improves performance under matched token budgets, with the largest gains appearing under aggressive compression regimes.
authors: Harshithanjani Athi, Sravan Kumar Ankireddy, Jianzhong Charlie Zhang, Hyeji Kim
bullets: Visual token counts make large VLM inference computationally expensive.
Existing query-aware pruning methods often rely on attention heuristics without modeling query–vision interaction structure explicitly.
QViD decomposes the query–vision interaction matrix into dominant latent modes that capture query-relevant semantics.
Experiments on image and video understanding benchmarks show consistent gains at matched token budgets, especially with aggressive compression.

figures.caption: Figure 2: QViD Pipeline. QViD performs query-aware visual-token pruning by explicitly modeling query–vision interactions. At pruning layer ℓ, it forms the interaction matrix M = QtxtK ⊤ vis, extracts its dominant low-rank modes with SVD, and scores each visual token by its participation in these modes. The top-K tokens are retained for subsequent reasoning, preserving query-relevant visual evidence while reducing sequence length. papers.abstract: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%. Project page and code: https://lems-svd.github.io
authors: Moritz Thoma, Maximilian Groezinger, Maximilian Forstenh\"ausler, Emad Aghajanzadeh, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Christos Anagnostopoulos, Pierpaolo Mori, Nael Fasfous, Alexander Frickenstein, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann

LEMS models layer-wise local/global importance and error propagation, then allocates ranks using an ILP.
KFAC-SVD uses token-wise statistics to mitigate rank deficiency during decomposition.
Evaluated on Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 families, with gains extending to models up to 70B parameters.
Reports up to 4.8 percentage-point zero-shot accuracy gains from LEMS and a 15% average perplexity improvement from KFAC-SVD.

papers.abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) offer strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities, but their high pretraining cost raises a practical sustainability question: does this upfront investment pay off over a full deployment lifecycle, compared to supervised standalone models that must be periodically retrained? We model the cumulative carbon cost of different approaches across a realistic industrial scenario: Chronos-2 amortizes its pretraining cost within months for large or frequently queried deployments, but a classical model remains cheaper indefinitely for small or rarely queried ones. For cases where reducing the TSFM's own cost matters, we show that removing a single encoder block (7.9% of parameters) via a gradient-free pruning criterion yields a consistent 6 to 9% reduction in FLOPs, CO2 emissions, and latency, at essentially no cost to zero-shot forecasting performance across a 25-task benchmark.
authors: C\'ecile Luc, Nathana\"el Lemonnier, Ievgen Redko
bullets: Frames TSFM sustainability as a lifecycle comparison between upfront pretraining and recurring retraining.
Chronos-2 amortizes its pretraining carbon cost within months for large or frequently queried deployments.
Classical standalone models remain cheaper indefinitely for small or rarely queried deployments.
Removing one encoder block (7.9% of parameters) cuts FLOPs, emissions, and latency by 6–9%.
Pruning preserves essentially unchanged zero-shot forecasting performance across 25 tasks.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token efficiency through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI iteratively refines companion harness configurations from training feedback, with validation selecting the configuration for deployment. A controller at the model-tool boundary reuses resolved decisions to replace later reasoning callbacks while actor weights remain fixed. Executable Decision Graphs store exact actions, literal arguments, causal dependencies, and public guards. Guarded Decision Reuse activates these persistent decisions from observed receipts; Certified Callback Substitution executes them through the native interface and records removal of the registered slow callback. New semantic decisions, unsupported evidence, and selector abstention invoke the original actor again. The representation restricts what feedback may change, while complete-task measurements establish quality and cost. On HumanEval, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82\% while reducing Tokens/task (k) from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54\% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success rises from 71.43\% to 85.71\% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93\% saving). A separate MBPP ablation measures 26.91\% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52\% lower cost than retained callbacks. These results establish guarded decision reuse as a practical way to reduce repeated reasoning in existing harnesses.
authors: Yuhua Jiang, Chang Xu, Feifei Gao, Li Zhao
bullets: Targets harnesses that unnecessarily re-invoke reasoning after tool feedback has already determined the next action.
Uses recursive self-improvement to refine harness configurations, with validation selecting the deployment configuration while keeping actor weights fixed.
Stores exact actions and dependencies in Executable Decision Graphs; guarded reuse and certified callback substitution replace eligible reasoning callbacks.
On HumanEval, preserves 90.82% success while reducing tokens per task by 29.54%; on DeepSeek Harness, raises success to 85.71% and cuts tokens by 87.93%.
MBPP ablations report lower cost than single-use graphs and retained callbacks, though reuse is bypassed for novel decisions, unsupported evidence, or selector abstention.

figures.caption: Figure 1: HarnessMM overview. papers.selection_reason: Introduces a method for improving token efficiency in LLM agent harnesses through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement, directly addressing token management and efficiency.
papers.title: HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency
papers.tldr: HarnessMM reduces repeated agent reasoning by safely reusing previously resolved tool decisions while preserving or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Split inference partitions a Vision Transformer between a resource-constrained edge device and a server. However, transmitting intermediate tokens across the communication channel is costly. Deploying fine-tuned backbones to every endpoint becomes expensive as well. We study token reduction for split inference under a frozen backbone, where only a small adapter is shipped. We observe that the CLS token plays a dual role: it acts as the global summary the receiver needs for classification, and it serves as a signal on which patches to keep. We propose Consomm\'e, a method utilizing both characteristics. There, an information bottleneck compresses the CLS token into a compact latent which is transmitted in place of the full CLS token and conditions a learned patch gate merging patches into exactly $k$ tokens via soft assignment. It reaches any budget in a single step, thus escaping the per-layer cap of bipartite matching (BPM). On DeiT-S/T, it leads all methods at aggressive token budgets and remains operable at shallow splits where BPM cannot operate, while matching fine-tuned methods at gentle budgets at a fraction of their deployment cost.
bullets: Targets split inference with a frozen backbone, avoiding deployment of separately fine-tuned backbones.
Uses an information bottleneck to transmit a compact CLS representation instead of the full CLS token.
Conditions a learned patch gate on this representation to softly merge patches into any desired token budget in one step.
On DeiT-S/T, performs best at aggressive budgets, works at shallow splits where BPM cannot, and matches fine-tuned methods at gentler budgets with lower deployment cost.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of Consommé. By leveraging the CLS token’s information via an IB, it serves as a selection mechanism for the soft-assignment merging gate in order to reduce the number of tokens to be transmitted.

Figure 3. We evaluate the classification accuracy on DeiT-S and DeiT-T for a token budget of k = 64 and k = 8, while varying the split layer. Consommé exhibits much better accuracy retention at shallow splits.

Figure 2. Consommé’s visualizations of different token budgets performed on DeiT-S on different split layers s ∈ {3, 6, 9} on samples from the ImageNet-1K validation set. The later the token reduction is performed, the more the tokens focus on the actual content and not on the background, thus identifying the more informative tokens which also aligns with the human-visual distinctive features. The biggest group which is non-colored corresponds semantically to a background group.

Table 7. Split 6 results of different token reduction methods on DeiT-S, DeiT-T, and ViT-B. ∗ indicates that the exact token count was not reached by the method. On all models, methods from all three tiers suffer from heavy performance degradation, with some even reaching single-digit top-1 accuracy. Consommé achieves superior results when reducing the token budget.

Table 8. Results on split layer 3. ◦ marks that the model did not converge. - shows that the token count was not reached by the method. Consommé satisfies all token budgets k on split layer s = 3, whereas all BPM methods, as well as some training-based methods, fail.

We report the performance of the tier-3 methods only on DeiT-S as a cost-agnostic reference point given their substantially higher deployment cost for SI settings and thus omit them for DeiT-T. papers.selection_reason: Proposes conditioned token merging for split inference, a clear token-level efficiency contribution.
papers.title: Consomm\'e: Conditioned Token Merging for Split Inference
papers.tldr: Consommé reduces communication in split-inference Vision Transformers by compressing the CLS token and conditionally merging patches into exactly k tokens using only a small adapter.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of video data has created an urgent need for efficient video understanding systems that can handle long and continuous visual inputs, posing significant challenges for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to severe memory bottlenecks. Moreover, existing compression methods often overlook the explosive accumulation of approximation errors. To address this issue, we propose Video-MemComp, a training-free and sensitivity-aware context management framework for memory-constrained streaming video understanding. Our method theoretically decomposes compression error into orthogonal local approximation error and layer-wise structural sensitivity via a first-order Taylor expansion. To minimize local approximation error, we perform token aggregation in a pre-RoPE safe zone with an attention-conserving logit bias, mitigating geometric distortions caused by RoPE rotations. To manage layer-wise structural sensitivity, we dynamically allocate the KV cache budget based on offline gradient priors and online context entropy, prioritizing high-sensitivity layers. Video-MemComp outperforms or achieves performance comparable to full-cache and state-of-the-art compression methods on benchmarks including MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema. Notably, it improves the overall accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-3B from 62.3% to 64.1% while reducing the KV cache to an equivalent of 6,000 tokens per layer, saving over 90% of KV memory.
authors: Yonghui Niu, Yuhao Ji, Chang Nie, Jiao Zhang, Yilong Li, Junlan Feng, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Chaoyou Fu
bullets: Targets memory bottlenecks and error accumulation in long-context streaming video understanding.
Uses a first-order Taylor expansion to separate local approximation error from layer-wise structural sensitivity.
Aggregates tokens in a pre-RoPE safe zone with attention-conserving logit bias to reduce geometric distortion.
Dynamically allocates KV-cache budgets using offline gradient priors and online context entropy.
Matches or exceeds full-cache and existing compression methods on MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema; Qwen2.5-VL-3B rises from 62.3% to 64.1% with over 90% KV-memory savings.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of our Video-MemComp Framework. Guided by Taylor expansion (top), we split global memory compression into two objectives. 1) Minimizing Local Approximation Error El (middle): Pre-RoPE Aggregation merges redundant tokens based on inter-frame filtering and intra-frame merging. Intra-layer KV Pruning selects key-value pairs using a dialogue-aware Proxy Query Qproxy. 2) Managing Structural Sensitivity Sl (bottom): A Tri-Hybrid Budget Allocation dynamically assigns the total memory budget Btotal using offline structural sensitivity, online information density, and uniform regularization to protect critical layers from aggressive pruning.

Figure 1 Our architecture. While standard Video-LLM models suffer from linear O(T ) memory growth, VideoMemComp maintains strictly O(1) memory via a Taylor-expansion-guided hybrid strategy, enabling efficient streaming video understanding. Specifically, we decompose the error via Taylor expansion into local approximation error El and layer-wise structural sensitivity Sl. To minimize El, we adopt Attention-Preserved Pre-RoPE Aggregation and Intralayer Sparsity-based KV pruning. Meanwhile, Sl is used to guide layer-wise budget allocation.

Figure 2 Performance on MLVU with Qwen2-VL-7B. Our method outperforms strong baselines across all memory budgets, and even surpasses the Full KV baseline at 6K, 12K, and 24K KV budgets, showing that Video-MemComp removes redundancy while preserving key semantics. See Section E.1 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 5 Accuracy-Memory trade-offs on Qwen2.5-VL-3B (VideoMME Long Video). Token Compression (Blue) excels in high-budget regimes, notably surpassing the dense baseline by mitigating attention dilution. Conversely, KV Compression (Orange) demonstrates robustness under strict memory constraints. Our Hybrid Method (Green) achieves the optimal Pareto frontier across all budgets, balancing redundancy removal with attention preservation. See E.4 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 6 Hyperparameter landscape of budget allocation. OVO-Bench accuracy is shown as a contour over uniform prior (λu) and structural sensitivity (λs); λe = 1 − λu − λs represents the dynamic entropy weight. The global optimum(star), revealing that a dominant structural prior combined with subtle dynamic adjustment yields superior performance compared to uniform allocation. See F.3 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 7 Joint Impact of Spatio-Temporal Compression Thresholds. The heatmap plots accuracy across varying Inter-frame (θinter) and Intra-frame (θintra) similarity thresholds. The landscape reveals a convex optimization zone, where the peak represents the optimal trade-off between aggressive redundancy filtering and semantic preservation. Notably, overly aggressive temporal pruning (low θinter) causes irreversible performance degradation. See F.4 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 4 Statistical Visualization on Qwen2.5-VL-3B. Layer-wise budget allocation (stacked bars) is shown under an average budget of 500 KV tokens per layer. Gradient Norm (Sl), Entropy (H), and Feature Magnitude (∥V ∥) are normalized for comparison. The strategy effectively assigns higher budgets to shallow layers, while more aggressively pruning deeper layers. See Appendix E.3 for details.

Table 1 Performance Comparison on Offline Video Understanding Benchmarks. We evaluate Video-MemComp against state-of-the-art compression methods and full-cache baselines. Avg Budget indicates the KV cache token limit; bold and underlined values mark the best and second-best results, respectively. Entries marked with * denotes reproduced

Table 3 System efficiency on LLaVA-OneVision-7B. Metrics include peak memory, visual encoder latency per frame, and time to first token (TTFT). Video-MemComp reduces memory and latency compared to retrieval-based baselines (ReKV), enabling OOM-free consumer-grade inference.

Table 11 Detailed hyperparameter configurations for different models across benchmarks. τinter and τintra denote the thresholds for inter-frame filtering and intra-frame merging, respectively. The budget allocation weights are denoted by λu (uniform), λs (static/structure), and λe (dynamic/entropy).

Table 4 Ablation study on intra-frame token compression. The inter-frame only baseline applies temporal filtering (θinter = 0.3) with standard KV pruning. Adding intra-frame compression improves performance on longer contexts by densifying spatial semantics, with a minor trade-off on short clips.

Table 13 Comprehensive Ablation Study on Budget Allocation Hyperparameters. We report the accuracy (%) for all subtasks on OVO-Bench. The configurations are sorted by the Uniform Prior weight (λu). The extreme cases (pure strategies) are located at the top and bottom. The new global optimal configuration is highlighted in bold with a gray background.

Table 10 Statistical Analysis of Structural Sensitivity (Sl) forQwen2.5-VL-3BBai et al. (2025b). Data is calculated based on LLaVA-Pretrain Liu et al. (2023). A higher Mean value indicates the layer is more sensitive to pruning errors. RSD (Relative Standard Deviation) reflects the fluctuation of importance across different samples.

Table 9 Distribution of Dynamic Metrics for Qwen2.5-VL-3B during Online Inference. Data is sampled from VideoMME streams. H denotes the Shannon entropy of the attention probability distribution, and log ∥V ∥ is the log-norm of the value vectors. Layers 3-28 exhibit extremely low entropy values, constituting the primary compression space.

Table 14 Ablation Study of Token Compression Thresholds on OVO-Bench. We report accuracy (%) for Backward, Realtime, and Forward tasks. The best configuration is highlighted in bold and gray background.

Table 12 Evaluation results on OVO-Bench. The table compares offline models and online streaming models separately. Bold indicates the best performance and underline indicates the second best within each group.
Table 6 Hyperparameter settings for different KV budgets. To achieve optimal performance under stricter budgets, we adopt slightly more aggressive filtering thresholds.

Table 8 Comparison of Compression Strategy Performance on VideoMME. We report model accuracy (%) under different KV budgets. The baseline performance of the original model (Qwen2.5-VL-3B without compression) is 50.56%.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses streaming-video KV-cache and token compression for efficient MLLM inference.
papers.title: Video-MemComp: Taylor-Guided Sensitivity-Aware Memory Management for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: Video-MemComp is a training-free method that compresses streaming-video KV memory by modeling sensitivity and approximation error, achieving over 90% memory savings with improved accuracy on Qwen2.5-VL-3B.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) read images through visual tokens, and under the small per-image budgets that efficient deployment requires, the fine text of documents, charts and infographics becomes illegible. Zooming in recovers the evidence, but the region must be chosen before the model answers. We find that MLLMs know where the evidence is, but not in a form that can be read before they answer: the answer tokens localize it from the middle layers on, whereas the attention available before answering does so only in the top layers, at a depth that varies across models, and diffusely. Supervising the pre-answer attention to point degrades reading, and the benefit of zooming is governed by each image's information gap. Building on these findings, we introduce ours, which lets an MLLM look where its answer would. A dedicated look token, processed in a single prefill and kept out of the answering pass, learns in hindsight to attend as the model's own correct answers do, extracting this knowledge into a concentrated pointer before any answer exists. Its hidden state then selects how to look, from no zoom to crops, square windows, windows that adapt to the pointer and foveated warps, supervised by the counterfactual outcome of every view. ours needs no box annotations, per-model layer search, external localizers or generation before the answer. On Qwen3-VL at three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it surpasses the strongest baseline by 4.8-9.1 points at 98 visual tokens per view and attention-guided zooming by 11.1-17.0 points, while running faster than attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.
authors: Zhensheng Hu, Guanglong Xu, Guanqiang Hu
bullets: Small visual-token budgets make fine text in documents, charts, and infographics difficult to read.
Answer tokens localize relevant evidence earlier and more clearly than pre-answer attention, whose useful depth varies by model.
OURS uses a dedicated look token trained from correct-answer attention to produce a concentrated pointer before answering.
The pointer selects among no zoom, crops, adaptive windows, square windows, and foveated warps using counterfactual view outcomes.

On Qwen3-VL across three scales and five text-rich benchmarks, it improves over the strongest baseline by 4.8–9.1 points and attention-guided zooming by 11.1–17.0 points at 98 visual tokens per view, while running faster than both attention-guided and grounding-based zooming.

figures.caption: Figure 4. Overview of LookZoom. (1) A dedicated <look> token is appended to the prompt and processed in a single prefill on the low-resolution view v. Its attention to the image tokens tells where to look, and its hidden state tells how to look. (2) The selected view transform is applied to the full-resolution image and re-encoded within the same per-view budget. (3) The reader answers from the low-resolution view and the selected view; the <look> token never enters this pass. Training: the <look> attention is distilled from the answer-time attention of the model’s own correct rollouts (hindsight distillation), the action head is supervised by the counterfactual outcomes of every view, and the reader is adapted with GRPO.

Figure 5. Qualitative results (Qwen3-VL-4B, 196 tokens). Top: input with the window selected by LookZoom (red). Middle: the zoomed view as the model reads it, re-encoded within the budget. Bottom: answers (green: correct, red: wrong). The selected views make units, numbers and brand names legible that the single view misreads.

Figure 1. The answer knows where to look (Qwen3-VL-4B, 196 visual tokens, V-CoT-Doc). (b) Before answering, the attention of the model’s middle layers barely touches the evidence (green box). (c) With the correct answer teacher-forced, the same layers attend to the evidence, but only once the answer is known. (d) Our <look> token concentrates on the evidence in a single prefill, and (e) the view it selects makes the value legible. Numbers give the fraction of attention inside the evidence box.

Figure 3. The information gap governs the value of looking again. Accuracy gain of a zoomed view (a 0.7 crop placed by the pre-answer attention of the base model) over the single view, against the information gap ρ (native over budget pixels). (a) Quintiles of ρ over 9,200 image–budget pairs per model (2,300 questions, 4 budgets). (b) Per benchmark (4B): the same images at budgets from 784 to 98 tokens.

Figure 2. Where the model looks before and while answering (V-CoT-Doc, 196 tokens). In the middle layers, the attention before answering places little mass on the evidence, while the attention of the answer tokens already localizes it. Before answering, comparable localization appears only in the top layers (best band of four layers per model). Our <look> token, read from the middle layers, concentrates the most mass on the evidence before any answer is produced.

Table 1. Main results under per-view visual-token budgets. Accuracy (%, official metrics) with at most B visual tokens per view; Views: views in the answering pass. Per-benchmark results use B=196; the last three columns average the five benchmarks at 196, 98 and 392 tokens. Baselines run on the base model, with the official settings where code is public; Ground-then-crop adds a crop of the evidence box named by the model, and GapSight† is our re-implementation (no public code), trained on the same images as our action head. Ours (replace) answers from the selected view alone. Best and second best per model in bold and underlined; ∆: Ours minus the best baseline.

Table 3. Ablations on Qwen3-VL-4B (five-benchmark average accuracy at 98 / 196 / 392 tokens); each block changes one component. Pre-answer: attention of the answer-start position at the layers of the <look> token or at the best top layers (†21–24, located with the evidence boxes of V-CoT-Doc).

Table 2. Cost on Qwen3-VL-4B at B=196 in the accounting of AttWarp [5]: MLLM passes, generation before the final answer, visual tokens processed and latency per sample (batch size 1, one RTX 4090). Acc.: five-benchmark average. †Our reimplementation.

Table 4. Training the pointer (Qwen3-VL-2B). Evidence mass of the pointer on V-CoT-Doc at 196 / 392 tokens, and five-benchmark accuracy averaged over 98 / 196 / 392 tokens for single-view reading and for the adaptive window placed by the pointer. Each row changes one element of training; the shared-attention variant trains the pre-answer attention instead of a <look> token.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a mechanism for MLLMs to intelligently zoom into images before answering, optimizing visual token usage. This addresses spatial intelligence (understanding where to look) and efficient AI (token budget management).
papers.title: The Answer Knows Where to Look: Zooming before MLLMs Answer under Visual-Token Budgets
papers.tldr: OURS lets MLLMs identify where answer-critical visual evidence lies before answering, enabling effective zooming under tight visual-token budgets.

papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GeoFMs) are costly to pretrain, yet model families often repeat this process across backbone scales and sensing modalities. We investigate feature distillation as a more efficient way to reuse existing representations. First, we distill frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers through patch-level feature matching. Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind Tiny, Small, and Base outperform their scale-matched released counterparts by 2.76, 3.02, and 1.87 mean IoU points, respectively; each also matches or exceeds the next-larger released model. Distilled CROMA-Base gains 2.05 points. TerraMind-Base required only 43 A6000 GPU-hours, approximately 0.5\% of the reported cost of independent pretraining. Second, we introduce TEDI, an unpaired multi-expert approach combining TerraMind for multispectral imagery and DINOv3 for high-resolution RGB. Separate patch embeddings route unpaired inputs into a shared Transformer trunk, removing the need for co-registered data. TEDI-Large achieves the highest single-model mean in our PANGAEA-9 comparison (62.51 mIoU), outperforming both teachers overall while retaining their modality-specific strengths. TEDI-Base reaches 61.75 mIoU with 72\% fewer parameters. These results show that distillation improves the GeoFM accuracy-compute frontier while consolidating complementary experts into a single versatile backbone.
authors: Mario Hamon, Pierre Adorni, Minh-Tan Pham
bullets: Distills frozen CROMA and TerraMind teachers into smaller Vision Transformers using patch-level feature matching.
Across nine PANGAEA tasks, distilled TerraMind and CROMA models improve over scale-matched released models and often reach the performance of larger ones.
TerraMind-Base distillation used approximately 0.5% of the reported cost of training an independent model.
TEDI combines TerraMind’s multispectral expertise with DINOv3’s high-resolution RGB features through separate patch embeddings and a shared Transformer trunk, without co-registered data.
TEDI-Large achieves the highest reported PANGAEA-9 single-model mean, while TEDI-Base offers a lower-parameter alternative with competitive performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Accuracy–compute trade-off. Released TerraMind models, their single-teacher distilled counterparts (TerraMind-KD), and multi-expert TEDI students are evaluated on the same nine PANGAEA tasks. Marker area indicates parameter count. Distillation shifts the entire model family toward a better trade-off; adding a complementary HR expert further improves average performance. TEDI-B1024 reallocates Base capacity toward a wider token embedding. Final comparisons use test scores; error bars show 3-run standard deviation.

Figure 3. Validation analyses. TerraMind-KD-Base val performance vs. distillation extent (left) and fraction of unique SSL4EO-S12 locations (right). Data-fraction runs hold update count fixed. Error bars show one sample standard deviation across three downstream runs.

Figure 2. TEDI training. Independent Sentinel-2 and HR samples are routed through modality-specific patch embeddings and a shared student trunk. Each sample is matched only to its corresponding frozen pretrained expert through a training-only projection head. Unlike a paired cross-modal objective, TEDI requires neither spatial correspondence nor a shared input representation across experts.

Table 5. Teacher-multiplicity ablation. Avg. test mIoU across three downstream runs, with standard deviation. Students use the same architecture and optimization budget. Two-student deployment: MS tasks to TerraMind-KD and HR tasks to DINOv3-KD.

Table 3. Multi-expert aggregation. Mean test mIoU on the nine PANGAEA-9 tasks. MS and HR average their respective five and four tasks, All over all nine. The expert oracle selects the better teacher independently for each task and therefore requires two deployed models. Results are averaged across three downstream runs, with one sample standard deviation shown below the mean. HLS=HLSBurnScars, MAD=Mados, PAS=PASTIS, S1F=Sen1Floods11, AI4=AI4SmallFarms, xV2=xView2, FBP=FiveBillionPixels, DEN=DynamicEarthNet, SN7=SpaceNet7.

Table 2. Single-teacher model-family derivation. Mean test mIoU on PANGAEA-9 across three downstream runs, with one sample standard deviation shown below the mean. Gains compare matched backbone sizes. CROMA results use its Sentinel-2 encoder.

papers.selection_reason: Demonstrates efficient feature distillation for geospatial foundation models, significantly reducing compute costs while maintaining or improving accuracy. This addresses both spatial intelligence (geospatial understanding) and efficient AI (distillation).
papers.title: Reuse, Don't Retrain: Efficient, Modality-Versatile Geospatial Foundation Models through Feature Distillation
