papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.

papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded memory for VLM-based robot planners that selectively retrieves frames, relevant to embodied memory, VLA, and token efficiency.
papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
papers.tldr: LogLook improves robot-planning memory by grounding it in execution logs and letting the model selectively inspect frames and demonstrations, reducing visual context while maintaining or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) can jointly process a broad range of modalities, such as text, audio, and video, enabling stronger multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities, but often at substantial inference cost. We observe that the benefit of additional modalities varies across queries, indicating that a fixed modality configuration can be inefficient. Motivated by this, we study query-wise modality selection, which keeps the underlying Omni-LLM fixed while adaptively selecting which modalities to provide for each query. We formulate the problem as an accuracy-cost optimization problem and develop a cost-sensitive learning approach for modality selection. We evaluate our approach on WorldSense using Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni under three inference-cost measures: input tokens, latency, and monetary cost. Across both models, query-wise modality selection consistently improves the accuracy-cost trade-off and can even outperform the standard setting in which all available modalities are provided to the Omni-LLM. For Qwen2.5-Omni, our cost-sensitive approach matches or exceeds this full-modality accuracy while requiring only approximately 41% of the input tokens, 39% of the latency, and 61% of the monetary cost.
authors: Shuqi Liu, Yuzhou Cao, Luke Ong
bullets: Additional modalities are not equally useful for every query, making fixed all-modality inference inefficient.
The method adaptively selects query-specific modalities while keeping the underlying Omni-LLM unchanged.
It formulates selection as an accuracy–cost optimization problem and uses cost-sensitive learning.
Evaluated with Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni on WorldSense across token, latency, and monetary costs.
For Qwen2.5-Omni, it matches or exceeds full-modality accuracy at about 41% of input tokens, 39% of latency, and 61% of monetary cost.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses efficiency in multimodal foundation models by proposing query-wise modality selection to optimize the accuracy-cost trade-off, which is a transferable technique for reducing inference costs in embodied agents.
papers.title: Efficient Omni-modal Large Language Model Inference via Per-Query Modality Selection
papers.tldr: Per-query modality selection makes Omni-LLM inference substantially cheaper while preserving or improving accuracy.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to predict human sentiments by integrating signals from different modalities such as text, video, and audio. However, raw multimodal sequences often suffer from semantic inconsistency--exhibiting redundancy or conflicts within and across modalities--which hinders robust understanding and increases computational cost. To this end, we introduce ConsMSA, which explicitly formalizes semantic distribution consistency across both $\textit{intra}$- and $\textit{inter}$-modality, providing a consistency-aware mechanism for robust and efficient multimodal sentiment prediction. Specifically, ConsMSA projects multimodal token features into a shared sentiment space to compute an Intra- and Inter-modality Consistency Score ($I^2CS$). By coupling this score with predictive relevance, we formulate consistency-aware importance signals that are utilized: (i) as a consistency regularizer to align latent distributions during training, (ii) to derive semantic-aware weights for adaptive multimodal token reweighting, and (iii) as a practical criterion to prune redundant or conflicting tokens. Extensive experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS demonstrate that ConsMSA achieves state-of-the-art performance while remaining robust under aggressive token compression--retaining only 10% of tokens yields comparable accuracy. These results establish semantic distribution consistency as a promising foundation for synergizing predictive robustness with computational efficiency.
authors: Pan Wang, Lipeng Ke, Huajun Ying, Pritish Mohapatra, Rohan Sarkar, Suresh Lakhani, Sankar Venkataraman, Jingtong Hu
bullets: Addresses semantic inconsistency, redundancy, and conflicts in text, video, and audio sequences.
Projects multimodal tokens into a shared sentiment space to calculate intra- and inter-modality consistency scores.
Uses consistency-aware signals for distribution regularization, adaptive token weighting, and token pruning.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance and comparable accuracy when retaining 10% of tokens.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the ConsMSA framework. The optimized tokens are finally concatenated in the Fusion Module for the final prediction. The system is optimized via a joint loss to achieve a robust balance between task accuracy (Ltask), semantic consistency (LI2CS), and modality-specific losses (LMS).

papers.title: ConsMSA: Semantic Distribution Consistency Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
papers.tldr: ConsMSA improves multimodal sentiment analysis by aligning semantic distributions across modalities while reweighting and pruning redundant or conflicting tokens.

papers.abstract: We consider the problem of model order reduction (MOR) in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs). We prove generalizations of well-known necessary interpolatory conditions for norm-optimal reduced-order models, originally stated for rational functions in $H_2$ Hardy-Hilbert spaces. We construct an alternative to the iterative rational Krylov (IRKA) algorithm for RKHSs with differentiable kernels to obtain norm-optimal reduced-order models. Then, we introduce generalized Malmquist-Takenaka (GMT) functions that can be used to define orthonormal bases in an arbitrary RKHS. Using GMT functions, we propose unitary transformations between separable RKHSs. This allows us to extend our optimality conditions and subsequent algorithms to MOR problems posed in RKHSs with non-differentiable kernels. The potential and versatility of the proposed MOR framework is demonstrated in several numerical experiments. We perform norm-optimal MOR on various machine learning models such as support vector machines and deep ReLU networks. In addition, we show how the proposed MOR framework can be used to solve seemingly unrelated problems. In particular, we provide an example for fitting high degree polynomials to data and also obtain a FEM-like method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with an optimal kernel basis.
authors: Tam\'as D\'ozsa, Andrea Angino, Rolf Krause, Matthias Voigt
bullets: Generalizes necessary interpolatory optimality conditions for reduced-order models in RKHSs.
Develops an IRKA alternative for differentiable kernels and uses generalized Malmquist–Takenaka functions for arbitrary RKHSs.
Constructs unitary transformations between separable RKHSs, extending the framework to non-differentiable kernels.
Demonstrates applications to support vector machines, deep ReLU networks, polynomial fitting, and PDE solution methods.
Numerical experiments illustrate the framework’s potential across these diverse problems.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents compact their context for the question at hand, but the compacted context must also serve questions that come later. We evaluate compaction on these later questions, using four corpora that annotate the evidence of several questions per text and recorded agent trajectories, and compare every method with random deletion at the same budget. On MultiRC, keeping the sentences that gpt-6-luna (through the OpenAI Decisions API) judges necessary for the current question raises its accuracy on that question by 11.4 points at 25% of the tokens. On the later questions, however, no method that selects sentences for the current question does detectably better than deleting sentences at random. Deleting words instead of sentences does better: LLMLingua-2, which ignores the question, beats random sentence deletion at the same token count by 12.5 points on the later MultiRC questions. It keeps about twice random deletion's share of the evidence's content words, and at equal content-word retention its gain shrinks to 7.3 points (exploratory). On FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text supports: the gain of sentence selection is no longer detected when answers are scored against the kept evidence, and the 21.0-point gain of LLMLingua-2 is not shown to rest on the kept text. The ranking also depends on the setting: on Evidence Inference sentence selection beats LLMLingua-2 at a nominal 25% budget, and on $τ$-bench trajectories, whose later tool calls need exact identifiers, it beats random deletion while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain. Scores on the question a compaction was made for do not reliably show how it serves later ones.
bullets: The study evaluates context compaction on later questions using four evidence-annotated corpora and recorded agent trajectories, with random deletion as a matched-budget baseline.
Selecting sentences for the current question improves current-question accuracy but generally performs no better than random deletion on later questions.
Question-agnostic word deletion with LLMLingua-2 improves later MultiRC performance over random sentence deletion, partly by retaining more evidence content words.
Results vary by setting: sentence selection helps on Evidence Inference and τ-bench, while LLMLingua-2 shows no detected gain on τ-bench.
Label accuracy can overstate whether the retained text supports an answer, especially on FEVER; evaluating only the original question is therefore insufficient.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates context compaction and token/sentence deletion methods for LLM agents, directly relevant to token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: Evaluating Context Compaction on the Questions That Come Later
papers.tldr: Context compaction optimized for the current question does not reliably preserve evidence for later questions, and performance depends strongly on the compression method and evaluation setting.

papers.abstract: Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.
bullets: Addresses the information bottleneck and limited performance of pooling- and projection-based sequence compression.
Computes regression coefficients in closed form during inference while learning the regression setup end-to-end with backpropagation.
Evaluated for block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging in multimodal large language models.
Achieves a large RULER improvement over attention-based compressors and matches an MLP merger using 55.6% fewer visual tokens.
Demonstrates test-time regression as a general compression primitive for efficient language and multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Processing long videos with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is bottlenecked by the quadratic cost of visual tokens, making long-form inference prohibitively expensive. While single-axis compression methods mitigate this, they hit a hard efficiency floor because they treat spatial and temporal redundancy independently. We present VETO (Video Efficient Token Optimization for Vision-Language Models), a training-optional plug-in that eliminates this bottleneck through dual-axis compression: (i) an intra-frame compressor that merges semantically similar tokens within each frame via optimal-transport inspired matching, and (ii) an inter-frame compressor that identifies and merges temporally redundant frames. The key design insight is hierarchical ordering: by first compressing spatial dimensions, VETO drastically reduces the cost of subsequent global temporal matching, bypassing the efficiency wall of single-axis approaches, with an advantage that grows with modern fully-fused attention infrastructure. Empirically, VETO achieves up to 45% faster inference (e.g., on LLaVA-OneVision-7B) while preserving or improving accuracy. Under extreme token starvation (10% budget), VETO outperforms VFlowOpt (54.9%), VisionZip (52.6%), and FastV (47.9%) with 55.7% accuracy. We demonstrate universal applicability across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA, with zero-shot accuracy preserved or improved in all cases.
bullets: Targets the quadratic visual-token cost that makes long-form video inference expensive.
Uses a training-optional dual-axis plug-in: optimal-transport-inspired intra-frame token merging followed by inter-frame redundant-frame merging.
Hierarchical ordering makes global temporal matching cheaper by first reducing spatial tokens.
Achieves up to 45% faster inference and maintains or improves zero-shot accuracy across LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL-2.5, and LongVA.
At a 10% token budget, reaches 55.7% accuracy, exceeding the cited VFlowOpt, VisionZip, and FastV results.

Second (Inter-Frame): Global frame-level redundancy is eliminated. Because the temporal similarity matrix is computed on the already spatially compressed dimension (N/k), computational overhead is minimized.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based models have shown strong performance across diverse tasks, but their reliance on self-attention mechanisms often leads to high computational costs. Token sparsification, which reduces the number of tokens processed in transformer layers, offers a promising solution to maintain performance while improving efficiency. However, although widely studied in the vision and language domains, token sparsification remains underexplored in audio, with existing work often limited to a single method, model size, or dataset. This work presents a comprehensive evaluation of token sparsification techniques for audio transformers. We assess a range of token pruning and merging strategies across multiple datasets and model sizes, under both post-training and fine-tuning settings. Furthermore, we introduce a novel sparsification approach that combines attention scores with spectral cues derived from the frequency content of token embeddings. Our experiments show that frequency-aware approaches, particularly those based on spectral flatness and low-frequency energy, consistently outperform attention-only methods. We also find that sparsification based on spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs. These results highlight the value of incorporating frequency-domain and input-specific information into sparsification strategies to enhance performance in audio tasks.
authors: Shreya Sajid, Fabrizio Julian Piva, Hiram Rayo Torres Rodriguez, Elif Ceren Gok Yildirim, Murat Onur Yildirim, Joaquin Vanschoren
bullets: Audio token sparsification is less explored than in vision and language, motivating a broader evaluation.
The study compares token pruning and merging across multiple datasets, model sizes, and post-training or fine-tuning settings.
It introduces a method combining attention scores with spectral cues from token-embedding frequency content.
Spectral-flatness and low-frequency-energy methods consistently outperform attention-only sparsification.
Spectrogram patch intensity is especially effective for longer audio inputs.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Post-training sparsification results on the AST-Base (Gong et al., 2021) model, evaluated on AudioSet-20K (Gemmeke et al., 2017) at a 50% keep rate. Methods that include frequencydomain cues, such as the proposed Spectral Flatness (SF) and the adapted Low-Frequency Energy (LFE) (Wang et al., 2022b), outperform others in terms of mean average precision (mAP), a standard metric for multi-label classification. The baseline (without sparsification) achieves an average mAP of 0.3572. The Pareto front is highlighted to illustrate the performance-efficiency tradeoff.

Figure 8. Performance comparison of frequency-based methods (LFE and SF) against attention-only baselines (TopK-Wt and TopK-CLS). SF slightly but consistently outperforms attention-based baselines across keep rates, while LFE shows competitive results but occasionally underperforms on ESC50 and AS-20K.

Figure 7. Sparsified Fine-tuning: Performance across varying keep rates. Frequency-based methods (SF, LFE), as well as pure attention-based pruning methods (Top-K, EViT), consistently maintain high performance across tasks. Most methods retain competitive performance down to a 50% keep rate. Overall, the performance differences between methods are not very significant, indicating that multiple sparsification methods can be equally effective when fine-tuned.

Figure 9. Token pruning performance as a function of input duration. Intensity Pruning consistently outperforms Top-K pruning for longer audio windows (> 2 seconds), suggesting that spectrogram intensity is a more informative proxy for longer audio samples.

Figure 3. Low-frequency Energy token pruning. Token embeddings are transformed to the frequency domain, where a Gaussian low-pass filter highlights low-frequency structure. The resulting energy scores are fused with attention scores to guide top-K token selection.

Figure 4. Spectral flatness-guided token pruning. Token embeddings undergo Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) along the embedding dimension to compute spectral flatness, capturing tonal richness. These scores are combined with CLS attention to rank token importance.

Figure 2. Intensity-guided token pruning. Tokens are divided into high- (H) and low- (L) intensity groups based on an applied threshold. The high-intensity set is then ranked using CLS attention scores, and the Top-K tokens are selected. If fewer than K tokens are available in H , the remaining slots are filled from the low-intensity set.

papers.selection_reason: Systematic study of token pruning and merging for audio transformers, directly matching token sparsification and efficiency interests.
papers.title: Muting Tokens: Exploring Token Sparsification for Efficient Audio Transformers
papers.tldr: A comprehensive study shows that frequency- and input-aware token sparsification can make audio transformers more efficient while preserving stronger performance than attention-only methods.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reads only a small subset of the key-value cache, and how to treat the unread tail remains a key challenge. Discarding the tail biases the output, and sampling it as previous approaches do fails at reads of 5% and below, where the tail likely holds heavy hitters the selector missed. Our key observation is that the simplest possible proxy, one token that folds the entire tail into its count-aware mean, already yields lower output error than a sample at every read behind a practical selector. We further show in closed form that at low reads sampling nearly doubles the weight error of discarding while a single proxy stays below it. Building on these findings, we explore approximating the dense attention distribution with a few proxies that target the tail. We propose OpenAttention, a pipeline of clustering, ErrorGate and top-k selection followed by a count-aware mean proxy. To implement clustering and selection both efficiently and effectively, we design training-free Query-Geometry Clustering (QGC) and a Query-Geometry Selector (QGS), which compress the keys while respecting the query directions. Additionally, unlike prior methods that rank clusters by centroid alone, ErrorGate allocates the exact read by the estimated weight error of each cluster. On RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B, OpenAttention retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read. It also achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across models, context lengths and datasets. Our customized attention kernel, OpenAttention.flash, runs the decode attention stage 10$\times$ faster than dense attention at a 1% read.
authors: Hyunwoo Yu, Jongbeom Lee, Hyunbin Kim, Sungjun Park, Jaemin Choi, Jincheol Yang, Seunghun Moon, Bongjoon Hyun, Kyomin Sohn, Kyeongbo Kong, Suk-Ju Kang
bullets: Sparse attention can be biased when unread tail tokens are discarded, while sampling performs poorly at very low read rates.
A single count-aware mean proxy for the entire tail reduces output and weight error more effectively than sampling.
The pipeline combines Query-Geometry Clustering, Query-Geometry Selection, ErrorGate, top-k selection, and tail proxies.
On RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B, it retains 99% of dense accuracy at a 1% read.
OpenAttention.flash reports 10× faster decode attention than dense attention at a 1% read.

papers.abstract: AI agents require interfaces to interact with external systems such as files, APIs, databases, and cloud services. Two competing paradigms have emerged: CLI (Command Line Interface), where agents execute shell commands directly, and MCP (Model Context Protocol), a structured JSON-RPC protocol providing governed, typed tool access. This paper presents a comparative analysis across 14 evaluation dimensions, supported by worked examples, security assessment against established compliance frameworks, and economic modeling. Our analysis indicates that CLI provides superior efficiency for single-user, local-only workflows, while MCP addresses requirements that CLI fundamentally cannot satisfy, including fine-grained access control, credential isolation, structured audit, and multi-tenant governance. We further examine how progressive disclosure techniques eliminate MCP's historical weakness (context window overhead), yielding token efficiency comparable to CLI while preserving its architectural benefits. A hybrid architecture is recommended for production systems. This analysis draws upon academic, government, and industry sources including NSA formal guidance (CSI U/OO/6030316-26), OWASP security standards, and economic modeling from BCG and Gartner.
authors: Arun Malik, Nitish Talasu, Bradley Klemick, Vineet Tushar Trivedi, Prachi Shah, Sanay Devi, Junjie Zhang, Kunal Sonawane
bullets: Compares CLI and MCP across 14 dimensions, including usability, security, governance, and economics.
CLI suits single-user, local-only tasks with direct shell access.
MCP provides typed, governed tool access with fine-grained permissions, credential isolation, structured auditing, and multi-tenant support.
Progressive disclosure can reduce MCP’s context-window overhead to near-CLI token efficiency.
The analysis recommends combining CLI and MCP in production architectures.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes the token efficiency and architectural trade-offs between CLI and MCP (Model Context Protocol) for tool integration, focusing on context window overhead and governance.
papers.title: MCP vs CLI for AI Agents: A Comparative Analysis of Tool Integration Strategies for Autonomous Systems
papers.tldr: CLI is efficient for simple local workflows, while MCP offers stronger governance and security for production AI agents; a hybrid approach is recommended.

papers.abstract: Every interaction between AI agents begins with a handshake: the initiating agent must locate its counterpart, learn what it can do, and establish a session before the first useful message can be sent. Surveys of agent communication protocols name handshake overhead as an efficiency criterion, yet none report measurements. This paper presents the first empirical, phase-decomposed benchmark of the handshake in three major agent protocols: MCP (in both its 2025 initialize and 2026 discover eras), A2A, and ACP. Using each protocol's official SDK, we instrument every request for round trips, per-phase latency, wire bytes, and token cost across cold-start, warm-repeat, capability-mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios (N=50 per cell, on loopback and under an emulated 50 ms RTT). Round-trip count dominates handshake cost. A legacy MCP handshake takes three round trips and 230 ms at 50 ms RTT; A2A needs one round trip and 61.0 ms. Round trips are not the whole bill: when an LLM reads the counterpart's metadata, handshake cost scales with the counterpart's capability inventory at 24-107 tokens per capability, so a 200-capability counterpart spends 11% of a 200k-token context window before the agent reads its own task. MCP's own 2026 revision cuts its handshake from three round trips to two and, with era pinning, to zero on warm reconnects, protocol evolution that corroborates the cost we measure. We release the full harness, raw data, and analysis at https://github.com/pvarshh/handshake-benchmark.
bullets: The study benchmarks handshake phases in MCP, A2A, and ACP across cold, warm, mismatch, and degraded-metadata scenarios.
Round-trip count is the primary cost driver: legacy MCP uses three round trips and takes 230 ms at 50 ms RTT, while A2A uses one and takes 61.0 ms.
LLM-readable metadata adds 24–107 tokens per advertised capability; a 200-capability counterpart can consume 11% of a 200k-token context window.
MCP’s 2026 revision reduces the handshake from three to two round trips, and era pinning enables zero-round-trip warm reconnects.
The authors release the benchmark harness, raw data, and analysis.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Cold-start latency to task-ready versus emulated RTT (S1 medians, N=20 per cell). Slopes track the number of delayed exchanges per handshake. Right-edge leader lines connect curves to labels and are not data.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures scale model capacity efficiently, yet their substantial memory footprint poses a major barrier to deployment. Expert pruning reduces this footprint, but most methods focus on which experts to remove and prune every layer equally. We propose SPARE (Sparsity Allocation via Routing Entropy), a training-free, selector-agnostic method that decides how many experts to remove from each layer using routing entropy, the entropy of tokens' normalized Top-K gate weights on calibration data. When a token's gate weight is spread evenly, removing one active expert discards little of it, so SPARE prunes layers with more diffuse routing more aggressively. A perturbation bound under random pruning formalizes this intuition, and controlled interventions with a fixed selector link concentrated routing to larger output changes. With the same selector and budget, SPARE improves average accuracy over uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, especially at high pruning ratios. At 50% expert pruning, it raises the eight-task average of Qwen3-30B-A3B from 57.2% to 63.8%, and the math, code, and science average of DeepSeek-R1 from 80.1 to 82.8.
authors: Yifan Yang, Hanling Yi, Dongquan Yang, Feng Lin, Rong Xiao, Aijun Li, Xiaotian Yu
bullets: Targets the memory cost of MoE deployment by choosing how many experts to remove per layer.
Uses token gate-weight entropy on calibration data: layers with more diffuse routing are pruned more aggressively.
Training-free and selector-agnostic; supported by a perturbation bound and controlled interventions.
Outperforms uniform allocation on Mixtral, Qwen3, and DeepSeek models, particularly at high pruning ratios.
At 50% pruning, Qwen3-30B-A3B improves from 57.2% to 63.8%, while DeepSeek-R1 improves from 80.1 to 82.8% on the reported task averages.

papers.abstract: Direct preference optimization (DPO) incurs training costs in output scoring, sequence execution, and backpropagation, so reducing supervision alone does not necessarily save computation. We introduce a unified framework for stochastic pruning of the DPO computation graph that independently samples response positions for scoring, response prefixes for execution, and preference branches for backpropagation. By making these selections before the corresponding operations, the framework omits computation at each stage of a training step. Our analysis characterizes the objective changes induced by position and sequence pruning and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain a conditionally unbiased single-branch gradient estimator for the sampled objective. Controlled measurements show that position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory, with most output-memory savings attributable to an implementation that retains full response supervision. Branch pruning yields a $1.426\times$ step-time speedup over a concatenated DPO baseline and reduces training time by about 30\% relative to stock DPO across two model families, with slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent changes in open-ended scores. These findings relate the resource benefits of stochastic graph pruning to the computation omitted and the resulting changes in the training objective.
authors: Yubing Wu, Wei Chen, Junmei Yang, Delu Zeng, Tiewen Pan
bullets: Targets DPO’s output scoring, sequence execution, and preference-branch backpropagation costs.
Samples response positions, response prefixes, and preference branches before their corresponding computations.
Uses inverse-probability weighting to produce a conditionally unbiased gradient estimator for the sampled objective.
Branch pruning provides the main speedup; position and sequence pruning primarily reduce peak memory.
Quality changes are modest but include slightly lower mean accuracy and benchmark-dependent open-ended scores.

papers.abstract: Full 3D attention is costly in video Diffusion Transformers. Block-sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only selected attention blocks. However, existing methods either overlook the potential to optimize sparsity allocation or rely on heuristic rules or local metrics to guide it. In this work, we observe that sparsifying attention in different layers and at different denoising steps affects final-video fidelity to substantially different degrees. Yet the identities of the most sensitive layer-step pairs remain nearly unchanged across inputs. Building on these findings, we propose Allocating Layer-step Latency by Output Tests (ALLOT), a training-free sparsity allocation method. Treating each layer-step pair as a cell, ALLOT estimates each cell's contribution to final-video error through (i) cell probing and (ii) trajectory calibration, then jointly optimizes cell densities under a measured-latency budget. It preserves existing selection strategies and kernels, replacing only the allocation component. At equal or shorter wall-clock time, ALLOT outperforms every compared allocation strategy with XAttention, with an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo. Extensive experiments across four additional published pipelines on Wan2.1, Wan2.2, and HunyuanVideo show that ALLOT outperforms or ties the default in all nine settings.
authors: Tianze Xia, Xiaoling Zhou, Ruya Lan, Yiqiao Liao, Chengru Song, Shiming Xiang
bullets: Full 3D attention is expensive, and different layer–step pairs have unequal effects on final-video fidelity.
ALLOT estimates each pair’s error contribution using cell probing and trajectory calibration.
It jointly optimizes sparsity densities under a measured-latency budget while retaining existing block-selection strategies and kernels.

Across five video diffusion pipelines and nine settings, ALLOT outperforms or matches the default allocation; with XAttention, it achieves an 11.8 dB PSNR gain on HunyuanVideo at equal or lower runtime.

papers.title: Sparsity Should Be ALLOTted by Output: Training-Free Allocation of Block-Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: ALLOT is a training-free method that allocates block-sparse attention across layer–denoising-step pairs to improve video diffusion quality under a latency budget.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment. Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model. We introduce VLA-ACL (Action Consistency Learning), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen. The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output. Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5x inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code is available at https://github.com/du-owen/VLA-ACL.
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of processing redundant visual tokens during robotic control.
Trains a lightweight pruning policy with action-level consistency supervision, using full-context predictions as a teacher and ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision.
Keeps the base VLA model completely frozen, avoiding costly end-to-end fine-tuning.
On LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks, prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5× inference speedup.
Demonstrates a stronger performance-efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of VLA-ACL. Modules with a snowflake symbol are kept frozen, modules with a flame symbol receive gradient updates. a) During training, two forward passes of the frozen LLM are performed. On the left, the full-vision-context teacher action is generated. On the right, vision embeddings enter our differentiable soft pruning gate and produce the soft-pruned action. b) During inference, the hard pruning gate only lets through K patches per view with the highest patch scores, obtained by the trained patch scorer. The pruned tokens never enter the VLA language backbone.

VLA-ADP and VLA-Cache both rely on full-context forwards during inference, while VLA-ACL sustains a much more aggressive pruning schedule at every control step, enabling lower latency while retaining similar performance across all LIBERO suites.

The logits pass through a soft Top-K function, which maps logits to [0, 1] scores summing to K. papers.selection_reason: Introduces VLA-ACL, a method for efficient visual token pruning in VLA models using action-level supervision without fine-tuning the base model.
papers.title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: VLA-ACL efficiently prunes visual tokens in frozen vision-language-action models by learning which tokens preserve the model’s control actions.

papers.abstract: Smart glasses can help users understand their activities and surroundings, but small vision-language models must preserve useful evidence within limited computation. This is difficult because redundant frames consume the visual budget, while aggressive spatial compression can discard relevant details. Although gaze identifies the wearer's focus, the question may require evidence from the surrounding scene. To address these constraints, we propose GazeLens, which combines frame selection with gaze- and question-guided token reduction. First, HOG transitions and image sharpness select frames before visual encoding. For each selected frame, Gaussian pooling then forms gaze-focused and complementary summaries. Because their relevance depends on the question, a lightweight gate blends them into a primary token. Together with a global scene token, this retains both focused and contextual summaries within two tokens per frame. On StreamGaze, GazeLens achieves higher macro and micro accuracy than the evaluated full-grid and token-reduction baselines, with lower input-forward FLOPs than the shared-backbone token-reduction baselines.
authors: Trong-Thang Pham, Anh Nguyen, Hien Van Nguyen, Ngan Le
bullets: Addresses limited computation in smart-glasses VQA while preserving both gaze-focused evidence and surrounding context.
Selects frames using HOG transitions and image sharpness before visual encoding.
Uses Gaussian pooling to create gaze-focused and complementary summaries, then applies a lightweight question-guided gate.
Represents each selected frame with a blended primary token plus a global scene token.
On StreamGaze, outperforms evaluated full-grid and token-reduction baselines in macro and micro accuracy while using fewer input-forward FLOPs than shared-backbone token-reduction baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed focus-aware, question-conditioned token reduction framework. (1) Dynamic Frame Selection. A continuous video stream is filtered using HOG transition and sharpness cues to retain informative frames while discarding small-change and blurry frames. This filtering process produces a dynamic input sequence V . (2) Focus-Aware Gaze Aggregation. Each selected frame is encoded into spatial features and combined with gaze (xt, yt) to produce a focus token gt, an unfocus token ct, and a global token mt. (3) Question-Conditioned Semantic Gating. Question token embeddings are mean-pooled and L2-normalized to t. A two-layer MLP and sigmoid then yield a scalar gate s ∈ [0, 1]. The gate modulates gaze-focused versus contextual information as pt = s · gt + (1− s) · ct. (4) Token Assembly and Training Objective. The per-frame tokens pt and mt are linearly projected, concatenated with the question, and fed into a language model to predict the answer, optimized with a cross-entropy (CE) loss.

Figure 1: Teaser of our gaze-driven adaptive token reduction framework for egocentric video QA. In the left panel, egocentric video and gaze data are inherently noisy and redundant, with dense frames and unstable gaze signals. In the middle panel, existing VLM approaches suffer from inefficient frame selection (too dense or too sparse) and often ignore gaze or rely on computationally expensive adaptive attention mechanisms. In the right panel, our approach combines (1) Dynamic Frame Selection, (2) Focus-Aware Gaze Aggregation, and (3) Question-Conditioned Semantic Gating. Together, these modules produce two visual tokens per frame. This design reduces the visual token budget and model computation while improving performance under strict token budgets.

papers.title: GazeLens for Efficient Egocentric Video Question Answering with Simple Gaze-Driven Adaptive Token Reduction
papers.tldr: GazeLens improves egocentric video question answering efficiency by selecting informative frames and compressing each into two question- and gaze-aware visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Token merging is an effective approach to reducing KV-cache memory consumption in autoregressive video generation by clustering temporally redundant tokens and retaining only a small set of representatives. Existing methods, however, typically apply a uniform merging ratio across all attention layers and heads. We observe that different layers and heads exhibit substantially different yet jointly correlated sensitivities to token merging, and that these sensitivity patterns remain consistent across prompts. Based on this observation, we introduce CALM, a Calibrated Allocation for Layer-Head Merging that uses offline calibration to improve online cache compression. Exhaustively evaluating all possible layer-head allocations is prohibitively expensive. To enable efficient calibration, we show that attention-output error strongly correlates with end-to-end video quality and can therefore serve as a lightweight proxy for allocation risk assessment. We evaluate different allocation strategies using this proxy and construct a fixed layer-head risk map offline. Given a cache budget at inference time, CALM uses dynamic programming to determine the best allocation of merging ratios. Experiments across three different autoregressive video models demonstrate that CALM consistently outperforms uniform token merging under the same memory budget, by reducing the LPIPS to original videos by around 21% with higher video-quality scores.
authors: Zhen Wang, Ning Lai, Qingtao Yu
bullets: Uniform token-merging ratios overlook substantial, prompt-consistent sensitivity differences across attention layers and heads.
CALM uses attention-output error as a lightweight proxy for end-to-end video-quality risk during offline calibration.
It builds a fixed layer-head risk map, then selects merging ratios dynamically for a given cache budget.
Across three autoregressive video models, CALM outperforms uniform merging, reducing LPIPS to original videos by around 21% while achieving higher video-quality scores.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.
authors: Injae Kim, Minseok Joo, Jihwan Park, Sehyung Kim, Minseong Bae, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Existing methods generate a dense Gaussian set before pruning, so inference cost remains nearly fixed regardless of the final budget.
RLSplat learns how to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians across local scene regions.
A resource-linear decoder refines Gaussians using efficient hierarchical neighbor search and local attention.
In zero-shot evaluation, it outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, including a stronger baseline with 4× fewer Gaussians.
At low budgets, RLSplat runs up to 4.1× faster and uses 9.6× less peak memory.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison under the same Gaussian budget. All methods use 8K Gaussians on RE10K. For each method, we show the rendered view and PSNR, a zoomed region and its local PSNR, the Gaussian centers in the highlighted region (red), and a 16×16 tile-wise map of the number of Gaussians. RLSplat places more Gaussians around the thin stair balusters (5,388 vs. 3,026 for F4Splat and 2,521 for EcoSplat), preserving the fine structure that the baselines blur.

Figure 2: Overview of RLSplat. Given uncalibrated context images, the geometry backbone predicts camera parameters and extracts anchor tokens {an} representing local 3D regions. papers.selection_reason: Proposes RLSplat, a resource-linear budget control method for 3D Gaussian Splatting. This addresses efficiency in 3D foundation models and falls under token/pruning strategies for resource management.
papers.title: RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: RLSplat makes feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting truly budget-controllable by reducing representation size, inference latency, and peak memory linearly with the requested Gaussian budget.

papers.abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.
authors: Liana Patel, Rishabh Ranjan, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, Carlos Guestrin
bullets: Addresses the high cost of processing every token across all layers during long-context prefill.
Uses a small drop-in component that learns token importance and prunes less relevant tokens.
Introduces token-gated attention to enable end-to-end training despite non-differentiable top-K pruning.
Reports 1.4–11.3× faster time-to-first-token and 1.5–3.4× lower peak memory with no accuracy degradation.
Supports standard and hybrid-attention transformers through lightweight adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes TokenGate, a learnable token pruning mechanism for LLMs, to achieve fast and memory-efficient prefill, directly addressing token pruning and memory efficiency.
papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.tldr: TokenGate adds lightweight learned token pruning to existing LLMs, substantially reducing long-context prefill time and memory without degrading accuracy.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.
bullets: Addresses unsupervised discovery of meaningful compositional hierarchies without structural supervision.
Recursively merges adjacent tokens into abstract representations through a variational information bottleneck.
Marginalises over possible binary trees with dynamic programming to jointly learn representations and structure.
Uses unsupervised consensus and distillation across independently trained models to improve training stability.
On held-out synthetic sequences, reaches 93% parse validity and exact reconstruction, versus 42% parse validity for the strongest trivial baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The three-stage pipeline. The same architecture is used as the base model in Stage 1 and as the distilled model in Stage 3; only Stage 1 uses the chart, while Stage 3 trains on the fixed silver trees.

Figure 3: The seed lottery. Held-out parse-validity of the 24 base models in each of the four seedvarying pools (labelled by their seeds, so s52-75 is pool 52–75). The spread within a pool is wide even though the models differ only in random seed.

Figure 5: Cosine similarity between the nineteen word embeddings, ordered by category, for the best base model (held-out parse-validity 1.000) and the distilled student (0.989). The base model groups words by category; the student does not, yet both parse well. A sweep of the student’s KL weight (holding latent size fixed) does not reproduce the clustering, so it is a by-product of how the base models induce structure, not of the bottleneck and not a prerequisite for parsing.

Figure 2: One chart cell for span (i, j) at split k. The two child spans are merged into a candidate parent, which the unmerger tries to invert; the negative squared error (“energy”) is the local score. The span score is the log-sum-exp over splits, and the highest-scoring split is stored as a back-pointer for parsing.

Figure 6: The four networks of the base model, with layers and dimensions. The lifter maps each token id to a leaf latent through two embedding tables (a mean and a log-variance) and the reparameterisation trick. The merger is the encoder step, a two-layer perceptron with a ReLU that combines two child latents into a parent; it is applied bottom-up at every internal node of the tree. The unmerger is the decoder step and an approximate inverse of the merger, predicting the two children from a parent, applied top-down; its squared error against the true children is the one-step energy that also scores splits in the chart. The unlifter is a single linear layer that reads a recovered leaf latent back to a distribution over the vocabulary. A single merger and a single unmerger are shared across all tree depths.

Table 2: Hyperparameters for the base models and the distilled student. Each pool trains 24 base models, of which the 8 with the highest peer agreement are selected; results are reported over seven independent pools. The KL weight is warmed up, so the base models, which stop at step 2500, end at β ≈ 0.032.

Table 3: Aggregation ablation. Twenty-four base models per mode on matched seeds and one data split, so initial weights and batch order are identical within each row and only the aggregation rule differs. Base-model figures are medians over the twenty-four models; consensus and student figures are for the pipeline built from them.

Table 5: Seven independent 24-model pools. The first four vary only the random seed on one data split; the last three redraw the data as well. The two consensus columns are the parse agreed over all 24 models and over the eight retained by peer agreement; both are measured on training surfaces. Student columns are held-out. Gold parses are used only to compute these numbers, never in training or selection.

Table 7: Four seeds that induce the grammar, each trained for 15,000 steps under three strategies that share the tight first 2500 steps and then differ in how training continues. Restart resets the learning rate to its maximum, continuous uses one smooth decay with no restart, and the loose arm drops the KL weight to 0.002. Base is the frozen base model. Reconstruction recovers with training but plateaus below the student’s 0.93, and no strategy keeps the grammar while reaching 0.93 reconstruction. Validity and reconstruction are held-out.

Table 1: Baselines on the held-out set (137 surfaces). “Random” is the exact expected validity of a uniformly random binary tree, obtained by enumeration rather than sampling. Overall figures are averaged over surfaces.

Table 6: Distilled students by sentence length, held-out, for the three seed-varying pools that were measured this way. Both metrics degrade at lengths seven and eight. The right-branching baseline over the same lengths is given for comparison.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder for unsupervised grammar induction, which is a form of token-level compression and structure discovery relevant to token pruning and efficiency.
papers.title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
papers.tldr: A recursive autoencoder learns hierarchical grammatical structure from compression alone, achieving 93% parse validity and exact reconstruction on a synthetic ambiguous grammar.

papers.abstract: Standard self-attention compares tokens by similarity but does not account for how much of a past state survives to the present. We introduce Dynamical Kernel Attention (DKA), which derives attention from robust estimation of a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics. As a past state decays toward equilibrium under the dynamics, the information it carries about the present vanishes, bounding the total evidence a head can draw. Unlike recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and guarantees a bounded error when old tokens are discarded. DKA preserves the parallel structure and computational cost of standard attention. We present the model and its theory; empirical evaluation is deferred to a subsequent version.
bullets: Standard self-attention measures similarity but ignores how much information from past states remains relevant to the present.
DKA derives attention by robustly estimating a latent state evolving under stochastic dynamics.
Information from past states decays toward equilibrium, limiting the total evidence an attention head can use.
Unlike simple recency biases, DKA can abstain when relevant evidence is weak and provides error guarantees when old tokens are discarded.
The abstract presents theory and the model; empirical evaluation is deferred to future work.

figures.caption: Figure 2: A single Isotropic DKA head. The dynamical model (blue) depends only on the lag and a few per-head scalars, and supplies the decay kernel E, the observation coefficient h = E2, and the conditioned covariance Σn. The query is compared in the key’s frame against the backward conditional mean EQ̃i. Weights are not softmax-normalized: m is the row maximum of L, and the proximal prior on the current estimate contributes a null slot e−mγ−2 to the denominator, so a head abstains when the accumulated information S̃ is small. The robust weight w may be the Student-t or exponential kernel, and the mask is causal (including the diagonal).

Figure 3: Counting evidence from distant tokens. One mode of the linear Gaussian model, with data drawn from its stationary distribution and nominal attention weights wij = 1 (µ = 0.05, v∞ = 2, η2 = 0.5). (a) Information about the current state assigned to a single token. DKA’s falls exponentially with lag; RFA’s levels off at 1/v∞, since each distant token restates the prior. The exact curve is the information a token adds given all newer tokens. (b) Total information in the N most recent tokens. The exact and DKA totals both saturate, DKA’s above the exact by a bounded factor; RFA’s grows linearly.

Figure 1: A distant token restates the prior. A latent state (black) evolves under stable linear dynamics around an equilibrium at zero; the star marks the current state xi. Each past token predicts the present by carrying its value forward under the dynamics (blue curves), and the error bars on the right show the uncertainty of each prediction at the present. A nearby token (dark) predicts the current state closely. A distant token (light) has decayed to the equilibrium, and its uncertainty has grown to the stationary spread √ v∞.

Figure 4: Accuracy and memory (setting as in Figure 3). We compare the estimates x̄i before the residual or proximal step. (a) MSE of each estimate of the current state, E [ (x̄i − xi) 2 ] /v∞; a value of one is what always guessing the equilibrium, x̄i = 0, achieves. With a few tokens, all three agree (RFA dips slightly below exact, trading a little bias for lower variance). Each further token adds a vote for the equilibrium in RFA’s average, so its error rises toward one. DKA’s levels off above the exact error, reflecting its bounded overcount. (b) Change in the estimate when only the T most recent tokens of a 2048-token context are kept (RMS over the stationary data, relative to √ v∞). DKA’s change falls exponentially at a rate set by µ, so tokens beyond a fixed window can be evicted for every query. RFA’s falls slowly, since a distant token’s weight in the normalizer is not decayed. The exact change falls fastest: once recent states are pinned down, older tokens add almost nothing.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an attention mechanism with bounded-error token discarding, directly relevant to efficient attention and token eviction.
papers.title: Dynamical Kernel Attention: Estimating the Present from a Record of the Past
papers.tldr: Dynamical Kernel Attention incorporates stochastic state dynamics into attention, enabling principled decay, abstention under weak evidence, and bounded error from discarding old tokens without added computational cost.

papers.abstract: Consumer phones and wearables increasingly collect physiological time-series data, yet most mobile systems treat these streams as summaries or text rather than as temporal evidence. This representation is poorly matched to personal health systems that need to retrieve, route, or summarize sensor evidence while preserving temporal structure. Cloud-hosted time-series language models avoid smartphone limits, but they repeatedly move sensitive physiology off the device and add latency and per-query compute cost. Mobile model alternatives that aggregate time-series data into statistical features or serialize raw samples as text either compress temporal structure or exhaust the context and memory budgets of small on-device models. We present PocketTSLM, a mobile-native deployment of OpenTSLM SoftPrompt, the soft-prompt variant of the OpenTSLM time-series language model. PocketTSLM runs fully on a consumer smartphone by injecting encoded time-series windows as embeddings instead of tokenizing time series as text. A numerical parity protocol verifies identical greedy-decoded token sequences between the Swift port and a Python reference using Apple's MLX machine-learning framework. Answers also match the PyTorch reference, although rationale wording can differ. An on-device context-economics benchmark compares the soft-prompt path with a text-serialized baseline on the same backbone. In our benchmark format, soft-prompting uses approximately 12 times fewer time-series tokens and reduces prompt-prefill cost. PocketTSLM processes 30-second Sleep-EDF electroencephalography clips for sleep staging and a 1,000-sample (10 s) 12-lead electrocardiogram clip from ECG-QA. In comparison, text-serialized baselines exceed the phone's context or memory budget at longer time-series windows. All inference runs entirely on the device, with no health data transmitted during inference.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between text-based mobile models and temporally structured physiological data, while avoiding cloud privacy, latency, and compute costs.
Injects encoded time-series windows as embeddings rather than serializing samples as text, preserving temporal input within mobile context limits.
Implements the OpenTSLM SoftPrompt model in Swift using Apple’s MLX framework and verifies numerical parity with a Python reference.
Processes Sleep-EDF EEG clips for sleep staging and 1,000-sample, 12-lead ECG clips from ECG-QA on a consumer smartphone.
Soft-prompting uses approximately 12× fewer time-series tokens than the text-serialized baseline and avoids context or memory overflow at longer windows.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The OpenTSLM-SP pipeline running fully on-device. Health time-series data are split into patches and encoded by a convolutional neural network (CNN) patch encoder and transformer (the timeseries encoder), projected into the LLM embedding space, and interleaved with the embedded text prompt. The combined sequence is decoded by a frozen pre-trained LLM with a low-rank adaptation (LoRA) adapter into a natural-language model rationale. The entire pipeline executes on the device through the MLX-Swift runtime on Apple silicon, with no health data leaving the phone. Figure adapted from Langer et al. [11].

Figure 2. On-device EEG sleep staging in the demo app, running on an iPhone Air in airplane mode. The app’s task menu (left), the Sleep-EDF prompt with its EEG input summary (center), and the model-generated rationale and answer (right).

Figure 3. On-device context economics (iPhone, Llama-3.2-1B, greedy decoding), for single-channel EEG (Sleep-EDF [34, 35]) and 12-lead ECG (ECG-QA [28]). (a) Time-series tokens vs. series length: text serialization costs approximately 12× as many tokens as soft prompts across evaluated lengths and both tasks (soft-prompt tokens are injected embeddings, not vocabulary tokens). (b) TTFT: soft-prompt TTFT is lower across the evaluated sweep, while the text arm grows steeply and drops out once its full prompt exceeds the 4,300-token on-device budget (𝐿 ≥ 250 for ECG, 𝐿 ≥ 1500 for EEG). Error bars show ± SD over five sweeps. Peak memory (Tables 1, 2) tracks the same token count.

Table 1. On-device context economics, EEG sleep staging (Sleep-EDF [34, 35], fixed raw sample, greedy, max 80 new tokens). The text and soft columns report only the time-series tokens. The full prompt adds a fixed ∼211-token pre/post scaffold shared by both arms. “n/a” marks a series whose full prompt exceeds the 4,300-token on-device budget and is skipped to avoid an uncatchable OS memory termination. TTFT is mean ± SD over five sweeps; peak memory varied by ≤ 3MiB across runs and is reported as the mean; soft-prompt tokens are injected embeddings, not vocabulary tokens.

Table 2. On-device context economics, 12-lead ECG (ECG-QA CoT [28], fixed bundled sample, greedy, max 80 new tokens). Columns as in Table 1 (time-series tokens; full prompt adds a fixed ∼533-token scaffold).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a soft-prompting approach for on-device time-series language models that significantly reduces the number of tokens required compared to text serialization, improving memory and context efficiency.
papers.title: PocketTSLM: Deploying an On-Device Soft-Prompt Time-Series Language Model for Privacy-Preserving Smartphone Reasoning
papers.tldr: PocketTSLM brings soft-prompt time-series language modeling to smartphones, enabling private on-device reasoning over physiological signals without transmitting health data.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.
authors: Siwei Cheng, Hao Wu, Zitong Qi, Xinming Zhang, Haoyu Xi, Peiran Yin, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: ReInsBench diagnoses how effectively vision-and-language navigators use historical observations through controlled continuation trials.
Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression removes temporal redundancy while preserving instruction-relevant visual context.
Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders prompt frozen navigators to revisit retained observations on a predefined schedule without extra model calls.
On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN reaches 64.27% and 64.44% success, improving over StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1 by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points.
Visual compression reduces prefill latency and KV-cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%; robot trials support broader sequential instruction-following use.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Overview of ReInsVLN. CIAC supports memory construction through Pre-LLM redundancy reduction and coverage-aware protection, followed by instruction-guided In-LLM token selection. FHR supports memory utilization by guiding the frozen navigator to revisit retained history through scheduled reminders, without additional model calls.

Fig. 2. Construction of ReInsBench. Episodes solved by exactly one of three frozen navigators contribute two unsuccessful rollouts each. Recorded prefixes are replayed to the state before the first disagreement with reference actions, yielding 812 model-specific checkpoints from 406 episodes. Matched continuations from each checkpoint compare neutral prompting (N) and history review with task restatement (R0); a 198-instance subset additionally includes controlled continuation without added text (B).

Fig. 5. Representative real-world navigation examples. Top: the Unitree G1 humanoid follows a sequence of landmark-dependent spatial instructions. Bottom: the Unitree Go2 quadruped navigates through repeated landmarks and stops beside the fifth potted plant in encounter order. Red text highlights instruction clauses, and numbered markers indicate the order of encountered plants.

Fig. 1. Navigation memory requires retaining and using relevant observations. Although the blue cabinet is no longer visible, its retained relation to the first armchair helps identify the next armchair as the stopping point.

Green and red spans mark revisited cues and unmet goals, ellipses mark omissions. Maps, cue diamonds, and goal stars are for illustration only, not navigator inputs or causal labels.

Fig. 6. Compression efficiency with reminders disabled. Bars are normalized to Native (100%): blue indicates compressed cost and gold indicates savings. Percentages report relative reductions; values below show Native → compressed means. Metrics are visual tokens after layer 20, LLM GPU prefill time, and end-of-call KV tensor storage excluding weights. Means cover 99 matched normal calls from 33 episodes, each repeated three times; each condition uses a distinct dedicated A100 40GB GPU.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free VLN with history compression and reminders, improving navigation while reducing KV cache; fits VLN, embodied memory, and token/cache efficiency.
papers.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: ReInsVLN is a training-free memory framework that compresses and periodically reactivates navigation history, improving VLN performance while reducing inference overhead.

papers.abstract: In this work, we address real-time fine-grained human activity recognition (HAR) in industrial assembly and introduce PDNet, a new framework that jointly exploits structured pruning and knowledge distillation for 3D convolutional networks. We start by training a 3D-CNN backbone in a supervised manner. Then, PDNet applies channel-wise structured pruning to obtain a more compact network. In the third step, our method is optimized using knowledge distillation from the large unpruned teacher to recover accuracy lost due to pruning. On the challenging MECCANO dataset with an X3D-M backbone, the pruned model without distillation reaches a Top-1 accuracy of 25.54 %, while PDNet raises this to 39.46 %, with only 6.90 MB model size and 3.78 GFLOPs. These results show that distillation within PDNet is highly effective in restoring pruned model performance and highlight its high potential for resource-constrained HAR in industrial assembly.
authors: Malek Baba, Thinesh Thiyakesan Ponbagavathi, Alina Roitberg
bullets: Targets real-time, fine-grained human activity recognition in industrial assembly.
Uses channel-wise structured pruning to reduce the 3D-CNN model, followed by distillation from the unpruned teacher.
On the MECCANO dataset with X3D-M, distillation improves Top-1 accuracy from 25.54% to 39.46% after pruning.
The resulting model is 6.90 MB with 3.78 GFLOPs, supporting resource-constrained deployment.
Scope is demonstrated on one dataset and backbone; broader generalization is not established in the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces PDNet, a framework that jointly exploits structured pruning and knowledge distillation for 3D CNNs in human activity recognition. This directly addresses efficiency in model size and computation.
papers.title: PDNet: Exploring Pruning and Distillation for Real-Time Worker Activity Recognition in Industrial Assembly
papers.tldr: PDNet combines structured pruning with knowledge distillation to make 3D-CNN-based industrial activity recognition more compact while recovering accuracy lost through pruning.

papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.
bullets: Targets the high cost of processing dense, long-form audio token sequences in Large Audio Language Models.
Scores tokens conditioned on the user’s question rather than relying on attention, similarity, or temporal-sampling heuristics.
Distills token rankings from a frozen LALM’s answer-gradient saliency and uses downstream answer supervision.
At 10% token retention, achieves the best or tied-best performance on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks.
Evaluated across speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification, among other tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Question-aware audio token pruning for large audio language models; directly fits token pruning/eviction and multimodal LLM efficiency.
papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.tldr: AudioScorer learns question-aware audio-token relevance to reduce LALM processing costs while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models enable parallel token generation, offering a promising alternative to sequential autoregressive decoding. Existing acceleration methods use predictive confidence to enable parallel token commitment while preserving generation quality. However, confidence-based selection prioritizes reliable token predictions without explicitly considering how token positions shape the remaining decoding schedule. Moreover, such ordering does not always reflect inter-token dependencies, suggesting that confidence need not be the sole criterion for token selection. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD), which favors central pivots within contiguous masked intervals and decodes the selected positions in parallel. Balanced pivots yield logarithmic decoding depth in the interval length. Our practical method accounts for model uncertainty by combining confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection. We evaluate the resulting quality-efficiency tradeoff on LLaDA and Dream across five mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DLM_random_pivot-EE62/
authors: Yejin Lee, Hyundong Jin, Yo-Sub Han
bullets: Confidence-only decoding overlooks the structure of remaining masked intervals and token dependencies.
BPD selects central pivots within contiguous masked spans, decoding selected positions in parallel.
Balanced pivoting provides logarithmic decoding depth with respect to interval length.
The practical strategy combines confidence-based prefilling with confidence-thresholded center selection.
Evaluated on LLaDA and Dream across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Balance-Aware Pivot Decoding (BPD). BPD first commits high-confidence tokens in parallel, then selects one pivot per remaining masked interval. It favors the most central confidence-eligible position to promote balanced splits and reduce decoding depth.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Recent methods explore step-level signals such as attention mass and step entropy to identify and suppress unnecessary steps. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. Experiments across two model scales and nine benchmarks show that IGPO achieves up to 62% average token reduction and better overall performance among compared methods.
authors: Guanda Li, Xuefeng Bai, Yulong Chen, Zhiyong Wang, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang
bullets: Long reasoning traces often mix useful and redundant intermediate steps.
Existing step signals describe model behavior but not each step’s causal contribution to the answer.
Interventional Step Credit (ISC) estimates step importance through targeted parameter-level interventions.
IGPO uses ISC to rescale reinforcement-learning advantages at fine granularity.
Across two model scales and nine benchmarks, IGPO reduces average tokens by up to 62% while improving overall performance versus compared methods.
