papers.selection_reason: Reduces redundant chain-of-thought steps in large reasoning models via interventional step credit, directly relevant to efficient LLM reasoning.
papers.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
papers.tldr: IGPO uses causal, intervention-based step credit to shorten chain-of-thought reasoning while preserving important steps and improving performance.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) supervises student-generated trajectories with a reference-conditioned version of the same base model. We ask whether every trajectory supplies distinct supervision that warrants its distillation cost. Gradient measurements on Qwen3-1.7B at initialization reveal that correct and incorrect responses have similar individual gradient magnitudes, but incorrect responses have approximately three times the coherent gradient share. Their estimated population-mean directions also largely overlap. A signal--noise model fitted at a small group size tracks alignment at larger group sizes without refitting. Motivated by these measurements, we introduce correctness-filtered OPSD (C-OPSD), which generates one response per problem and distills only a subset of incorrect responses. Removing unselected rows before both distillation forwards avoids their teacher/student forward and student backward work. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, C-OPSD achieves on-par performance with full OPSD. In a measured micro-batch-size-four implementation, executed rows decrease by approximately 68%, and with retained rows packed into full micro-batches, training takes about 40% less time while rollout generation remains unchanged. Together, the measurements and training results connect outcome-conditioned supervision redundancy to more compute-efficient distillation.
authors: Harrison Zhao, Lei Huang, Fei Liu, Wen Shi, Zijian Jin
bullets: Incorrect responses provide more coherent gradient signal than correct responses despite similar individual gradient magnitudes, suggesting supervision redundancy.
C-OPSD generates one response per problem and distills only a selected subset of incorrect responses.
Filtering rows before teacher/student forwards and student backpropagation reduces executed rows by approximately 68%.
Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, C-OPSD performs on par with full OPSD.
With packed retained rows, training takes about 40% less time; rollout generation is unchanged.

papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache is the main memory bottleneck of long-context LLM inference. Token eviction methods such as SnapKV, H2O, AdaKV and L2Norm shrink it, but they give every transformer layer the same budget, although layers differ in which tokens they need. We present MOSAIC, a multi-objective neural architecture search that learns per-layer KV-cache budgets for any eviction method. One search maps the trade-off between average budget and task score; its best allocation transfers to every target budget without further search, and an optional budget-constrained search refines it. Across four eviction methods on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, MOSAIC beats uniform allocation in 146 of 154 (task, method, budget) settings, by up to +48 points on RULER and +11.9 on LongBench (LCC). On both models, it reaches the score of uniform allocation with up to 4x less KV cache (75% smaller). Against EvolKV, MOSAIC explores a ~10^40 x larger search space with 4x fewer evaluations and 18% fewer GPU-hours per budget, and scores higher in 5 of 6 settings. The learned allocations consistently favour a small set of middle layers.
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of assigning every transformer layer the same KV-cache budget despite differing token needs.
Uses multi-objective neural architecture search to find per-layer allocations compatible with existing eviction methods.
A single search captures the budget–task-score trade-off and transfers across target budgets; an optional constrained search further refines allocations.
Across four eviction methods and two LLMs, it outperforms uniform allocation in 146 of 154 evaluated settings and can match uniform performance with up to 75% less cache.
Allocations consistently concentrate cache on a small set of middle layers; compared with EvolKV, MOSAIC searches a much larger space with fewer evaluations and GPU-hours.

Stage 4 optionally refines each budget with constrained BO seeded by the rescaled winner. Bar profiles are schematic.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face significant scalability challenges in long-video understanding due to quadratic attention complexity and context window constraints. Existing retrieval-based approaches typically rely on supervised learning from static keyframe annotations. However, these label priors often fail to align with the actual information required by downstream MLLMs for complex reasoning, creating a misalignment between the training target and inference needs. To bridge this gap, we propose a probabilistic framework that reformulates frame selection as latent-variable inference. We first initialize a lightweight policy using supervised learning to capture general visual saliency. Then, we treat a frozen MLLM as a task environment and use its answer likelihood as dense task evidence to refine the policy via Bayesian Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Within this formulation, the negative log-likelihood (NLL) over ground-truth answer tokens provides a principled dense reward, while a prior-matching KL term preserves semantic consistency with the elicited label prior. This process transitions the selection principle from static label priors to task evidence. Extensive experiments on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench demonstrate that our selector achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based scorers while retaining the inference efficiency of lightweight methods. The selector is trained once with a frozen MLLM environment and transfers directly to multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining. Code is available at \url{github.com/Miraclecsc/Frame_Selection_GRPO}.
authors: Shuochen Chang, Bingjie Gao, Qingyang Liu, Qianli Ma, Yibo Miao, Haonan Zhao, Zhaohe Liao, Xiaofeng Zhang, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static keyframe-label supervision and the evidence needed for complex downstream reasoning.
Initializes a lightweight saliency policy with supervised learning, then refines it against a frozen MLLM environment.
Uses answer-token negative log-likelihood as a dense reward and a KL term to preserve consistency with the learned prior.
Achieves competitive accuracy with MLLM-based frame scorers while retaining lightweight inference efficiency on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench.
The selector is trained once and transfers across multiple downstream MLLMs without retraining.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The overall framework of our methods. (a) Keyframe Selector. The lightweight selector (fθ) comprises stacked Video-Text Fusion Transformers. It modulates frame features with query semantics to output importance logits, then parameterizing a Plackett-Luce distribution. (b) Stage I: Label Prior Elicitation. We utilize keyframe label annotations to construct a Label Prior. The selector is trained via pairwise ranking loss to align its predicted logits with the label logits, establishing a robust initialization. (c) Stage II:Task-Evidence Posterior Inference. We freeze the MLLM and treat it as a frozen task environment. The selector performs Group Sampling to propose discrete frame subsets (z). The MLLM evaluates these subsets to provide dense NLL rewards (R) and advantages (A). The policy is refined via Bayesian GRPO to maximize task evidence while maintaining KL-regularization towards the label prior.

papers.abstract: Understanding when during a video a model makes its critical observations is essential for interpreting video-understanding systems. However, existing attribution methods often spread evidence diffusely across near-duplicate frames. We introduce Sufficient Frame Subsets: compact sets of frames in which all other frames are masked, yet each subset independently preserves the model's prediction. We evaluate our method on two complementary benchmarks, UCF101 and Something-Something v2, using both CNN- and transformer-based architectures. Our results show that the proposed algorithm identifies highly compact and effective frame subsets for explaining model decisions. We also find that models capable of relying on a greater number of sufficient frame subsets tend to perform better, possibly because they are more robust, consistent with prior research. Finally, the extracted frame subsets help us analyze model failure cases, reveal which aspects of a video the model has learned to emphasize, and identify opportunities for improving future training procedures.
bullets: Addresses diffuse attribution across near-duplicate frames in video understanding.
Masks all frames outside each candidate subset and tests whether the prediction is preserved.
Evaluated on UCF101 and Something-Something v2 with CNN- and transformer-based models.
Finds highly compact, effective subsets and links reliance on more sufficient subsets with better model performance.
Supports failure analysis, inspection of learned visual emphasis, and future training improvements.

papers.abstract: We show that a video can be represented with just a few keyframes without sacrificing a given model's belief about the video. Our method is the first of its kind that extracts these keyframes conditioned on the model's prediction, which is massively helpful for building explainable video models. We then fairly distribute the importance of the video to the model among the keyframes with game theoretically fair Shapley values. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that keyframe attribution is superior to the traditional frame attribution. Further, we conduct preliminary exploration on highlighting the important changes among the frames by looking at the differences between adjacent keyframes.
bullets: Extracts keyframes conditioned on the model’s prediction.
Represents videos with few keyframes without changing the model’s belief.
Uses game-theoretic Shapley values to distribute importance fairly across keyframes.
Experiments show keyframe attribution outperforms traditional frame attribution.
Also explores highlighting important changes between adjacent keyframes.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. We show that this coupling breaks an intrinsic inference pattern in MLLMs. Through layer-wise attention analysis, we identify \textbf{Visual Backtracking}: visual pivots remain spatially stable, yet in middle layers they actively retrieve context from tokens that appeared unimportant earlier. Thus, early low-saliency tokens can be inactive for computation while still being useful for later reasoning. Motivated by this finding, we propose \textbf{ReTrace}, a backtracking-aware compression framework that introduces a dormant token state. ReTrace caches non-pivot tokens outside expensive layer-wise computation, restores them during the backtracking window, and prunes only after their information has been absorbed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 demonstrate nearly 90\% reductions in FLOPs and KV cache, a 2.83$\times$ prefilling speedup, and strong performance retention across complex vision-language benchmarks.
authors: Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Yifan Yu, Miao Liu, Panwang Pan, Wentao Zhu
bullets: Visual token compression can harm reasoning by permanently deleting tokens that appear unimportant in early layers.
Layer-wise analysis reveals visual backtracking: stable visual pivots later retrieve context from previously low-saliency tokens.
ReTrace adds a dormant token state, caching non-pivot tokens outside expensive computation and restoring them during a backtracking window.
Tokens are pruned only after their information has been absorbed, preserving more visual context for reasoning.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 report nearly 90% lower FLOPs and KV-cache usage, a 2.83× prefilling speedup, and strong benchmark performance retention.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overall architecture of ReTrace. ReTrace follows a cache–inject–prune schedule. (1) Pivot Buffer Construction builds a compact active receiver buffer at the encoder output while caching the remaining tokens as dormant context. (2) Backtracking-Aware Context Injection restores the missing pivot-to-context retrieval route at the backtracking layer through similarity-based routing. (3) Post-Absorption Task Pruning removes task-irrelevant enriched pivots after context absorption.

papers.abstract: Weather transformers process dense reanalysis fields whose reliability varies across variables, locations, and weather regimes. Token merging can reduce computation, but feature similarity alone does not account for this heterogeneous input uncertainty. We introduce UtoMe, an observation-uncertainty-guided token merging framework that combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data assimilation spread as a relative input-reliability proxy. The resulting importance score protects selected tokens as anchors and calibrates bipartite matching between the remaining tokens. Three variants use external uncertainty at both training and inference, during training only, or neither stage. In ERA5 72-hour forecasting at two spatial resolutions, UtoMe improves Overall error over train-time ToMe at matched token budgets. At $1.40625^\circ$ and 50% token reduction, UtoMe-E lowers Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at the same 0.55x encoder FLOPs. Small reductions remain close to the full-token baseline; larger reductions incur measurable accuracy losses. Component ablations and spatial uncertainty controls support combining dynamics with aligned uncertainty when allocating a weather transformer's token budget.
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Janet Wang, Xi Xiao, Jihun Hamm, Xiao Wang
bullets: Weather inputs have heterogeneous reliability, which similarity-only token merging does not capture.
UtoMe combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data-assimilation spread to score token importance and protect anchor tokens.
It supports uncertainty use during both training and inference, training only, or neither.
In ERA5 72-hour forecasting, UtoMe-E reduced Overall error from 67.32 to 53.00 at 50% token reduction and 0.55× encoder FLOPs.
Accuracy remains near the full-token baseline for small reductions but declines at larger compression levels.

figures.caption: Figure 1: UtoMe overview. UtoMe uses observation uncertainty to guide training-time token merging for transformer-based weather forecasting. It first turns weather-state saliency and low observation uncertainty into a patch-level token score, then uses that score to protect forecast-sensitive anchors and merge lower-importance redundant tokens. The framework supports three uncertainty-availability regimes: external uncertainty at both stages, during training only, or neither stage.

Figure 2: 5.625◦ case summary. The figure shows the complete merge-decision pipeline: weather state, observation uncertainty, dynamics saliency, importance score, patch-level token score, and the final anchor or merge-candidate overlay.

Figure 3: 1.40625◦ high-resolution case study. The observation-uncertainty field contains coherent bands and high-spread structures. After saliency combination and patch aggregation, these structures produce a heterogeneous token score for uncertainty-guided merging.

Figure 4: Cosine-only matching can select merge edges in high-importance regions because feature similarity alone does not encode observation uncertainty. UtoMe protects anchors and penalizes importance-incompatible pairs, shifting the merge budget toward lower-importance regions.

Figure 7: Predictor visualization for UtoMe-P and UtoMe-S. The learned predictors recover the broad spatial structure of their supervision targets, which explains why the predictor-based variants remain close to UtoMe-E in the main results.

Figure 9: Additional 1.40625◦ case study. The panels show how a high-resolution weather state and its aligned observation-uncertainty field are converted into the importance and token-score maps used by UtoMe.
Figure 8: Additional anchor and merge-candidate overlay at 5.625◦. Blue squares denote merge candidates and black squares denote anchors selected from the patch-level token score.

Figure 5: Motivation for uncertainty-guided token merging at 1.40625◦. The observationuncertainty field is not uniform noise; it contains coherent spatial structure. After patch aggregation and combination with dynamics saliency, the token-score grid separates low-uncertainty high-saliency regions from high-spread merge candidates.

Figure 6: Additional importance-score decomposition. From left to right, the figure shows the input weather state, dynamics saliency, observation uncertainty, teacher importance, and predicted importance for a held-out 5.625◦ case.

papers.abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) have shown strong performance on dynamic graph learning tasks by continuously updating node memories from evolving interactions (i.e., events) and leveraging these memories for downstream predictions. As graphs grow rapidly in modern applications, training requires processing an increasing number of events; meanwhile, each event can update node memories used by later events, creating dependencies that constrain parallel execution and limit the benefits of additional computing resources. These costs motivate an upstream question: Are all events, and the dependencies they introduce, necessary for learning? We investigate this question through two roles of temporal events: prediction targets and historical events sampled as inputs. We observe that targets involving stable node memories tend to exhibit lower prediction loss, while filtering historical events associated with stable memories can retain similar training-loss trajectories in several evaluated settings. Together, these observations suggest an opportunity to identify input redundancy through changes in node memories. Building on this opportunity, we propose RAFT, a redundancy-aware input-filtering framework for TGNN training. RAFT tracks memory changes during training and uses them to guide two filters: a root-event filter removes selected prediction targets before training, and a support-event filter excludes selected historical context during sampling. Filtering inputs before their downstream preparation and processing reduces the work they trigger. Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%, while reducing recorded training time by up to 52.56\% with negligible changes to model precisions.
authors: Yue Dai, Sarah Zhou, Youtao Zhang
bullets: TGNN training becomes costly because rapidly growing event streams create sequential memory dependencies that limit parallelism.
RAFT identifies redundancy through the stability of node memories associated with prediction targets and historical inputs.
A root-event filter removes selected prediction targets, while a support-event filter excludes redundant historical context during sampling.
Across three TGNN models and five datasets, RAFT reduces training inputs by 35.23% on average and up to 97.11%.
Recorded training time falls by up to 52.56% with negligible changes to model precision.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a redundancy-aware input filtering framework for training Temporal Graph Neural Networks. This falls under Efficient AI (Token Pruning and Eviction) and offers a method to reduce computational load in dynamic graph learning, which is transferable to other sequential data processing tasks.
papers.title: RAFT: Redundancy-Aware Input Filtering for Temporal Graph Neural Network Training
papers.tldr: RAFT accelerates temporal graph neural network training by filtering redundant target and historical events based on node-memory changes, substantially reducing processing with negligible precision loss.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning aims to reduce inference cost while preserving the capabilities of the original VLM. Yet existing evaluations rely on aggregate task accuracy and retained token count as proxies for pruning quality and actual efficiency. We reveal two limitations: 1) Aggregate accuracy can obscure whether a pruning method truly identifies critical visual tokens; many examples remain solvable under arbitrary token removal and models can exploit textual shortcuts when visual evidence is degraded. 2) Retained token count is an unreliable proxy for efficiency, as identical token budgets can incur different end-to-end costs depending on where and how pruning is performed. Consequently, comparisons based on aggregate accuracy and retained token counts fail to recover the global performance-efficiency Pareto frontier across methods. We introduce PAA-Bench, a plug-and-play evaluation framework for existing benchmarks, to evaluate whether pruning succeeds through meaningful token selection and whether this success translates into real speedup. To determine when token choice actually matters, we propose Random-Pass@k to measure how often an example remains correct under random pruning, enabling comprehensive evaluation across different levels of selection difficulty. To compare efficiency fairly, we introduce Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) to report the maximum end-to-end speedup each method achieves under a shared preservation target. Experiments across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks show that stronger token compression does not necessarily yield greater speedup, method differences widen on examples where token selection matters, and efficiency rankings change with the preservation target.
authors: Geng Li, Guohao Chen, Shilin Shan, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Aggregate accuracy can hide arbitrary token removal and reliance on textual shortcuts.
Equal retained-token budgets can produce different real inference costs depending on pruning location and procedure.
Random-Pass@k measures how often examples remain correct under random pruning, revealing when token selection matters.
Preservation-Constrained Speedup (PCS) compares maximum end-to-end speedup at a shared preservation target.
Across 8 methods, 3 VLM backbones, and 9 benchmarks, compression strength, speedup, and method rankings do not consistently align.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.
authors: Lei Tian, Chunzheng Zhu, Kai Wu, Yifan Zhang, Haihua Yang
bullets: Native MLLMs tokenize image patches directly, creating substantial visual-token redundancy that existing ViT-oriented compression methods do not address.
Analysis finds redundancy is heterogeneous and independently distributed across height and width, while early-layer tokens are broadly indiscriminable.
PACE estimates direction-aware spatial importance by decoupling Multimodal-RoPE attention along height and width with negligible overhead.
It allocates token budgets through Pareto optimization across performance, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage.
Experiments report near-lossless performance at 25–50% visual-token retention, with improvements on several benchmarks and over 2× FLOPs reduction.

papers.abstract: Long video understanding requires VideoLLMs to answer queries about videos spanning tens of minutes to hours, but such long videos produce far more visual tokens than current VideoLLMs can process. To address this issue, keyframe selectors are proposed to select the most query-relevant frames by computing the similarity between frame and query embeddings. Existing selectors either encode frames independently without temporal context or process chunks in isolation with ranking objectives that are difficult to optimize. To alleviate those limitations, we propose FrameScout with two core designs: (i) a streaming selector architecture that leverages a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to produce temporally-contextualized frame embeddings; (ii) a frame-query contrastive objective that aligns frame and query embeddings in a shared space, directly training the selector to distinguish relevant frames from irrelevant ones. Extensive experiments on three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs demonstrate that FrameScout consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Hubert-1102/FrameScout.
authors: Haonan Hu, Shuhao Chen, Weisen Jiang, Lizhao Gao, James Kwok, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets the excessive visual-token cost of videos lasting tens of minutes to hours.
Uses a sliding-window KV cache and successor aggregation to encode frames with temporal context.
Trains frame and query embeddings with a contrastive objective to distinguish relevant from irrelevant frames.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance across three long-video benchmarks and six base VideoLLMs.
Scope: focuses on query-guided frame selection for long-video question answering.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning is increasingly used to reduce the memory and inference costs of vision-language models. Existing work has largely focused on designing method-specific selectors and demonstrating incremental improvements over prior methods at selected token budgets. It remains unclear whether the resulting performance reflects an inherent limit of visual token pruning or the limitations of current token-selection algorithms. We take a complementary perspective and ask: \emph{how well can visual token pruning perform when offline search cost is not the primary constraint?} We formulate pruning for general image understanding as selecting, under a fixed budget, one shared visual-token subset that supports a broad distribution of questions about an image. We approximate this utility with a finite auxiliary QA set generated by a frontier VLM and optimize a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen. Motivated by the conceptual monotonicity and diminishing returns of adding visual evidence, we construct nested subsets greedily and introduce \emph{QA mini-batch greedy} (QA-MBG), which estimates token marginal gains from randomly sampled QA components at each step. Empirically, QA-MBG is both cheaper and more effective than full greedy. With one frontier-VLM call and approximately $0.5$ H100 GPU-hours per image, it produces a nested subset trajectory covering keep ratios up to $0.3$. Across Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma~4 E4B on $900$ images from nine benchmarks, we find significant headroom over evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation, while the searched subsets substantially narrow the gap to full-token inference.
authors: Janghoon Cho, Shubhankar Borse, Reza Pourreza, Juntae Lee, Jihwan Bang, Munawar Hayat, Fatih Porikli
bullets: Frames pruning as selecting one shared, fixed-budget visual-token subset per image for diverse downstream questions.
Uses auxiliary QA generated by a frontier VLM and a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen.
Introduces QA mini-batch greedy, which builds nested subsets by estimating token gains from sampled QA components.
On Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma 4 E4B across 900 images from nine benchmarks, searched subsets outperform evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation.
Scope: optimization requires substantial offline computation—one frontier-VLM call and about 0.5 H100 GPU-hours per image—and covers keep ratios up to 0.3.

papers.abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
bullets: KV-cache memory grows with context length, while existing non-uniform head compression methods can be unstable across workloads.
The method finds that active-head composition shifts between prefill and decode but remains stable across later content tokens after filtering format tokens.
PeekKV performs a one-token peek to jointly score head groups and token importance, then allocates cache budgets and retains the highest-scoring tokens.
It applies directly to unseen workloads and models because it requires neither offline profiling nor additional training.
Across four benchmarks, it is closest to full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench; reported retention reaches 95.7% and 95.9% of full-cache accuracy at low memory budgets on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models(VLMs)have advanced Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) by enabling OCR-free, multi-vector representations. However, these models generate excessive tokens to preserve dense visual details, which severely limits retrieval scalability. Existing compression methods mitigate this overhead but rely on isolated heuristics that fail to balance token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage capacity. We propose a visual token compression framework formulated as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem. Our approach unifies these three objectives into a single alternating optimization process. Furthermore, we theoretically show that minimizing the transport cost upper-bounds the MaxSim retrieval error, ensuring ranking stability. Extensive experiments on the ViDoRe V1 and V3 benchmarks demonstrate that our method preserves fine-grained document semantics and improves the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off over state-of-the-art base-lines. Code is available at https://github.com/shhhhhyy/Unbalanced-Optimal-Transport-for-EVDR.
authors: Hoyeon Shin, Jeongyeon Kim, Yeong Jun Koh, Yeoneung Kim, Hanul Kim
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem caused by excessive tokens in OCR-free, multi-vector VLM-based visual document retrieval.
Formulates token compression as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport problem balancing token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage.
Uses alternating optimization to jointly optimize these compression objectives.
Provides a theoretical guarantee that lower transport cost bounds MaxSim retrieval error, supporting ranking stability.
Experiments on ViDoRe V1 and V3 show a better efficiency–effectiveness trade-off than existing baselines while retaining fine-grained semantics.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing inference-time visual token pruning methods often irreversibly remove low-ranked tokens, although the set of visual tokens receiving high query-conditioned attention can change across decoder depth. Recoverable routing preserves skipped tokens for later reconsideration, but re-admits them with stale representations after bypassing intermediate transformations. We further find that replacing stale re-admitted states with their current-depth oracle states from a full-token reference trajectory substantially improves grounding performance. We therefore propose CatchUp, a training-free framework for depth-aware visual-token re-admission. CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned visual relevance, processes only selected visual tokens through each decoder interval, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission. Upon re-admission, CatchUp approximates missed representation evolution using reference-to-current transition signals from semantically and spatially related visual tokens. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention in both benchmark groups at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget with 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, CatchUp retains 92.17% of the full model's performance on average across six multimodal benchmarks while reducing end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp
bullets: Problem: Irreversible visual-token pruning can discard tokens that become relevant later, while recoverable routing may re-admit them with stale representations.
Method: Re-evaluates query-conditioned token relevance at each decoder interval, processes only selected tokens, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission.
Key idea: Uses transition signals from semantically and spatially related tokens to approximate the representation evolution missed by skipped tokens.
Results: Across three grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets.
At 64 tokens, it uses 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, retains 92.17% of full-model performance on average, and reduces end-to-end latency by 8.0%.

papers.abstract: Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST (Brain-Encoding-Speech-Text), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources. On the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural-audio-text alignment pathway.
authors: Zehui Feng, Weichuan Wang, Xiaohan Chen, Cuntai Guan, Ting Han
bullets: Speech BCI data are scarce, noisy, and costly, making the value of model scaling uncertain.
BEST uses two stages with hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that maps neural activity to text.
It reports 6.19% and 1.62% WER on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks, respectively, using 3.85% of the parameters of comparable methods.
The study finds that decoder scaling has non-monotonic benefits, cross-modal alignment matters more than model size, and overfitting harms sequence-level performance.
Representation analysis indicates a consistent neural–audio–text alignment pathway, supporting efficient deployment in low-resource settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall illustration of BEST. papers.abstract: Visual information worth extracting from an image and the token budget it warrants depend on the text query. Yet modern vision and vision-language models largely encode images independently of the query and allocate a fixed visual token budget to every input. We introduce the Query-Adaptive Recurrent Tokenizer (QART), a backbone-agnostic module that makes visual representations both query-steerable and budget-adaptive. QART steers the visual representation toward query-relevant evidence while adapting its token budget to the amount of information required. Its key principle is simple. Additional tokens are allocated until the visual features relevant to the query are represented with sufficient fidelity. Starting from frozen encoder features, QART recurrently constructs a compact representation and uses reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support to control token allocation. On Visual7W and VQAv2, QART achieves 81.96% and 76.37% accuracy using only about 29 visual tokens, reducing token counts by 20-25x relative to dense VLM inputs. It further reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%. Together, these results show that visual representations need not be fixed in either content or capacity and can instead adapt to what each query requires.
authors: Bavesh Balaji, Pranav Gopinath, Pouya Sadeghi, Sirisha Rambhatla
bullets: Addresses fixed, query-independent visual representations and token budgets in vision-language models.
Uses frozen encoder features and recurrently builds a compact representation steered toward query-relevant evidence.
Controls token allocation through reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support.
Achieves 81.96% on Visual7W and 76.37% on VQAv2 with 20–25× fewer tokens than dense inputs.
Also reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of QART. Given an image and a text query, frozen encoders provide visual and linguistic features V and T respectively. A relevance module Hϕ selects query-relevant patches VA; QART then recurrently refines a small set of query-conditioned slots S by passing them along with VA and T to the shared transformer Fθ. After each round r, a shared decoder Dψ reconstructs the visual features, and reconstruction quality determines whether more slots are added or recurrence halts. Only slot states propagate across rounds.

Figure 1: QART combines query steerability with budget adaptivity. Fixed patch tokenizers use the same representation and token budget for every query. Adaptive tokenizers change how many tokens are allocated, while steerable methods change what visual information is emphasized. QART does both, steering the representation toward the query while adapting its capacity to the required visual evidence. The clear regions represent the tokenizers’ focus.

Figure 4: Recurrent refinement and inference efficiency. (a) QART’s recurrence refines representations even upon disabling token growth. (b–c) The compact visual sequence increasingly improves throughput and language-model prefill as batch size grows.

Figure 3: QART steers visual representations while preserving transferable visual information. (a) On CORE, QART redirects visual representations toward queried content. (b) The same representation transfers zero-shot to natural images on GeneCIS without dataset-specific tuning. (c) Replacing the sample-specific query with fixed conditioning substantially degrades Winoground performance. (d) On PODS, coarse conditioning preserves fine-grained instance information beyond the prompt.

Figure 5: Representation refinement across recurrent rounds. Each row shows the spatial support of an active QART slot over successive rounds for a different query. The support progressively shifts toward the query-relevant region, including the foreground backpack, the person in plaid, and jersey number 13.

Figure 7: QART adapts its token budget across image–query pairs. Representative examples span the allocation range from K = 2 to K = 32. Localized queries can be represented with only a few active tokens, while broader or more spatially distributed visual evidence receives a larger representation.

Table 1: Reasoning and grounding under aggressive visual compression. QART preserves strong downstream performance with approximately 29 visual tokens on both VQAv2 and Visual7W. Visual7W additionally reports the average token count processed across language-model layers for methods that prune within the LLM.
Table 3: Data mixture used for QART pretraining. VG is separated into native Visual Genome images and images overlapping with COCO.

Table 2: Ablation of the two roles of query conditioning in QART on CORE. Query conditioning helps steer the visual support used during recurrence and independently control the evidence used for slot growth and halting.
Table 4: VQAv2 results for QART with SigLIP2 and DINOv2 visual backbones. Both variants use the same LLaVA-1.5-7B integration and projector-training protocol.

Table 5: Sensitivity to the relevance threshold. Lower thresholds generally increase the selected visual support, but performance does not vary monotonically with the resulting token budget. Mean K denotes the average number of active QART slots.

papers.selection_reason: Query-adaptive recurrent token allocation for efficient VLM inference.
papers.title: Query-adaptive Recurrent Tokenization
papers.tldr: QART makes visual tokenization query-aware and dynamically allocates only as many tokens as each query requires, achieving strong performance with about 29 tokens.

papers.abstract: Token merging improves the efficiency of Vision Transformers by combining redundant tokens, but existing methods largely rely on feature similarity to determine which tokens to merge. This criterion is effective for semantic segmentation, yet can fail in instance segmentation, where adjacent objects of the same class often have highly similar features. We identify this failure mode as cross-instance token fusion. We introduce MaskMerge, an instance-aware token merging method that uses coarse intermediate mask predictions to constrain feature-based merging and preserve instance boundaries. We evaluate MaskMerge on two diverse instance segmentation domains characterized by high inter-instance visual similarity: PanNuke and iSAID. Against the SOTA token merging method ALGM, MaskMerge improves mAP from 30.1 to 32.1 on PanNuke while reducing computation from 229 to 153 GFLOPs and running 1.18x faster, and from 33.1 to 36.2 on iSAID while reducing computation from 198 to 182 GFLOPs and running 1.23x faster. Additionally, we also test it on Cityscapes and match ALGM's performance while using fewer FLOPs. The gains also transfer to an MAE pretrained backbone, demonstrating that instance-aware merging enables more aggressive compression when appearance similarity alone cannot reliably preserve object identity.
authors: Bavesh Balaji, Letian Jiang, Alexander Wong, David Clausi, Sirisha Rambhatla
bullets: Feature-similarity merging can blur boundaries between adjacent same-class instances, causing cross-instance token fusion.
MaskMerge constrains feature-based token merging with intermediate mask predictions to preserve instance identities.
On PanNuke and iSAID, it improves mAP while reducing computation and increasing speed relative to ALGM.
On Cityscapes, it matches ALGM’s performance with fewer FLOPs.
The approach also transfers to an MAE-pretrained backbone, supporting more aggressive compression when appearance similarity is ambiguous.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overall pipeline of MaskMerge. Given an input image I ∈ RH×W , the standard patch tokens X0 ∈ RN×D of the image are initially passed through L1 layers of the transformer encoder. After that, similar tokens within a small neighbourhood are merged together using the local merge module resulting in X′ L1 ∈ N′ × D where N ′ < N . After this, the model is passed through Lm transformer layers to get X′ Lm where our object-level adaptive token merging (OLAM) module further reduces tokens from N ′ to N ′′ while preserving instance identities. These reduced tokens are prcoessed by the rest of the transformer encoder layers and then unmerged back to the original dimensions before being fed to the segmentation head.

Figure 2. Cross-instance token fusion in similarity-based token merging. (a) ALGM frequently merges tokens across different nuclei instances, whereas MaskMerge constrains merges within predicted instances. (b) At the same merge budget, ALGM produces 5.7× and 2.9× more cross-instance merges than MaskMerge on PanNuke [17] and iSAID [62], respectively, demonstrating that instance-aware constraints enable safer token reduction.

Figure 1. Throughput–accuracy Pareto frontier on PanNuke [17] across ViT-S, ViT-B, and ViT-L backbones. MaskMerge consistently achieves a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than ToMe [1] and ALGM [43] across model scales, indicating that instance-aware merging enables more aggressive token reduction while better preserving instance segmentation accuracy.

papers.title: MaskMerge: Structure-aware Token Merging for Efficient Instance Segmentation
papers.tldr: MaskMerge makes token merging more efficient for instance segmentation by using coarse masks to prevent tokens from different objects being fused.

papers.abstract: Speed-limit sign recognition on an automotive camera system-on-chip (SoC) must fit a detector and a classifier (the reader) into the memory, arithmetic, and energy budgets of the device. In our two-stage recognizer, the detector, a YOLO-family network with ReLU and hard-sigmoid operators, is compressed by channel replay: an iterative pruning cascade identifies the channels to remove, the recorded deletions are replayed on the original task-trained network, the parent, and one continuous knowledge-distillation recovery follows. On a YOLOv5n, replay removes 60.3% of the parameters at the accuracy of the parent and, in validation mAP50-95 over five matched seeds, outperforms iterative pruning and training from scratch, and its per-step variant (per-step replay) is the most accurate pruning method. On a YOLOv8n, replay and per-step replay outperform every other method and the unpruned parent. The reader, a five-layer CNN with 18k parameters, and the post-processing of the YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n heads use integer arithmetic only. With 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations (W4A8), the reader matches FP32 accuracy in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory, and an executable streaming model reproduces the INT8 class predictions of its runtime on all 9,850 test crops. On a Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only in the implicit formulation of TensorRT, and the replay detector runs fastest on the deep-learning accelerator (DLA). Trained on public data only, the combined system of 0.72 M parameters recognizes 95.2% of the signs of a held-out automotive camera at 90% precision and 94 frames per second.
authors: Se Un Park, Kyungkeon Chung, Huigeol Kim, Junyoung Park
bullets: Channel replay removes 60.3% of YOLOv5n parameters while maintaining parent accuracy; replay variants outperform competing pruning methods on YOLOv5n and YOLOv8n.
A five-layer, 18k-parameter reader achieves FP32-equivalent accuracy with 4-bit weights and 8-bit activations in 12.1 KB of on-chip memory.
Integer-only post-processing and reader inference support executable streaming deployment, reproducing runtime INT8 predictions on all 9,850 test crops.
The combined 0.72M-parameter system reaches 95.2% sign recognition at 90% precision and 94 frames per second on a held-out automotive camera.
On Jetson AGX Orin, INT8 is faster than FP16 only for TensorRT’s implicit formulation; replay detection runs fastest on the DLA.

Marker shape gives the width M (the five layers have M , 2M , 2M , 4M , and 8M channels, the suffix h halves the last layer, 4.7k to 240k parameters) and marker color the precision, where sh. denotes power-of-two scales. Filled markers are QAT and hollow markers PTQ, with three seeds per point. The dashed line is the reader of width 8h in FP32 (90.5±0.3%), the deployed width.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes replay pruning and few-bit integer inference for hardware-efficient speed-sign recognition, relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Replay Pruning and Few-Bit Integer Inference for Hardware-Efficient Speed-Sign Recognition
papers.tldr: A replay-pruned detector and few-bit integer reader enable accurate, real-time speed-sign recognition within automotive SoC memory and compute constraints.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) for visual question answering (VQA) often pass long visual-token sequences to the language model, making visual-token pruning attractive but risky for medical images, where answers may depend on localized boundary and texture evidence. We study training free pre-decoding pruning and treat pruning as a subspace stable evidence preservation problem. The retained tokens should remain close to the dominant visual evidence subspace induced by the full token set. To this end, we propose \emph{Subspace-Transition Token Pruning} (\method{}), which estimates each token's spectral support from principal component space and constructs a compact representation subspace. To better reflect medical image structure, \method{} further uses a bounded token-grid transition prior to promote boundary and texture sensitive tokens. We evaluate \method{} on the closed-ended SLAKE and OmniMedVQA benchmarks and on RadImageNet-VQA, which provides both closed-ended and open-ended evaluations, using Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones. \method{} delivers consistently strong performance on both the closed-ended and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations. These results show that \method{} is an effective training free pruning framework for medical domain VQA.
authors: Mengchen Fan, Qizhen Lan, Xi Xiao, Lin Zhao, Liang He, Tianyang Wang, Xiaoqian Jiang, Pulin Che, Baocheng Geng
bullets: Medical VQA often uses long visual-token sequences, but pruning can remove localized evidence needed for accurate answers.
MedSTP estimates tokens’ support in principal-component space to preserve the dominant visual evidence subspace.
A bounded token-grid transition prior promotes tokens capturing medical-image boundaries and textures.
Evaluated on SLAKE, OmniMedVQA, and RadImageNet-VQA with Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B.
It shows consistently strong performance on both closed- and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MedSTP for medical VQA token pruning. Given a medical image-question input, the frozen VLM encoder produces visual tokens before decoding. MedSTP constructs a compact retained subspace from principal projection participation and incorporates a bounded token-grid transition multiplier. The selected compact subset is passed to the frozen VQA decoder for answer prediction.

Figure 5. VQA accuracy under increasing pruning strength with Lingshu-7B. All methods use matched pruning insertion points and fixed visual-token budgets. Dashed horizontal lines denote full-token accuracy.

Figure 1. Qualitative comparison under the same compact token budget. The dashed red circle marks the relevant abnormal region; MedSTP keeps boundary and texture evidence that generic pruning may miss.

Figure 4. As retained-token budgets shrink, MedSTP stays nearer the low-drift, high-accuracy corner than the competing pruners. Subspace drift versus answer accuracy on SLAKE with Lingshu7B; accuracy is reported as a percentage, and larger markers indicate larger retained-token budgets.

Figure 3. Across most pruning rates, MedSTP keeps the retainedtoken eigenspace closer to the full-token visual eigenspace than the competing pruners. Subspace preservation diagnostic on SLAKE with Lingshu-7B; lower drift is better, and 0% pruning is the zero-drift identity case.
Figure 6. Moderate transition weighting works best on OmniMedVQA at 10% keep ratio with Lingshu-7B: β = 0.1 − 0.3 gives higher accuracy, while larger weights reduce accuracy.

papers.title: MedSTP: Preserving Subspace and Transition Evidence for Medical VQA Token Pruning
papers.tldr: MedSTP is a training-free medical VQA token-pruning method that preserves dominant visual evidence while retaining boundary- and texture-sensitive tokens.

papers.abstract: Existing video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) organize observations primarily in time, but embodied spatial reasoning requires organizing them in space. Consequently, their visual representations can remain locally consistent across nearby frames while lacking a persistent spatial context that is stable across viewpoints and time. We exploit depth and camera pose, which are naturally available to embodied agents, to explicitly establish this spatial correspondence. We introduce Cambrian-BEV, which extends Cambrian-S with a parameter-free geometric tokenization scheme that back-projects visual patch features from each frame into a shared bird's-eye-view (BEV) coordinate frame and averages features that fall within the same spatial cell. Thus, observations of the same physical location, regardless of viewpoint or time step, are aggregated into a common spatial token. In addition to providing a persistent scene representation, this formulation acts as an efficient compression mechanism: 128 frames containing approximately 100K DINOv3 patch features are consolidated into a fixed 27$\times$27 grid of only 729 BEV tokens, cutting LLM prefill time by $2.9\times$ and peak memory by $3.6\times$. Cambrian-BEV requires no architectural modification beyond BEV tokenization and uses a frozen DINOv3 vision encoder with a trainable multimodal projector and LLM. On VSI-Bench, our model reaches 63.48, $+8.5$ points over an identically fine-tuned frame-token control with $12.6\times$ fewer visual tokens, with particularly large gains on room size ($+24.5$) and relative direction ($+34.1$). On ReVSI, it reaches 44.68, $+4.5$ over the corresponding control.
authors: Faizan Siddiqui, Nirav Savaliya, Sahith Reddy Chada, Enna Sachdeva
bullets: Addresses the lack of stable spatial context in video MLLMs that primarily organize observations over time.
Back-projects visual patch features using depth and camera pose into shared BEV coordinates, averaging features within spatial cells.
Compresses 128 frames and roughly 100K patch features into 729 BEV tokens without architectural changes beyond tokenization.
Reduces LLM prefill time by 2.9× and peak memory by 3.6×.
Outperforms the matched frame-token control on VSI-Bench and ReVSI, with especially strong VSI-Bench gains in room-size and relative-direction reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Cambrian-BEV architecture. Patch tokens leave the frozen encoder and the vision-to-language projector already in the language embedding space, so the parameter-free geometric module (steps 1–6) can pool them directly into a metric BEV grid whose cells become the BEV tokens that replace the frame tokens in the LLM context. The BEV projection (green) is introduced only in the final fine-tuning stage (stage 5, Tab. S3); the encoder, projector, and LLM are inherited from the unmodified four-stage Cambrian-S recipe, which trains on frame tokens.

Figure 1. From frame-indexed tokens to BEV visual tokens. Top: A conventional video MLLM represents each frame independently, producing repeated evidence for regions observed from multiple viewpoints. Bottom: We use depth and camera pose to back-project patch features into a shared metric coordinate frame and aggregate them on a fixed 27 × 27 bird’s-eye-view grid. Repeated observations of the same spatial region are fused into common BEV cells, replacing approximately 9K frame tokens with 729 spatially indexed tokens at the LLM interface.

Figure 3. Patch-level text similarity, SigLIP2 vs. DINOv3. SigLIP2 distributes evidence for the queried object (row label) across the image, whereas DINOv3 more closely follows the object’s extent. Warm colors indicate higher similarity; color scales are normalized per panel. Details in Sec. H.

papers.selection_reason: BEV tokenization compresses video MLLM visual tokens while improving embodied spatial reasoning, combining spatial intelligence, token merging, and video understanding.
papers.title: Thinking from Above: Efficient Spatial Reasoning with Bird's-Eye-View Visual Tokens
papers.tldr: Cambrian-BEV improves embodied spatial reasoning by aggregating multi-view video features into a compact, persistent bird’s-eye-view representation.

papers.abstract: Token merging has emerged as an effective training-free strategy for accelerating diffusion models by reducing redundant token computation while minimizing generation degradation. A key challenge is determining which tokens can be safely merged and which should be preserved for subsequent computation. Existing method addresses this by preserving prompt-aligned foreground regions, thereby protecting semantically relevant structures. However, this text-relevance criterion overlooks background objects, local details that are not explicitly mentioned in the prompt, leading to degraded structural coherence. In this work, we propose Dynamics-aware Token Merging (DaTMe), a training-free framework that grounds token merging in the underlying diffusion dynamics. Our key insight is that token importance should reflect whether a token remains unresolved during denoising and whether it carries structural information. To this end, DaTMe constructs a dynamics- aware importance map from the Tweedie denoised estimate. The map combines a temporal signal, measuring inter-step changes in the predicted clean image, with a structural signal, capturing local high-frequency content such as boundaries and fine details. Using this map, DaTMe adaptively assigns tokens into merging roles under a given compression ratio: important tokens are preserved as anchors, while tokens that are both temporally stabilized and structurally homogeneous are selected as safe merge candidates. Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX demonstrate that DaTMe maintains visual fidelity across the entire image, highlighting diffusion dynamics as an effective token-level merging decision in efficient generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/SeungJuCha/DaTMe.
authors: SeungJu Cha, Ye-Chan Kim, HyunGee Kim, Sungho Koh, Dong-Jin Kim
bullets: Existing token-merging methods prioritize prompt-aligned foregrounds but may lose unmentioned background objects and local details.
DaTMe is a training-free framework that builds token-importance maps from Tweedie denoised estimates.
Its map combines temporal changes across denoising steps with local high-frequency structure such as boundaries and fine details.
Important or unresolved tokens are preserved as anchors, while temporally stable and structurally homogeneous tokens are merged.
Experiments on PixArt-a and FLUX show maintained visual fidelity under compression.

Figure 11: Additional FLUX results under different compression ratios. Unlike prior methods, DaTMe more faithfully preserves the fine details present in the original image.
Figure 10: Additional PixArt-α results under different compression ratios. Unlike prior methods, DaTMe more faithfully preserves the fine details present in the original image.
Figure 13: SDXL results under different compression ratios. Unlike prior methods, DaTMe more faithfully preserves the contents of the original image especially background details.
Figure 12: SD 1.5 results under different compression ratios. Unlike prior methods, DaTMe more faithfully preserves the contents of the original image.

Figure 1: (a) Comparison under different compression ratios. CFG-based merging [9] often overlooks background details and structures, whereas our method better preserves background integrity. (b) Spatial distribution of top-ranked tokens over denoising timesteps. CFG-based importance remains concentrated on the foreground object with limited temporal variation. In contrast, our score-based signals (Score Slope and Tweedie Diff) progressively shift from object regions to fine-grained spatial details, better matching the pseudo-GT pattern. Here, pseudo-GT is defined as the difference between the final denoised latent and the Tweedie estimate at each timestep. (c) Non-prompt region blind spot. Low-ranked tokens under the CFG-based signal consistently overlap with structurally salient regions in text-irrelevant areas (red).

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison under compression ratio 0.5 on FLUX. DaTMe better preserves structural details with lower quality degradation.

(Bottom) Spatial distributions: the difference term captures structured token-level changes, whereas the scale term remains spatially unstructured.

papers.title: Which Tokens to Merge? Diffusion Dynamics for Efficient Image Generation
papers.tldr: DaTMe accelerates diffusion image generation by merging tokens according to denoising dynamics and structural importance, preserving visual fidelity across the image.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Chengyuan Qian, Zhengzhong Tu, Yang Sui, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets VLA inference bottlenecks caused by hundreds of visual tokens from high-resolution, multi-view observations.
Ranks tokens using task-to-vision attention rather than generic visual saliency.
Adapts compression rates from attention-distribution uniformity using an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration.
Evaluated across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT in LIBERO, SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
Reduces simulation backbone FLOPs by 35–59% and action latency by 9–32% while maintaining success; real-robot end-to-end latency drops 20% at comparable success.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of FastVLA, our temporally adaptive, training-free visual token compression framework for Vision-Language-Action models. At each action prediction step, FastVLA estimates task-conditioned patch importance via attention, measures distributional uniformity over selected vision tokens, and dynamically adjusts the compression rate using an online sliding-window calibration. By retaining task-relevant yet information-diverse tokens across timesteps, our approach reduces LLM backbone computation while preserving action performance.

Figure 5. Qualitative rollouts on two manipulation domains. Top: a long-horizon task from the LIBERO-Long suite (simulation). Bottom: a real-world pick-and-place task. In each strip, eight frames are sampled uniformly over time (left to right) from the external thirdperson camera, where the full observation is shown alongside its masked/pruned counterpart processed by FastVLA. We further provide complete rollout videos with pruning effect by FastVLA in the supplementary material.
Figure 3. Visual token importance distributions across action steps in a single trial on the LIBERO-Long benchmark.

Figure 2. Average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark under different visual token pruning rates, comparing three attentionbased importance scoring strategies: task-to-vision, vision-tovision, and all-to-vision.
Figure 4. Temporal comparison of Shannon entropy and inverse Simpson concentration measures over action prediction steps in a single trial on the LIBERO-Long benchmark.

Table 1. Comparison of different VLA acceleration methods on the LIBERO benchmark. For FastVLA, ρ is set per suite and backbone: on OpenVLA-OFT, ρ=0.8 (Spatial), 0.7 (Object), 0.75 (Goal), 0.6 (10); on OpenVLA, ρ=0.35 (Spatial), 0.5 (Object), 0.4 (Goal), 0.3 (10). papers.selection_reason: Task-aware and temporally adaptive visual token compression for efficient VLA inference, directly relevant to VLA and token pruning.
papers.title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FastVLA accelerates vision-language-action robot control by selecting task-relevant visual tokens and adapting their budget over time without retraining.

papers.abstract: Byte-level language models such as the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) run their large global model once per patch and start a patch where a small model's next-byte entropy is high. This rule rarely starts a patch at in-line computed results, such as the number after "=" in a worked solution, and accuracy on them collapses under tight patch budgets. We propose novelty patching, motivated by LZ77-style compression: start a patch where the upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent context. The rule is a lookup table over the previous two bytes, fitted in seconds on raw text with no labels, reference model or losses. In BLT-style models trained from scratch on a 1.9 GB math corpus at a matched ~11% patch rate (3 seeds each), it has no clear effect at 1M parameters, raises final-answer accuracy from 47% to 72% at 12M, and at 50M raises computed-result accuracy from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90%; a table fitted on the raw pretraining corpus keeps the gain. Outside math the advantage shrinks: novelty lowers bits per byte on prose and ties entropy on source code and on synthetic execution traces. An analysis of where boundaries fall explains the pattern. Computed results have ordinary surprisal for the patcher's model, so surprisal-seeking rules pass over them: entropy concentrates patch starts on high-surprisal bytes most strongly of all rules (boundary enrichment 1.61) and is the worst on computed results, while the best rules sit near chance enrichment. Novelty works where new content begins at segment starts close to the computation, as in written math; a learned chunker (H-Net) finds such structure on its own, in math and in code. We also report what did not work: typed uncertainty as a training rule, switching rules after training, and a context-aware novelty predictor.
bullets: Entropy-based patching often misses inline computed results because they have ordinary surprisal for the patching model.
Novelty patching starts patches where upcoming bytes are unlikely to repeat the recent two-byte context, using a label-free lookup table fitted on raw text.
At 50M parameters, computed-result accuracy rises from 21% to 57% and final-answer accuracy from 60% to 90% at a matched ~11% patch rate.
The benefit is strongest in written math, shrinks on prose, and ties entropy on source code and synthetic execution traces.
Typed uncertainty, post-training rule switching, and a context-aware novelty predictor did not work; learned chunking finds related structure in math and code.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes compute-efficient patch selection for byte-level language models, relevant to token-level efficiency and LM architecture.
papers.title: Patch where the text is new: a compression view of where byte-level models should spend compute
papers.tldr: Novelty-based byte patching directs compute toward new content near mathematical computations, substantially improving computed-result and final-answer accuracy under fixed patch budgets.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformer architectures have showcased impressive performance on semantic segmentation, yet their quadratic attention complexity hinders practical applications. Recent works have focused on merging tokens to reduce sequence length and thus improve transformer efficiency. However, existing token merging methods primarily rely on feature similarity to identify similar tokens, overlooking spatial consistency, which may introduce segmentation errors in semantic segmentation. In this work, we propose SCMerge, a training-free token merging method that jointly considers feature similarity and spatial consistency in pairing similar tokens. The pairwise tokens are then merged within the encoder, and the resulting token sequences are reconstructed onto the original patch grid after decoding. The proposed method is flexible and can be plugged into existing vision Transformer-based semantic segmentation pipelines. Extensive experiments on the benchmark datasets ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show that SCMerge consistently achieves a better trade-off between segmentation accuracy and efficiency than baseline methods.
authors: Junfeng Ren (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yi Gong (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yuan Zeng (Shenzhen Technology University)
bullets: Addresses the quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers in semantic segmentation.
Pairs tokens using both feature similarity and spatial consistency to reduce segmentation errors from spatially inconsistent merges.
Merges tokens in the encoder and reconstructs the decoded sequences onto the original patch grid.
Plug-and-play with existing Vision Transformer semantic segmentation pipelines.
Experiments on ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than baseline methods.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SCMerge. SCMerge is a plug-and-play module that can be inserted into multiple ViT encoder blocks to reduce the token sequence length while maintaining a merge map. It combines feature similarity with a spatial-consistency penalty to guide similar token pairing and merging. The reduced token sequence remains compact throughout decoding and is reconstructed onto the original dense prediction grid only after the decoder.

Figure 3. Qualitative segmentation comparison on ADE20K. Prediction and error maps show that SCMerge produces fewer segmentation errors than the baseline token-merging methods, achieving the lowest pixel error rate.

Figure 2. Token-reduction and spatial-consistency visualization. SCMerge selects spatial-consistency token pairs with lower boundary sensitivity Bij and neighborhood consistency Dij than competing methods.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free token merging with spatial consistency for efficient semantic segmentation directly fits token pruning/merging.
papers.title: SCMerge: Spatial-Consistency-Aware Token Pair Merging for Efficient Semantic Segmentation
papers.tldr: SCMerge is a training-free token-merging method that improves Vision Transformer segmentation efficiency by combining feature similarity with spatial consistency.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.
authors: Inseok Kong, Geunyoung Jung, Jiyoung Jung
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in 3D point clouds without source data or backpropagation.
Computes token abnormality from attention and geometric relation graphs.
Uses Otsu-based separability to derive each sample’s retained/pruned token partition.
Routes to the pruned prediction only when keep-ratio-penalized entropy favors it.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overall pipeline of SATOR. Token abnormality scores are computed from attention and geometric relation graphs and adaptively fused based on their Otsu separability. A sample-specific token partition is then derived directly from the fused score distribution via sorted-split Otsu thresholding, eliminating iterative purge-size search. A keep-ratio-calibrated routing mechanism selects between the original and pruned token sequence predictions, accounting for the keep ratio in the routing criterion.
Figure 2. Fused token abnormality scores on ModelNet40-C. The clean example (left) is unimodal under GMM-BIC; the corrupted example (right) is bimodal, with Otsu threshold τ⋆.

Table 3. Top-1 classification accuracy (%) across all 15 corruption types in ScanObjectNN-C. The highest mean accuracy is highlighted in bold and the second highest is underlined.

papers.selection_reason: Source-free 3D test-time adaptation with sample-adaptive token routing; fits test-time learning and token pruning.
papers.title: SATOR: Backpropagation-Free 3D Test-Time Adaptation via Sample-Adaptive Token Routing
papers.tldr: SATOR enables efficient backpropagation-free 3D test-time adaptation by routing tokens using sample-specific decisions instead of costly purge-size searches.

papers.abstract: Although Graph Neural Networks are widely used in various domains, they remained mostly unexplored in computer vision. Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers were leading the field, until the quite recent introduction of Vision Graphs (ViG) that treat images as a set of nodes and apply graph convolution on their k-NN graphs. ViGs show impressive accuracy on image classification but their computational cost remains relatively high. Inspired by optimization methods for GNNs, we present CoViG, a novel approach combining graph coarsening and ViGs. Our method introduces an additional MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks. By simplifying the intermediate graphs and thus decreasing the number of nodes of specific blocks, our approach considerably reduces the computational cost of ViG during inference. We evaluated our approach on ImageNet with several ViG architectures, and we obtained accuracies equivalent to the original ViG models with only about 51\% of FLOPs.
authors: Martial Guidez, Stefan Duffner, Christophe Garcia
bullets: Vision Graphs model images as nodes connected through k-NN graphs, but their computational cost is relatively high.
CoViG adds a MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks.
Graph coarsening reduces the number of nodes processed in selected blocks.
On ImageNet across several ViG architectures, CoViG achieves comparable accuracy using about 51% of the original FLOPs.

Figure 3. Overview of the Vision Graph Neural Network (ViG) architecture.
Figure 5. Effect of coarsening depth on MinCUT assignment quality: near-hard spatial assignments at block 0 vs. soft semantic aggregation at block 6.

Figure 4. Visualization of the graph representation learned by the ViG [14]. From left to right: the input image overlaid with the 14×14 graph nodes, the dynamically constructed k-NN graph based on feature similarity, and a PCA projection of the learned node features into RGB space. Subfigures a) and b) correspond to different backbone blocks, illustrating the evolution of graph connectivity and feature representations throughout the network.
