papers.title: CoViG: Coarsened Vision GNN for Image Classification
papers.tldr: CoViG reduces Vision Graph Network inference cost by coarsening intermediate graphs while maintaining accuracy comparable to standard ViGs.

papers.abstract: Point-cloud streams are central to autonomous driving and robotics, yet existing segmentation networks process every frame from scratch, although consecutive frames largely overlap. We observe that the intermediate features of point-cloud transformers remain semantically consistent across frames for the same spatial region, especially in deep stages. Building on this, we present SpaceCache, a training-free feature cache that reuses these features across frames. Tokens of previously observed regions skip a sequence of transformer blocks and take their cached features, only the remaining tokens are computed, and the full token layout is restored for dense prediction. Lightweight cache management keeps reused features reliable by limiting each entry's age and evicting low-confidence entries. Unlike token merging, SpaceCache selects tokens at negligible cost and runs its cache operations once per encoder stage. On both outdoor and indoor benchmarks, such as nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet, with two transformer backbones of Utonia and LitePT-B, SpaceCache achieves up to 1.65x speedup with less than 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.
authors: Dongheon Yang, Beomseok Kang, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Addresses redundant frame-by-frame processing caused by substantial overlap in consecutive point-cloud streams.
Uses a training-free cache to let previously observed tokens skip transformer blocks while computing only new or changed tokens.
Maintains reliability by limiting cache-entry age and evicting low-confidence features; cache operations run once per encoder stage.
Evaluated on nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet with Utonia and LitePT-B backbones.
Achieves up to 1.65× speedup with less than a 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of SpaceCache. Inference pipeline with the Mask, Reuse, and Commit Gates. Cache-hit tokens bypass the selected transformer blocks, while cache-miss tokens are computed through the blocks. The Reuse Gate restores the full token layout, and the Commit Gate updates the cache after prediction. Each cached stage has its own SpaceCache.

Figure 6: Accuracy-efficiency trade-off on outdoor streams. Curves sweep the merge ratio (ToMe, GitMerge3D), similarity threshold (ALGM), or confidence threshold θ (SpaceCache), plotting mIoU against FLOPs (top) and latency (bottom). Solid line and star–backbone; dashed lines–1and 2-point mIoU drops; Rings–fewest-FLOPs point of each method within the 1-point drop.

Figure 7: Latency and memory breakdown on the representative scenes of Waymo with Utonia, each method within a 2.0-point mIoU drop. (a) Latency per frame, split into the backbone layers and the policy overhead. (b) Policy overhead per frame, split into its components. (c) Peak memory with flash-attention, split into the model weights, the activation memory, and the cache.

Figure 1: Increasing temporal overlap across encoder stages. Visualization on the Waymo dataset using the stage-wise downsampling ratios of the Utonia and LitePT-B models. Both have five encoder stages (S0–S4). Each grid cell represents the voxel region corresponding to a single token, and its color indicates the ground-truth semantic class of that region. Magenta highlights voxels in frame t+1 that overlap with frame t. As progressive downsampling increases the voxel size at deeper stages, tokens represent larger spatial regions and exhibit higher cross-frame overlap.

Figure 2: Temporal-reuse opportunity in point-cloud encoders. (a) A multi-stage encoder, where stage l runs Bl blocks over a fixed token set and downsampling between stages shrinks the token set while enlarging the region each token covers. (b) The median fraction of stage-l overlapping tokens, whose region already appeared in the previous frame, grows substantially with depth. (c) The Reuse Agreement of stage-l overlapping tokens also increases with depth, indicating that the overlapped previous-frame token and the corresponding current-frame token predict the same class (Appendix A.2).

Figure 4: Operation details of SpaceCache. Each entry stores a region index, cached feature, and age. Read: Current-frame tokens are mapped to global region indices and queried at the Mask Gate to identify cache hits; the corresponding cached features are then retrieved for reuse at the Reuse Gate. Write: Newly computed cache-miss features become candidate entries at the Reuse Gate; after prediction, the Commit Gate evicts invalid entries, commits valid candidates, and re-sorts the cache for the next-frame lookup.

Figure 5: Reuse Agreement of cache entries (Stage-3, Waymo with Utonia). (a) By region confidence c(v) at L=8 for all, cached, and candidate entries; the dashed line marks θ=0.85. (b) By entry age with L=∞.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free feature cache for point-cloud transformer segmentation with token reuse and eviction; relevant to efficient AI and 3D perception.
papers.title: SpaceCache: Intermediate Feature Reuse for Efficient Semantic Segmentation on Point Cloud Streams
papers.tldr: SpaceCache accelerates point-cloud stream segmentation by reusing reliable intermediate transformer features from previously observed spatial regions.

papers.abstract: Occupancy predictors rely on large persistent banks of Gaussians or learned queries whose size is fixed by hand. Common pruning proxies, such as opacity, activation frequency, or parameter magnitude, do not measure whether removing a row changes the model's voxel decisions. We introduce Decision-FLIP, a budget-free compilation framework whose scoring and structure selection need only unlabeled calibration inputs. Exact Mean-FLIP scores each persistent row by the number of voxel argmax decisions that change when the row is removed from the readout; a guarded Otsu split of the log-score distribution selects the survivor count without a target and abstains when the split is unsupported; and the survivors are physically compiled into a smaller checkpoint, so camera sampling, attention, and aggregation shrink with the bank. For streaming banks, scores are integrated over each row's lifecycle through warp, death, and refill. Across four Gaussian-bank model-dataset settings and one persistent-query transfer, the automatically selected cuts remove 12-79% of eligible rows and cut bank/query-dependent latency by 7-45% across settings with component profiles, with whole-model savings of up to 8.0% on the primary endpoints bounded by fixed-cost image, voxel, and sensor modules and peak-memory savings of up to 16.6%. Under matched one-epoch recovery controls, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point. Same-$K$ controls show that the ranking, not only the bank size, matters: random removal collapses GaussianFormer-1 and OccFormer, while label-free Mean-FLIP matches or outperforms supervised Taylor ranking on all five settings where that control was run. The method applies when removable primitives keep a stable checkpoint-row identity; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.
authors: Jingxing Li, Anurag Paul, Subhasis Das, Cindy Xu
bullets: Scores each persistent row by how many voxel argmax decisions change when it is removed, rather than using opacity, activation, or parameter magnitude.
A guarded Otsu split selects survivors automatically and abstains when the score distribution does not support a reliable split.
Across five model–dataset settings, it removes 12–79% of eligible rows, reducing bank/query-dependent latency by 7–45% and peak memory by up to 16.6%.
With matched one-epoch recovery, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point; ranking quality matters, as random removal can collapse models.
Applies to removable primitives with stable checkpoint-row identities; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Decision-FLIP. (a) On unlabeled calibration frames, removing row i from the cached full readout and recomputing the all-class argmax gives per-frame Decision-FLIP; scores aggregate as Mean-FLIP or lifecycle Mean-FLIP. (b) Guarded log-Otsu selects a survivor set only when η ≥ 0.5, otherwise retaining the full bank. (c) The same survivor indices are gathered across aligned tensors, strict-loaded, and compared with the unpruned reference under matched one-epoch recovery and official evaluation.

papers.title: Decision-FLIP: Budget-Free Structured Pruning for Gaussian Occupancy Models
papers.tldr: Decision-FLIP uses unlabeled calibration inputs to identify and physically remove Gaussian or query rows that do not affect voxel decisions, automatically shrinking occupancy models without a preset pruning budget.

papers.abstract: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget
authors: Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
bullets: Addresses the costly, empirical selection of numerical resolution for pretrained flow-based generators.
Uses training-free, simulation-free interpolation probes of learned dynamics to estimate normalized one-step discretization error.
Derives budget estimators for Euler and Heun ODE solvers and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama SDE sampling.
Maps a target numerical tolerance to an NFE budget using solver order and relates ODE estimates to terminal integration error.
Evaluated across SiT, FlowDCN, and Rectified Flow models and formulations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Analysis of FLOWBUDGET budget estimation.

Table 1: FLOWBUDGET-predicted budgets and corresponding FID, reported as mean ± std over three seeds. Reference FID uses NFE = 250 for SiT-XL/2, FlowDCN-XL/2, and RF-UNet, and NFE = 1 for 1-RF, 2-RF, and 3-RF.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficiency in generative models by estimating sampling budgets for flow matching, a technique relevant to both video generation and efficient inference.
papers.title: FlowBudget: Training-Free Sampling-Budget Estimation for Flow Matching Models
papers.tldr: FLOWBUDGET estimates the sampling NFE budget needed by flow-matching models without repeated sample generation or FID-versus-NFE sweeps.

papers.abstract: With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents have achieved promising performance in interacting with real-world interfaces through screenshot-based grounding. However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. A lightweight selector is optimized through policy learning while the VLM backbone remains frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that \papername achieves a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff under low token budgets. At 21% token retention, it preserves 77.7% of full-token performance while reducing inference latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%. Results on Android in the Wild further suggest that the method transfers to mobile GUI environments.
authors: Shuo Wang, Sifan Zhou, Xiaobo Wang, Tianyu Fu, Chenxu Zhao, Anyang Su, Hanning Wang, Ping Jiang, Minghui Wu
bullets: Addresses inference overhead from high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn visual histories.
Uses query-guided token scoring with spatial window-level selection to avoid fragmenting small GUI elements.
Trains a lightweight selector with policy learning while keeping the VLM backbone frozen.
On Online-Mind2Web, retaining 21% of tokens preserves 77.7% of full-token performance, reducing latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%.
Results on Android in the Wild suggest transfer to mobile GUI environments.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the STP-GUI pipeline. Given the task instruction and visual tokens, STP-GUI scores token relevance and performs window-level selection under a token budget before the retained tokens are fed into the LLM. The resulting compact visual representation is then used for downstream action prediction.

Figure 1: Compared to existing VLM token pruning methods, our framework for Web-GUI agents aggregates fine-grained scores into non-overlapping spatial windows and uses a Plackett–Luce policy during training to select complete, contiguous patches. This helps suppress background noise while preserving local semantic and geometric structure, enabling the frozen VLM backbone to retain action-relevant evidence for downstream decisions.

papers.abstract: Transformers can perform in-context reinforcement learning without parameter updates. However, existing theoretical constructions often require context sizes that grow with the number of sampled transitions, leading to increasing memory costs in large-scale problems. This raises a fundamental scalability question: how much context is intrinsically necessary to carry out such learning? We answer this question for fixed-policy TD evaluation. We show that, with a shared linear decoder, the minimum context dimension required to exactly reproduce the first $L$ TD iterates is the Krylov dimension induced by the sampled transitions. When the available context dimension $m$ falls below this threshold, exact reproduction is no longer possible. In this regime, we characterize the optimal approximation error and show that it decays as $\Theta(\gamma^m\max\{1,1/(m(1-\gamma))\})$ where $\gamma$ is the discounting factor. Moving from representation complexity to actual memory cost, we characterize the optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations as $\Theta(nk_L)$ and show experimentally that on a sampled task whose exact rank is full but whose numerical rank is small, a context accurate to $10^{-2}$ is $88.7\%$ smaller than the sparse sufficient statistics of TD. Finally, we establish the learnability of the shared executor through pretraining by proving global convergence of an auxiliary objective over effective attention parameters under suitable task diversity. Experiments across diverse TD evaluation problems validate parameter recovery and the predicted context--accuracy tradeoff.
authors: Yajie Zhao, Yingjun Mo, Zhiyong Wang, Bo Tang, Chao Xu, Fang Kong
bullets: For fixed-policy TD evaluation with a shared linear decoder, exact reproduction of the first L TD iterates requires context dimension equal to the transitions’ induced Krylov dimension.
Below this threshold, exact reproduction is impossible; the optimal approximation error decays as Θ(γ^m max{1, 1/[m(1−γ)]}).
The optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations scales as Θ(nk_L).
On a sampled task with full exact rank but low numerical rank, context accurate to 10⁻² used 88.7% less memory than TD’s sparse sufficient statistics.
The paper also proves global convergence for pretraining the shared executor under suitable task diversity, with experiments validating parameter recovery and the context–accuracy tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models combine parameter reuse with sparse computation to improve performance under matched budgets. Prior work demonstrates that different loop visits can play different roles even when they share parameters. To probe the contributions of different loop visits, we learn separate residual coefficients in a model that applies a shared block twice, observing a smaller scale in the first visit. Fixed coefficient experiments show that reducing the first visit's scale preserves or improves performance, whereas the same reductions to the second hurt it. This asymmetry motivates us to explore asymmetric compute allocation. We propose \textbf{LatentLoop}, which compresses the first visit's sequence, retains full resolution in the second, and reallocates saved computation to increase the hidden size. We further learn how strongly the first visit updates the full sequence, and share MoE weights across visits while using separate attention parameters to accommodate their different sequence resolutions. Across 15 configurations spanning 1.3B--7B parameters, with the largest budget exceeding $10^{21}$ FLOPs, LatentLoop consistently lowers validation NLL. At a fitted NLL of 1.988, predicted compute savings are 19.0\% and 7.9\% relative to vanilla MoE and the looped baseline. It also improves average scores on nine benchmarks at all sizes in 0-shot and 5-shot settings. These results suggest asymmetric compute allocation is a promising direction for looped MoE models.
authors: Zefeng He, Yunkai Chai, Xiaoyang Chen, Tong Zhu, Zongliang Wu, Yun Luo, Yafu Li, Yu Cheng
bullets: Different loop visits contribute asymmetrically: reducing computation in the first visit is less harmful than reducing it in the second.
The method compresses the first visit’s sequence, keeps the second at full resolution, and increases hidden size with the saved compute.
It learns the first visit’s update strength, shares MoE weights across visits, and uses separate attention parameters for differing resolutions.
Across 15 configurations from 1.3B to 7B parameters, it consistently lowers validation NLL and improves average scores on nine benchmarks in 0-shot and 5-shot settings.
At fitted NLL 1.988, it predicts 19.0% and 7.9% compute savings versus vanilla MoE and the looped baseline, respectively.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune, a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs. Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups. At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of 1.19-1.27x while improving task success rates. At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.29-1.33x average speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.
authors: Baekseung Kim, Junhoo Lee, Sohyeon Hong, Suhyun Jeon, Minkyu Kim, Seungyeon Kim, Donghoon Han, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses high inference latency from dense future-frame token processing in world action models.
Uses instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens during early denoising, without training.
An entropy-based phase mechanism keeps dense computation during precision-sensitive phases.
At 35% pruning, it delivers 1.19–1.27× speedups while improving task success rates.
At 50% pruning, it reaches 1.29–1.33× speedups on simulation benchmarks with success within 1.0 percentage point of baseline.

papers.abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.
authors: Chenxu Wang, Hangyi Kuang, Bo-Wen Yin, Yuxuan Li, Quan-Sheng Zeng, Yang Zhang, Xu Guo, Xiang Li, Qibin Hou
bullets: Dense-scene autoregressive detectors can repeatedly emit identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted.
The proposed Compressed Window Auto-Regression limits token-level attention to the current generation window.
Each previous window is compressed into fixed latent tokens, preserving cross-window dependencies while reducing historical-coordinate interference.
On RSDense, WinARDet raises F1 at IoU 0.5 from 32.16 to 39.36 and lowers redundancy from 35.48% to 13.00%.
The approach also extends to parallel box decoding and polygon generation across varying scene densities.

papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.
authors: Zefan Yang, Zheyuan Zhang, Boris Maihe, Yikang Liu, Hang Yu, Ankush Mukherjee, Xiao Chen, Pingkun Yan, Terrence Chen, Shanhui Sun
bullets: Addresses the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments for robotic ultrasound, where small probe motions can cause large image changes.
Learns video dynamics from about 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames and grounds them to 6-DoF probe poses using a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset.
Uses staged training with latent-action-conditioned video diffusion, pose grounding, and distribution-matching distillation for causal long-horizon generation.
Evaluated pose-following, round-trip consistency, axis-specific control, and user-study performance on held-out tracked scans.
Correctly ranked target-directed motion over equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials.

(b) A fixed sensor-to-tip calibration transforms the measurements to probe-tip poses, such that the resulting motion corresponds to that of the imaging plane. (c) Consecutive probe-tip poses are converted to relative motions expressed in the preceding probe frame, yielding 6-DoF actions used to condition SonoWorld.

papers.abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.
authors: Yiheng Su, Junyi Jessy Li, Matthew Lease
bullets: Addresses the underexplored problem of predicting multiple regression outputs from text with LLMs.
Extracts broad and output-specific representations, then combines them through a dual-branch architecture.
Evaluated across five heterogeneous tasks and eight LLMs, including models up to 122B parameters.
Outperforms seven supervised baselines while fitting substantially fewer parameters; gains persist with limited training data.
Ablations show complementary value from both evidence types and effective lightweight shared predictors.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.
authors: Woosang Lim, Haneul Yoo, Vincent-Daniel Yun, Sungjoo Yoo
bullets: Targets reasoning degradation caused by conventional structured pruning on long-form tasks such as AIME.
Identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features without gradients or recovery training.
Evaluated across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, outperforming existing pruning methods in most settings.
Improves average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP.
On Qwen3-14B, delivers 1.24× faster prefill and 19.7% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model while preserving reasoning ability.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.
authors: Mei Okonkwo, Owen Castellanos, Ingrid Solberg, Yusuf Demirel
bullets: Motivation: LoRA applies every rank-one component to every token, although many responses appear to be cross-talk on a Gaussian noise floor.
Method: A router-free mechanism estimates each token’s robust noise level and soft-thresholds component responses, allowing the active rank to vary without a preset rank budget.
Thresholds are chosen per module using Stein’s unbiased risk estimate; an explaining-away step suppresses redundant components and favors complementary ones.
Theory: The method is near-optimal up to a logarithmic factor, has risk-consistent threshold selection, and provides coherence-based error control for joint sparse coding.
Experiments across reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE tasks report gains over LoRA and a mixture baseline while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SQUELCH, a router-free method for efficient token-level adaptation in LoRA, improving efficiency and performance in LLMs through noise-floor squelching and explaining-away mechanisms.
papers.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
papers.tldr: SQUELCH dynamically selects only the rank-one LoRA components each token needs by thresholding noise and removing redundancy, improving performance while using fewer components.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have advanced rapidly, but most remain optimized for single-image inputs. Multi-image reasoning is costly because each image adds many visual tokens, increasing encoding and attention demands. Existing techniques that address the above issue, including visual token pruning, token merging, visual token compression, learned resampling, hierarchical compression, retrieval-augmented visual reasoning, and memory-based architectures, have largely been designed for single-image scenarios, where redundancy is primarily spatial and local. Multi-image reasoning introduces additional challenges: redundancy may occur across images, task-relevant evidence may be sparse or distributed, and aggressive per-image compression can remove details needed for comparison, counting, temporal reasoning, retrieval, or evidence grounding. Moreover, existing token-reduction methods are often either (i) training-free but inference-inefficient, typically relying on accessing attention matrices to get token-importance that may be impractical to access with memory-efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention, or (ii) training-dependent, requiring the base MLLM to be retrained or adapted to a new compressed-token paradigm. In this work, we study scalable multi-image reasoning and understanding without retraining the base model and without accessing attention matrices at inference time. To this end, we propose mmVB, a lightweight plug-and-play module that assigns query-conditioned per-image token budgets via cross-image context, adding only 1.6M trainable parameters while reducing visual input tokens by 9x. This reduction yields 5x faster time-to-first-token and 7x fewer prefill FLOPs, while maintaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight multi-image reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Aimon Rahman, Joymallya Chakraborty, Vidit Bansal, Abhishek Dan
bullets: Multi-image inputs are expensive because each image contributes many visual tokens, with relevant evidence potentially sparse or distributed across images.
mmVB uses cross-image context to assign query-conditioned, per-image token budgets.
The lightweight plug-in adds 1.6M trainable parameters and reduces visual input tokens by 9×.
It delivers 5× faster time-to-first-token and 7× fewer prefill FLOPs while retaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight benchmarks.
The approach targets multi-image reasoning without modifying or retraining the base model.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Introduction and Motivation. Existing multi-image methods scale poorly: dense attention breaks FlashAttention and excludes API-only models, token merging disrupts positional encodings and cross-image reasoning, and video-style compression assumes frame similarity. Our pre-encoding predictor instead assigns query-conditioned token budgets using only pixels, enabling compatibility with any MLLM, including closed models.

Figure 2: mmVB architecture. Frozen EfficientNetB0 encodes N images, while frozen LLM embeddings encode the query through mean pooling and a 64- dimensional bottleneck. A two-layer, four-head Transformer processes all N+1 tokens, after which a shared MLP maps each image token to four ordinal logits.

papers.title: Visual Tokens on Demand: Visual Budgeting for Scalable and Efficient Multi-Image Reasoning in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: mmVB enables efficient multi-image reasoning by dynamically allocating visual-token budgets across images without retraining the base multimodal LLM or accessing attention matrices.

papers.abstract: Image-token compression must reduce computation without hurting the semantics. We introduce Varest, guided by semantic fungibility: tokens within a coherent semantic region can be summarized coarsely, while object boundaries and literal text require finer distinctions. Object and text localizers guide variable-resolution merging, preserving spatial coverage and finer detail at boundaries and text. Learned [REL] registers then prune visual tokens after early decoder processing. Training across budgets enables one checkpoint per backbone. Across three backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 15 baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, retaining 86.10-92.33% of full-token performance with only 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image-token count.
authors: Tianhao Fu, Austin Wang, Charles Chen, Roby Aldave-Garza, Victor Xie, Xiyue Jiao, Yucheng Chen, Martin Tin
bullets: Targets lower computation without sacrificing semantic understanding.
Uses semantic, variable-resolution token merging guided by object and text localization.
Preserves spatial coverage and finer distinctions at object boundaries and literal text.
Learned [REL] registers perform additional relevance pruning after early decoder processing.
Across 3 backbones and 13 benchmarks, retains 86.10–92.33% of full-token performance using 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image tokens, outperforming 15 baselines at every evaluated budget.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Varest. Object boundaries and textness are passed through the Varest tokenizer with post-projector visual tokens, which are then partitioned into Km semantic regions and each region is merged into one image token. At layer L/2, 4 learned [REL] registers (the figure is not to scale) produce a score for each image token and keep the Kp image tokens that are most relevant to LLM reading. Optional adaptive halting removes all remaining image tokens once the information horizon has been detected.

papers.selection_reason: Image-token compression via semantic merging and relevance pruning directly targets token-level efficiency for vision-language models.
papers.title: Just Respect the Semantics: Image-Token Compression via Pre-LLM Semantic Variable-Resolution Tokenization and In-LLM Relevance Pruning
papers.tldr: Varest compresses image tokens by preserving fine detail for objects and text while coarsening redundant regions, then pruning less relevant tokens inside the LLM.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Fengyu Zhou, Yijuan Liang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Existing pruning methods can retain strong overall performance but substantially harm OCR and visual grounding.
Bifocal uses mixed-granularity pruning with separate query-focused and image-intrinsic token budgets plus a pooled whole-image representation.
It matches question words to regions, balances this with norm-debiased image saliency, maximizes coverage, and applies density-adjusted text-to-image attention pruning inside the LLM.
Using roughly one-quarter of the visual tokens, it retained over 90% of unpruned performance in every evaluated ability group across three MLLM families.
The method was evaluated across ten pruning methods, five ability groups, and nine model-budget settings; code is publicly available.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage visual token pruning method. Stage 1 runs before the LLM and retains a mixed-granularity representation: fine evidence at native-patch resolution, of two kinds, query-focused evidence selected for the question and image-intrinsic evidence selected from the image itself, and coarse tokens obtained by average pooling. Stage 2 keeps the top-K tokens by text-to-image attention inside the LLM.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free visual token pruning for MLLMs, directly relevant to efficiency and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Bifocal: Training-Free Mixed Granularity Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Bifocal is a training-free visual-token pruning method that preserves fine-grained and general MLLM abilities by combining query-focused, image-intrinsic, and coarse image evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.
authors: Vatsal, Soumil Malhotra, Priyanshu Chahal, Sanjeev Kumar
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of token interactions and limited understanding of robustness in training-free token reduction.
Uses class-attention pruning to remove less-important tokens and similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy.
Introduces Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) to assess robustness under image transformations.
Evaluated on pretrained ViT and DeiT models, it achieves competitive compute reduction with better accuracy than existing token-reduction methods.
Finds that hybrid token reduction preserves prediction stability and does not produce hallucination-like behavior for common transformations.

Stage 1 (pruning) filters out background tokens based on class-attention scores kp, while Stage 2 (merging) aggregates redundant salient tokens using bipartite matching km.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes training-free token pruning and merging for Vision Transformers, directly matching token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
papers.tldr: A training-free prune-and-merge strategy compresses Vision Transformer tokens while reducing computation and preserving accuracy and prediction stability.

papers.abstract: We propose a unified spatial-density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full-pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM-Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill-probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM-Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity.Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL-3.5, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-1.5) and three full-pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three-way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density-based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top-k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM-Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL-3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM-Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full-pipeline validation for any decode-phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/TwinPrune
authors: Kai Liu, Anqi Li, Junxian Li, Zhixin Wang, Zhikai Chen, Renjing Pei, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Prefill-only probes can hide severe decode-phase quality degradation, so pruning claims require full-pipeline evaluation.
Method: Apply density-based scoring for bipartite visual-token merging during prefill and top-k visual KV eviction during decode.
Contribution: Establishes separate benchmarks and evaluation guidance, recommending MM-Vet or DocVQA for decode-pruning validation.
Results: Prefill selection is up to 100× faster at high resolution; decode pruning outperforms H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM across tested retention ratios.
Scope: Evaluated across seven model variants and multiple vision-language benchmarks; performance gains are reported for both stages.

figures.caption: Figure 3: TwinPrune pipeline. A single spatial density signal ρ, defined as each visual token’s average cosine dissimilarity to its w×w neighborhood (b), drives both phases. Prefill bipartite-merges low-ρ source tokens into high-ρ destination anchors, cutting FLOPs (c). Decode ranks visual KV by ρ and keeps the top-k with original RoPE positions, cutting KV memory (d). One signal, two levers, and a three-axis Pareto trade-off over compute, KV, and accuracy (a).

Figure 2: Prefill-probe benchmarks are structurally insensitive to decode-phase KV eviction across three VLM families. Left: accuracy vs. visual KV kept on InternVL-3.5-8B. Right: prediction mismatch at DALL grouped by (benchmark, model). Details in Sec. 3.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes density-aware token pruning and KV eviction for vision-language models, directly addressing efficiency in both prefill and decode phases.
papers.title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: TwinPrune uses spatial-density-aware token pruning separately for prefill merging and decode KV eviction, improving the compute–memory–accuracy trade-off while exposing pitfalls in phase-specific evaluation.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers incur high computational costs when processing long visual token sequences. Existing reduction methods typically rank tokens independently and discard those deemed unimportant or redundant. We propose a reconstruction-guided framework for visual token condensation (ReConV), which summarizes the complete visual sequence with a compact Summary Bank (SMB) and retains tokens whose information is not adequately captured by the SMB, as indicated by their reconstruction residuals. At each compression layer, a lightweight position-conditioned decoder reconstructs the current tokens, leaving shared information compressed in the SMB while explicitly preserving poorly reconstructed details. Experiments on image classification and multimodal understanding demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs: ReConV surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48\% fewer GMACs on ImageNet and enables reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference. Code is available at TokenDrop.
authors: Xiaoya Tang, Shilong Liu, Daniel Smolyak, Xiwen Li, Quynh Nguyen, Tolga Tasdizen
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of Vision Transformers on long visual token sequences.
Uses a position-conditioned decoder to reconstruct tokens from a Summary Bank at each compression layer.
Retains tokens with large reconstruction residuals, rather than ranking tokens independently.
Achieves favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs in image classification and multimodal understanding.
On ImageNet, surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48% fewer GMACs and supports reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ReConV, the proposed reconstruction-guided token pruning framework. Given N token embeddings from a vision encoder or transformer layer, each compressive layer uses a small set of learned summary bank (SMB) tokens to summarize the input via cross-attention, reconstructs the original tokens using the SMB representation and positional information, and retains the top-k tokens with the largest reconstruction residuals (approximately N · r, where r is the keep ratio). Tokens that are well reconstructed are dropped as redundant, while the retained tokens are passed to the next layer. For classification, the model uses the CLS token when available, or pooled SMB features otherwise; for other tasks, it uses the retained visual tokens with SMBs.

Figure 3: Patch-to-SMB assignments for tokens entering the first, second, and third compression layers of our A1A3A5 classification model, which use keep ratios of 0.75, 0.25, and 0.0, respectively. The model’s performance is reported in Table 2. Green numbers identify the SMB tokens assigned to reconstruct the corresponding patches, and patches assigned to the same SMB are masked with the same color. Unnumbered patches have been dropped by preceding layers. Examples are randomly selected from the ImageNet validation set.

Figure 6: Patch-to-SMB assignments in our single-layer A5 classification model with a keep ratio of 0.0 and our three-layer A1A3A5 classification model with keep ratios of 0.75, 0.25, and 0.0. From left to right, the figure shows the patch-to-SMB assignments and corresponding color-coded masks at the single compression layer of the A5 model, followed by the patch-to-SMB assignments for the tokens entering the first, second, and third compression layers of the A1A3A5 model. For example, the visualization at the first layer therefore includes all input patch tokens; this layer subsequently drops 25% of them, and the retained tokens enter the second compression layer. Green numbers identify the SMB tokens assigned to reconstruct the corresponding patches, with patches assigned to the same SMB sharing the same color. Patches without a number have been dropped by preceding compression layers. The examples are randomly selected from the ImageNet validation set.

Figure 7: Samples are randomly selected from the MME evaluation set, covering five subtasks from left to right: artwork, existence, landmark, OCR, and scene. The figure visualizes the 64-token setting of our model, which contains 56 kept tokens and 8 SMBs. From top to bottom, the panels show: the question-answer pair, the input image, SMB allocation at the first compression layer, SMB allocation at the second compression layer after the first token-dropping step, and the final SMB allocation after the second token-dropping step. The color from light to dark yellow indicates SMB indices from 0 to 8. The letters on each patch indicate the assigned SMB index, while patches without letters have already been dropped.

Figure 4: Examples from the MT-VQAv2 test split, where the number of questions associated with each image varies across samples. In the multi-turn setting, each image is encoded and optionally compressed only once, and the resulting visual embeddings are reused across all associated questions.

Figure 1: Illustration of visual token pruning. Prompt-independent saliency emphasizes irrelevant regions, while prompt-conditioned pruning can still discard task-relevant details, especially at high pruning ratios. ReConV instead preserves information through SMB summaries and residual tokens.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes reconstruction-guided visual token condensation, directly fitting token pruning/eviction for efficient vision and multimodal inference.
papers.title: Bottlenecked semantic compression by representation reconstruction
papers.tldr: ReConV compresses long visual token sequences by reconstructing shared information in a compact summary bank and retaining tokens with unrecovered details, improving efficiency while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Video language models represent a video as a long sequence of visual embeddings in a decoder's input. Every visual embedding is processed by every decoder layer during prefill, stored in the key value cache, and attended by every generated token, so a long video raises prefill, memory, and generation cost at once. We present WIRE (Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding), which reduces this recurring cost by moving part of the video conditioned computation of a frozen video language model from its input activations into a temporary low rank update of its weights. WIRE keeps a short explicit visual context, so the update acts as a correction rather than a replacement of the video. WIRE first compresses the full resolution embeddings of each frame into a small set of carrier tokens using a question conditioned bidirectional selective scan, and physically contracts the decoder input so every decoder layer, cache entry, and decoding step operates on the shorter sequence. Hypernetworks at selected decoder layers read the compressed forward pass together with a readout of the full resolution features removed by contraction and generate LoRA updates to the attention and feedforward projections. The updates are merged after prefill, so autoregressive decoding runs the unmodified frozen backbone. On Qwen3-VL-8B, WIRE with 16 carrier tokens per frame contracts the visual stream by $3.5\times$, reduces decoder prefill time by $3.35\times$ at 256 frames and $4.14\times$ at 1024 frames, shrinks the key value cache proportionally, and keeps per token decoding latency approximately constant. Across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames, it obtains the highest average accuracy among efficient video language models we evaluate under a common 256 frame budget.
authors: Ameen Ali, Tamim Zoabi, Lior Wolf, Chaim Baskin
bullets: Addresses the rising prefill, KV-cache, and attention costs caused by long video embedding sequences.
Compresses each frame into carrier tokens using a question-conditioned bidirectional selective scan, then contracts the decoder input.
Uses hypernetworks to generate LoRA updates from compressed features and removed full-resolution information at selected decoder layers.
Merges updates after prefill, allowing autoregressive decoding to use the unmodified frozen backbone.

On Qwen3-VL-8B with 16 carrier tokens per frame, achieves 3.5× visual-stream contraction, 3.35–4.14× faster prefill, proportional KV-cache reduction, and top average accuracy across nine benchmark settings at 256 frames.

figures.caption: Figure 2: WIRE overview. The frozen vision encoder produces nt full resolution visual tokens for frame t. Bilinear resampling initializes kt carrier tokens, and a bidirectional Mamba2 scan refines the carrier tokens while reading the full resolution visual stream and the question. The carrier tokens replace the original frame tokens in the decoder prefix. At selected decoder layers, a hypernetwork uses the contracted decoder state and a full resolution per frame readout to generate LoRA updates for selected attention and MLP projections. The updates are merged after prefill. Decoding then uses the frozen backbone over the contracted prefix.

Figure 3: Qualitative examples at 256 frames. On a question about a video’s global subject, WIRE matches the uncompressed backbone while the efficient baselines pick locally plausible distractors. On a temporally localized question all systems answer correctly.

Figure 1: Latency versus video length. Times are measured on one B200 GPU at batch size one in bfloat16, excluding video file decoding. Left: total model time to first token. Right: decoder prefill only. WIRE contracts the sequence before the first decoder layer, so its advantage grows with frame count and it continues to run beyond input lengths where several baselines exhaust memory.

papers.selection_reason: Presents a method to compress visual tokens and reduce KV cache/prefill cost in frozen video LLMs, directly targeting efficiency in multimodal inference.
papers.title: WIRE: Weight Space Implicit Representation Encoding of Frozen Video LLMs
papers.tldr: WIRE makes frozen video LLMs more efficient by replacing most long visual inputs with a short context plus temporary low-rank weight updates that preserve video information.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.
authors: Shengzhen Li, Yongkang Li, Hao Gao, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited representation quality and high latency caused by generic visual pretraining and dense patch processing.
Distills complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models.
Adapts the encoder to multi-frame driving and stores spatiotemporal context in register tokens for planning.
Uses register-guided token compression to reduce redundant patch computation while improving planning performance.
Reports 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation.

papers.title: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: ConDenseDrive distills diverse visual knowledge into a token-sparse encoder that improves planning while delivering 2.0× faster inference for end-to-end autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Visual token compression has emerged as a critical technique for reducing the inference cost of Vision-Language Models. Existing methods select tokens based on text relevance, visual diversity, or a fixed combination of both---treating the relevance-diversity balance as a universal constant independent of the input. We conduct a systematic analysis to challenge this assumption. At the dataset level, grid-searching the optimal relevance-diversity weight per benchmark reveals substantial cross-task variation. More critically, we further maximize per-sample answer likelihood to recover sample-level oracle weights, finding that their distributions not only differ markedly across benchmarks but also exhibit high within-benchmark variance. Based on these observations, we propose SAVER, a framework for Sample-Aware relevance-diversity balanced Visual tokEn Reduction. We first derive a Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens to infer a sample-specific relevance-diversity weight, and then apply this weight to jointly select tokens via a Weighted Text Centroid (WTC) for relevance scoring and a Visual Marginal Coverage Gain (VMCG) for diversity. SAVER requires no additional training and achieves sample-aware balancing entirely at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAVER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, retaining 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B with only 11.1% of the original visual tokens, and further generalizing to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.
authors: Yihang Huang, Peisong Wen, Chenhao Zhou, Difu Feng, Qianqian Xu
bullets: Fixed relevance–diversity weights vary substantially across tasks and even among samples within the same benchmark.
SAVER infers a sample-specific weight from the spatial concentration of text-relevant tokens using a Geometric Intent Prior.
It combines Weighted Text Centroid relevance scoring with Visual Marginal Coverage Gain diversity selection.
The training-free method retains 96.5% of full-model performance on LLaVA-1.5-7B while using 11.1% of the original visual tokens.
It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT and Mini-Gemini.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the SAVER framework. Given a multimodal input, we compute the Geometric Intent Prior (GIP) from the spatial distribution of high-relevance visual tokens, which dynamically weights text relevance (via WTC) and visual diversity (via VMCG) in a unified greedy selection process.

papers.title: When 1+1 Backfires: Rethinking Relevance-Diversity Balancing for Sample-Aware Visual Token Reduction
papers.tldr: SAVER improves visual token compression by adapting the relevance–diversity trade-off to each input sample at inference time.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity efficiently by activating only a small subset of experts for each input, while still requiring all parameters to be stored in memory, resulting in substantial memory overhead. Expert merging techniques have recently emerged as a promising compression paradigm that reduces this overhead by consolidating multiple experts into a smaller set. However, existing approaches have two key limitations: (i) direct convex interpolation in parameter space is not generally guaranteed to yield meaningful interpolation of expert functions; and (ii) estimating expert similarity or merging coefficients often relies on calibration data, introducing dependence on the calibration distribution. To address these limitations, we propose Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging (SLEM), a calibration-free expert merging framework that occurs in a structured latent representation of expert weights using a VAE. SLEM groups experts within and across layers based on latent similarities and derives merging coefficients from expert weight spectra. It then performs geometry-aware latent interpolation and decodes the resulting representations into merged expert weights. Compared with existing expert merging methods, SLEM achieves comparable or better performance on general knowledge benchmarks and higher average performance on generation benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and code generation.
authors: Dohyeon Kim, Bedionita Soro, Bruno Andreis, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: MoE models reduce computation but retain all expert parameters, creating substantial memory overhead.
Existing merging methods may produce poor function interpolation and depend on calibration data.
SLEM uses a VAE-based latent representation, grouping experts by latent similarity within and across layers.
It derives merge coefficients from expert weight spectra and applies geometry-aware latent interpolation.
The method achieves comparable or better general-knowledge performance and higher average performance on math-reasoning and code-generation benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses memory efficiency in Mixture-of-Experts models through expert merging in a latent space, relevant to efficient AI and LLMs.
papers.title: SLEM: Spectrum-Aware Latent Expert Merging
papers.tldr: SLEM compresses Mixture-of-Experts models without calibration data by merging experts in a spectrum-aware latent space.

papers.abstract: Hour-long videos, streaming feeds, and movie-length content are pushing vision-language models (VLMs) past their breaking point -- the standard recipe of encoding each frame into visual tokens yields sequences that grow linearly with video length, causing prohibitive memory consumption and inference latency. Existing approaches, such as token reduction and keyframe selection, shorten the token sequence but leave the O(n) scaling intact, failing to resolve the fundamental bottleneck. We propose FramePack-U, a strikingly simple, training-free frame packing framework that compresses arbitrarily long videos into a fixed size visual representation at constant memory cost. FramePack-U requires no fine-tuning or architectural modification -- it plugs directly into off-the-shelf VLMs at inference time. Inspired by FramePack from the generation literature, we propose a content-aware compression strategy for visual understanding under a fixed token budget. Specifically, FramePack-U (1) scores each frame by its semantic similarity to the text prompt and ranks frames in a diversity-driven manner, and (2) packs the selected frames at varying resolutions into a fixed-length context window. This concentrates the memory budget on frames that are both instruction-relevant and visually diverse. While FramePack-U can in theory pack arbitrarily many frames into the fixed budget, we identify an empirical instantiation that generalizes robustly across settings. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME show that FramePack-U consistently outperforms full-resolution baselines and prior token reduction and keyframe selection methods across diverse model families, parameter scales, and frame budgets. Notably, on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, FramePack-U yields gains of +12.9\%, +10.6\%, and +9.7\% over the official model on the three benchmarks, respectively.
authors: Shuo Gao, Chenhao Zheng, Zhongzheng Ren
bullets: Addresses the linear memory and latency growth caused by encoding every video frame as visual tokens.
Uses a training-free, inference-only strategy that ranks frames by prompt relevance and diversity, then packs them at varying resolutions.
Works with off-the-shelf VLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
Experiments on LongVideoBench, MLVU, and Video-MME report consistent improvements over full-resolution, token-reduction, and keyframe-selection baselines.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B with a 128-frame budget, gains are 12.9%, 10.6%, and 9.7% on the three benchmarks, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of FramePack-U. Given a long video and a text query, FramePack-U selects query-relevant and visually diverse frames, then packs them with heterogeneous resolutions under a fixed memory budget. Higher-priority frames are kept at higher resolution, while lower-priority frames are progressively compressed. The packed frames are fed into the VLM for answer generation.

papers.title: Elephant in the Fridge: Constant-Memory Frame Packing for Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: FramePack-U enables VLMs to understand arbitrarily long videos with constant memory by packing prompt-relevant, diverse frames into a fixed-size visual representation.

papers.abstract: Adaptive image tokenizers compress an image into a variable number of tokens matched to its complexity, and recent work makes this allocation controllable: conditioned on a target reconstruction error, the tokenizer itself decides how many tokens an image needs. However, the fidelity measure guiding this allocation shapes which aspects of the image are preserved under compression. The pixel-wise error used in prior work is blind to the spatial structure that carries an image's meaning, and under heavy compression such tokenizers are prone to abruptly discarding tokens that encode essential content. We introduce GIST (Guided Image Semantic Tokenizer), an adaptive tokenizer that can be steered toward a requested semantic fidelity. Its token allocation is jointly controlled by pixel-level and semantic target errors, with semantic error measured in the feature space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. This joint control enables semantic protection: with the semantic target fixed at zero, the reconstruction target can be relaxed to discard pixel detail while preserving what the image depicts. In a controlled comparison on ImageNet-100, GIST outperforms its pixel-controlled counterpart KARL at every token count, with up to $30\%$ lower LPIPS and $37\%$ lower DreamSim. On average, lowering its semantic target reduces LPIPS $2\times$ faster per token than lowering the reconstruction target, and up to $5\times$ in the low-token regime. Semantic fidelity is thus an effective control signal for adaptive tokenization: it lets a tokenizer see, and so preserve, what an image depicts.
authors: Danilo de Goede, Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani, Yuki M. Asano, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Pixel-wise error can discard semantically important content when token budgets are tight.
GIST uses a frozen DINOv3 feature space to measure semantic error alongside reconstruction error.
Fixing the semantic target while relaxing pixel fidelity enables detail removal without losing what the image depicts.
On ImageNet-100, GIST improves over KARL at every token count, with up to 30% lower LPIPS and 37% lower DreamSim.
Semantic targets reduce perceptual error faster per token, especially in low-token settings.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Semantic conditioning makes tokens more semantically informative. (a) kNN accuracy of GIST, KARL†, and GIST-1 as we vary each method’s target values (same setup as Figure 3), with accuracies linearly interpolated at matched mean active token counts. GIST and GIST-1 outperform KARL† at every token count, and GIST-1 performs best despite performing on par with KARL† and worse than GIST on reconstruction quality. (b) kNN accuracy trajectories of GIST as we vary one target with the other held fixed (shown by color). Lowering ϵsem increases kNN accuracy at a much steeper rate than lowering ϵrec. Accuracies are computed by mean pooling over the active tokens; Appendix I reports the same comparison under max pooling.

Figure 4: Semantic protection keeps the subject recognizable under heavy token compression. For each sample (Goldfish reef, top; Black swan, bottom), the upper row shows KARL† reconstructions as we vary ϵrec, and the lower row shows GIST reconstructions with ϵsem fixed at 0 and ϵrec varied over the same values. The far-left image is the original; token budget is fixed at T = 256; per-cell strips report the active token count and LPIPS. papers.abstract: Quantization plays a crucial role in efficiently deploying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices. Post-training quantization does not require access to the original dataset or retraining the full model. Current methods that achieve high performance close to baseline results typically require INT8 fixed-point integers. However, achieving higher model compression with lower bit-widths often leads to significant performance degradation. In this paper, we propose VLCQ, a post-training quantization method that relaxes the fixed-point encoding constraint, enabling more flexible exploration of quantization techniques through variable-length encoding. This approach achieves competitive or improved performance while reducing bit-widths, without requiring access to training data or model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on image classification, segmentation, and object detection demonstrate that VLCQ improves model compression and accuracy compared with state-of-the-art post-training quantization approaches. For per-channel quantization, VLCQ surpasses FP32 accuracy and Piece-Wise Linear Quantization (PWLQ) on most evaluated models, achieving up to 6x compression compared with FP32 and up to 1.7x compared with PWLQ. When prioritizing compression with limited accuracy loss, VLCQ achieves up to 12.25x compression compared with FP32 with less than 4% performance degradation. For per-tensor quantization, VLCQ is competitive with Data-Free Quantization (DFQ), while providing greater flexibility to achieve lower bit rates across different tasks and models.

papers.abstract: Foundation models like V-JEPA are increasingly deployed across a heterogeneous edge-cloud continuum spanning smart glasses, phones, robots, and servers. Yet, they are typically trained as rigid, fixed-capacity networks bound to one device, supporting neither reconfigurable compute budgets nor collaborative execution. Existing approaches address only one axis at a time: slimmable and NAS-based methods provide width elasticity but assume single-device inference, whereas split-computing methods enable cross-device collaboration only for fixed partitions and static capacities. We introduce Elastic V-JEPA (EV-JEPA), a single model trained once and deployable everywhere along the continuum. Its width is reconfigurable, and it is natively partitionable across heterogeneous devices. At its core is Transition-Aware Triplet Training (T3). At each step we pick a narrow and a wide width, and train three paths: each width alone, plus a hybrid path that runs the early layers narrow and the rest wide. The hybrid switch point is where one device hands off to another, so the same weights learn both single-device and cross-device execution. Across various benchmarks, EV-JEPA falls within 1 accuracy point of independently trained baselines while improving over previous elastic training approaches by up to 11 accuracy points. Narrow-to-wide cross-device hybrid execution recovers to within 1.1 points of the highest-capacity standalone model and supports many-to-one, any-to-any, and variable-split configurations. Finally, we show that the elastic principle extends beyond the backbone to an elastic token compression mechanism that exposes controllable trade-offs among on-device computation, latency, and accuracy.

bullets: Supports reconfigurable model widths for different device compute budgets.
Enables native cross-device execution with flexible split points and many-to-one or any-to-any configurations.
Uses Transition-Aware Triplet Training to jointly train narrow, wide, and hybrid narrow-to-wide execution paths.
Matches independently trained baselines within 1 accuracy point and improves prior elastic methods by up to 11 points.
Extends elasticity to token compression, trading on-device computation and latency against accuracy.

papers.abstract: Speech large language models (LLMs) are often built using pretrained acoustic encoders as an audio interface to an LLM decoder. However, LLMs scale poorly with input sequence length, while acoustic encoders tend to produce substantially longer sequences than typical textual inputs. This motivates learning to compress encoder outputs while preserving task-oriented information. To this end, we introduce ASSET, a reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework that learns to adaptively compress encoder outputs by first partitioning them into variable-duration segments and then pooling each segment into a continuous audio token. We use group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) to train a segmenter with task performance feedback and a token-rate penalty. In automatic speech recognition (ASR) experiments, ASSET achieves performance comparable to a transcript-assisted character-boundary oracle with approximately 25% fewer audio tokens on English LibriSpeech, while improving on a phone-boundary oracle at a similar token rate on Mandarin AISHELL. Exploratory experiments on non-ASR tasks further illustrate how learned segmentation changes when the framework is adapted to tasks beyond transcription.
authors: Cihan Xiao, Yuan Tseng, Matthew Wiesner, Desh Raj, Leibny Paola Garcia Perera, Sanjeev Khudanpur, David Harwath
bullets: Addresses the sequence-length mismatch between long acoustic-encoder outputs and speech LLM inputs.
